breakdown.how_to_read: A plaint alleging fraud in conclusory terms ("the defendant fraudulently induced the plaintiff") without particulars of who said what, when, and how it was false is classically vulnerable to a Rule 16 strike-out application or an Order VII Rule 11 rejection argument — always plead fraud/undue-influence particulars as a checklist, not an afterthought.

sections.title: Order VI, Rule 6 — Condition precedent
sections.raw_text: 6. Condition precedent.—Any condition precedent, the performance or occurrence of which is intended to be contested, shall be distinctly specified in his pleading by the plaintiff or defendant, as the case may be; and, subject thereto, an averment of the performance or occurrence of all conditions precedent necessary for the case of the plaintiff or defendant shall be implied in his pleading.

breakdown.plain_summary: A party need not expressly plead that every condition precedent to his claim or defence has been performed or has occurred — that is implied automatically. But if a party wants to contest the opponent's compliance with a condition precedent, he must distinctly specify that contestation in his own pleading.
essential_elements: General rule: performance/occurrence of conditions precedent is implied in a pleading without express averment.
Exception the pleader must invoke: to contest a condition precedent, it must be distinctly specified in the contesting party's pleading.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The implication only covers conditions "necessary for the case" being pleaded — it does not relieve a party of pleading facts that are themselves part of the cause of action, only the background compliance conditions.
breakdown.how_to_read: If a defendant wishes to argue that a contractual precondition (e.g., prior notice, an escalation step, exhaustion of an internal remedy) was not satisfied, that must be expressly pleaded in the written statement — silence is treated as an admission that all conditions precedent were duly performed.

sections.title: Order VI, Rule 7 — Departure
sections.raw_text: 7. Departure.—No pleading shall, except by way of amendment, raise any new ground of claim or contain any allegation of fact inconsistent with the previous pleadings of the party pleading the same.

breakdown.plain_summary: A party cannot, in a later pleading, spring a brand-new ground of claim or allege facts inconsistent with what they pleaded earlier — except through a formal amendment under Rule 17. This prevents a party from quietly shifting their case as the suit progresses.
essential_elements: Bars raising a new ground of claim in a subsequent pleading without amendment.
Bars pleading facts inconsistent with the party's own earlier pleading, again absent amendment.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The bar does not apply where the party formally seeks and obtains leave to amend under Rule 17 — amendment is the lawful route to change or add to one's case.
breakdown.how_to_read: A classic cross-examination and final-argument tool: if an opposing party's evidence or arguments depart from their pleaded case without a corresponding amendment, Rule 7 (read with the principle that parties are bound by their pleadings) is the basis to object that the new case cannot be looked into.

sections.title: Order VI, Rule 8 — Denial of contract
sections.raw_text: 8. Denial of contract.—Where a contract is alleged in any pleading, a bare denial of the same by the opposite party shall be construed only as a denial in fact of the express contract alleged or of the matters of fact from which the same may be implied, and not as a denial of the legality or sufficiency in law of such contract.

breakdown.plain_summary: If one party pleads a contract and the other party simply denies it without more, that bare denial is read narrowly — as disputing only the factual existence of the contract (or the facts from which it could be implied), not as also disputing whether the contract is legally valid or legally sufficient.
essential_elements: A bare denial of an alleged contract denies only its factual existence/implication.
A bare denial does NOT, by itself, raise a challenge to the contract's legality or legal sufficiency.
exceptions_and_qualifications: A party wishing to challenge legality or legal sufficiency (e.g., void for illegality, insufficient consideration, violates a statute) must plead that specifically — it will not be read into a generic denial.
breakdown.how_to_read: If you intend to argue a contract is illegal or legally insufficient (not just factually non-existent), draft the written statement to say so explicitly — relying on Rule 8's default construction of a bare denial will not preserve that argument.

sections.title: Order VI, Rule 9 — Effect of document to be stated
sections.raw_text: 9. Effect of document to be stated.—Wherever the contents of any document are material, it shall be sufficient in any pleading to state the effect thereof as briefly as possible, without setting out the whole or any part thereof, unless the precise words of the document or any part thereof are material.

breakdown.plain_summary: When a document's contents matter to a pleading, it is enough to summarise the document's effect briefly — there is no need to reproduce the whole document or any part of it, unless the document's precise wording itself is what matters.
essential_elements: General rule: plead the effect/substance of a material document briefly.
Exception: where the precise words themselves are material, those precise words (or the relevant part) must be set out.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Determining whether "precise words" are material is fact-specific — e.g., in a defamation suit the exact words used are almost always material and must be quoted verbatim, unlike a generic commercial contract where summarising suffices.
breakdown.how_to_read: Over-pleading by annexing and reciting entire contracts verbatim clutters a plaint unnecessarily; better practice is to summarise the effect under this Rule and rely on the document itself (filed as an exhibit) for precise terms, reserving verbatim quotation for clauses that are genuinely in dispute.

sections.title: Order VI, Rule 10 — Malice, knowledge, etc.
sections.raw_text: 10. Malice, knowledge, etc.—Wherever it is material to allege malice, fradulent intention, knowledge or other condition of the mind of any person, it shall be sufficient to allege the same as a fact without setting out the circumstances from which the same is to be inferred.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where a party's mental state — malice, fraudulent intent, knowledge, or similar — matters to the case, it is enough to simply allege that state of mind as a fact, without pleading out all the circumstantial detail from which it is to be inferred.
essential_elements: Permits bare allegation of mental-state facts (malice, fraudulent intention, knowledge) without reciting the inferential circumstances.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This simplification is for pleading purposes only — at trial, the party will still need to lead evidence of the surrounding circumstances to actually prove the alleged state of mind; Rule 4's particulars requirement for fraud allegations should also be read alongside this Rule.
breakdown.how_to_read: Useful in malicious-prosecution or fraud-adjacent pleadings to keep the plaint concise — allege "the defendant acted with knowledge that the representation was false" as a fact, and save the evidentiary circumstances for trial, while still giving enough particulars under Rule 4 to satisfy that separate requirement.

sections.title: Order VI, Rule 11 — Notice
sections.raw_text: 11. Notice.—Wherever it is material to allege notice to any person of any fact, matter or thing, it shall be sufficient to allege such notice as a fact, unless the form or the precise terms of such notice, or the circumstances from which such notice is to be inferred, are material.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where notice to a person of some fact or matter is material, it suffices to simply allege that notice as a fact — except where the form, precise terms, or the circumstances from which the notice is to be inferred are themselves material, in which case those details must be pleaded.
essential_elements: General rule: allege notice as a bare fact.
Exception: plead form/precise terms/inferential circumstances where those are themselves material to the case.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Statutory notice requirements (e.g., Section 80 notice to Government, or contractual notice clauses) often make the precise terms and manner of notice material — in such cases the bare-fact shortcut does not suffice and full particulars of the notice must be pleaded.
breakdown.how_to_read: Where a claim depends on a statutory or contractual notice (termination notice, default notice, Section 80 CPC notice), plead the date, mode, and content of that notice specifically rather than relying on this Rule's general shortcut, since the notice's adequacy is likely to be contested.

sections.title: Order VI, Rule 12 — Implied contract, or relation
sections.raw_text: 12. Implied contract, or relation.—Whenever any contract or any relation between any persons is to be implied from a series of letters or conversations or otherwise from a number of circumstances, it shall be sufficient to allege such contract or relation as a fact, and to refer generally to such letters, conversations or circumstances without setting them out in detail. And if in such case the person so pleading desires to rely in the alternative upon more contracts or relations than one as to be implied from such circumstances, he may state the same in the alternative.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where a contract or relationship is to be implied from a series of letters, conversations, or other circumstances, it is enough to allege the resulting contract/relation as a fact and refer generally to those letters/conversations/circumstances, without reciting each one in detail. The pleader may also plead, in the alternative, more than one possible implied contract or relation arising from the same circumstances.
essential_elements: Allows a general reference to the correspondence/conversations/circumstances rather than a detailed recitation.
Expressly permits alternative pleading of multiple possible implied contracts or relations from the same facts.
exceptions_and_qualifications: As with Rules 10-11, this is a pleading-stage simplification; the underlying letters/conversations will still need to be proved as evidence at trial.
breakdown.how_to_read: Useful where a commercial relationship was never reduced to a single signed contract but grew out of an exchange of correspondence — plead the implied contract as a fact, optionally in the alternative (e.g., "a contract of agency, or alternatively a contract for commission on each transaction"), rather than quoting every email.

sections.title: Order VI, Rule 13 — Presumptions of law
sections.raw_text: 13. Presumptions of law.—Neither party need in any pleading allege any matter of fact which the law presumes in his favour or as to which the burden of proof lies upon the other side unless the same has first been specifically denied (e.g., consideration for a bill of exchange where the plaintiff sues only on the bill and not for the consideration as a substantive ground of claim).

breakdown.plain_summary: A party need not plead a fact that the law already presumes in his favour, or a fact for which the burden of proof rests on the opposite side — unless the other side has specifically denied it. The Code's own example: a plaintiff suing on a bill of exchange need not plead consideration, since the law presumes consideration for a bill, unless the defendant specifically denies consideration.
essential_elements: No need to plead facts the law presumes in the pleader's favour.
No need to plead facts on which the burden of proof lies on the other side.
Exception triggering a need to plead: once the other side specifically denies the presumed fact, it becomes a live issue.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The illustrative example (consideration on a bill of exchange) shows the Rule's operation is tied to specific statutory/legal presumptions — e.g., under the Negotiable Instruments Act — not a general licence to omit material facts.
breakdown.how_to_read: Plaintiffs suing on negotiable instruments can keep the plaint lean by not separately pleading consideration; but the moment a written statement specifically denies consideration, the plaintiff should be ready to meet that issue with evidence, since the presumption is rebuttable, not conclusive.

sections.title: Order VI, Rule 14 — Pleading to be signed
sections.raw_text: 14. Pleading to be signed.—Every pleading shall be signed by the party and his pleader (if any): Provided that where a party pleading is, by reason of absence or for other good cause, unable to sign the pleading, it may be signed by any person duly authorized by him to sign the same or to sue or defend on his behalf

breakdown.plain_summary: Every plaint or written statement must be signed by the party itself and by the pleader (advocate), if the party has one. If the party cannot sign — because of absence or other good cause — someone duly authorised by the party to sign, or to sue/defend on the party's behalf, may sign instead.
essential_elements: Default rule: signature of both the party and the pleader (if engaged) is required.
Proviso: a duly authorised person may sign in the party's place where the party cannot sign due to absence or other good cause.
exceptions_and_qualifications: "Other good cause" is not defined and is left to be assessed case-by-case (e.g., illness, incapacity); the authorisation to sign must be proved if challenged.
breakdown.how_to_read: A pleading signed only by counsel without the party's signature (or a valid authorised signatory's signature backed by a power of attorney/authorisation) is technically defective — check this before filing and keep authorisation documents on record to pre-empt a maintainability objection.

sections.title: Order VI, Rule 14A — Address for service of notice
sections.raw_text:
14A. Address for service of notice.—(1) Every pleading, when filed by a party, shall be accompanied by a statement in the prescribed form, signed as provided in rule 14, regarding the address of the party.
(2) Such address may, from time to time, be changed by lodging in Court a form duly filled up and stating the new address of the party and accompanied by a verified petition.
(3) The address furnished in the statement made under sub-rule (1) shall be called the “registered address” of the party, and shall, until duly changed as aforesaid, be deemed to be the address of the party for the purpose of service of all processes in the suit or in any appeal from any decree or order therein made and for the purpose of execution, and shall hold good, subject as aforesaid, for a period of two years after the final determination of the cause or matter.
(4) Service of any process may be effected upon a party at his registered address in all respects as though such party resided thereat.
(5) Where the registered address of a party is discovered by the Court to be incomplete. false or fictitious, the Court may, either on its own motion, or on the application of any party, order—
(a) in the case where such registered address was furnished by a plaintiff, stay of the suit, or
(b) in the case where such registered address was furnished by a defendant, his defence be struck out and he be placed in the same position as if he had not put up any defence.
(6) Where a suit is stayed or a defence is struck out under sub-rule (5), the plaintiff or, as the case may be, the defendant may, after furnishing his true address, apply to the Court for an order to set aside the order of stay or, as the case may be, the order striking out the defence.
(7) The Court, if satisfied that the party was prevented by any sufficient cause from filing the true address at the proper time, shall set aside the order of stay or order striking out the defence, on such terms as to costs or otherwise as it thinks fit and shall appoint a day for proceeding with the suit or defence, as the case may be.
(8) Nothing in this rule shall prevent the Court from directing the service of a process at any other address, if, for any reason, it thinks fit to do so.

breakdown.plain_summary: Every pleading must come with a statement of the party's address, which becomes that party's "registered address" for all service of process in the suit, any appeal, and execution, valid for two years after final determination (changeable by lodging an updated, verified form). If the Court finds the registered address incomplete, false, or fictitious, it can stay the plaintiff's suit or strike out the defendant's defence; the affected party can get that order set aside by furnishing the true address and showing sufficient cause for the earlier failure, on the Court's terms as to costs.
essential_elements: Sub-rule (1): mandatory address statement must accompany every pleading, signed per Rule 14.
Sub-rule (3): the furnished address becomes the "registered address", valid for service for two years post-final-determination.
Sub-rule (4): service at the registered address is treated as valid as though the party actually resided there.
Sub-rule (5): a false/incomplete/fictitious registered address can trigger stay of the suit (if plaintiff's) or striking out of the defence (if defendant's).
Sub-rules (6)-(7): the affected party can seek restoration by furnishing the true address and showing sufficient cause, with the Court having discretion on costs and terms.
Sub-rule (8): preserves the Court's power to direct service at any other address regardless of the registered address.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Sub-rule (8) is itself an express carve-out letting the Court bypass the registered-address regime entirely when it thinks fit, for any reason.
breakdown.how_to_read: Always double-check the client's registered address statement for accuracy before filing — a false or stale address risks the drastic sanction of stay/striking-out under sub-rule (5), and while sub-rule (7) offers a cure, it comes with costs and delay that are entirely avoidable by getting the address right the first time.

sections.title: Order VI, Rule 15 — Verification of pleadings
sections.raw_text:
15. Verification of pleadings.—(1) Save as otherwise provided by any law for the time being in force, every pleading shall be verified at the foot by the party or by one of the parties pleading or by some other person proved to the satisfaction of the Court to be acquainted with the facts of the case.
(2) The person verifying shall specify, by reference to the numbered paragraphs of the pleading, what he verifies of his own knowledge and what he verifies upon information received and believed to be true.
(3) The verification shall be signed by the person making it and shall state the date on which and the place at which it was signed.
(4) The person verifying the pleading shall also furnish an affidavit in support of his pleadings.

breakdown.plain_summary: Every pleading must be verified at its foot — by a party, or by someone proven to the Court's satisfaction to know the facts — specifying paragraph-by-paragraph what is verified from personal knowledge versus what is verified on information believed to be true, signed with date and place, and (by later amendment) backed by a supporting affidavit.
essential_elements: Verification by the party, a co-party, or a knowledgeable person proved to the Court's satisfaction.
Paragraph-specific split between personal-knowledge verification and information-and-belief verification.
Signature with date and place of signing.
Supporting affidavit now mandatory under sub-rule (4).
exceptions_and_qualifications: Sub-rule (1) itself opens with "save as otherwise provided by any law for the time being in force" — special statutes can prescribe their own verification regime overriding this default one.
Commercial disputes are governed by the stricter Rule 15A Statement-of-Truth regime instead of/in addition to this Rule.
breakdown.how_to_read: A defectively verified pleading (no paragraph-wise knowledge/belief split, missing affidavit, wrong signatory) is a frequently raised technical objection — verify this checklist before every filing, especially in writ-adjacent or urgent interim-relief matters where verification defects can be fatal to urgency arguments.

sections.title: Order VI, Rule 15A — Verification of pleadings in a commercial dispute
sections.raw_text:
*15A. Verification of pleadings in a commercial dispute.— (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in Rule 15, every pleading in a commercial dispute shall be verified by an affidavit in the manner and form prescribed in the Appendix to this Schedule.
(2) An affidavit under sub-rule (1) above shall be signed by the party or by one of the parties to the proceedings, or by any other person on behalf of such party or parties who is proved to the satisfaction of the Court to be acquainted with the facts of the case and who is duly authorised by such party or parties.
(3) Where a pleading is amended, the amendments must be verified in the form and manner referred to in sub-rule (1) unless the Court orders otherwise.
(4) Where a pleading is not verified in the manner provided under sub-rule (1), the party shall not be permitted to rely on such pleading as evidence or any of the matters set out therein.
(5) The Court may strike out a pleading which is not verified by a Statement of Truth, namely, the affidavit set out in the Appendix to this Schedule.

breakdown.plain_summary: For commercial disputes, Rule 15A overrides the ordinary verification Rule with a mandatory "Statement of Truth" affidavit in the prescribed Appendix form, signed by a party or a duly authorised, knowledgeable person. Amendments must be similarly re-verified unless the Court orders otherwise. Failure to comply means the pleading cannot be relied on as evidence, and the Court may strike it out altogether.
essential_elements: Sub-rule (1): overrides Rule 15 — mandatory prescribed-form Statement of Truth affidavit for every commercial-dispute pleading.
Sub-rule (2): signed by a party or a duly authorised, knowledgeable person.
Sub-rule (3): amendments require re-verification in the same form, absent contrary Court order.
Sub-rule (4): non-compliance bars reliance on the pleading (or its contents) as evidence.
Sub-rule (5): non-compliant pleadings are liable to be struck out entirely.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Sub-rule (3)'s re-verification requirement can be dispensed with by specific Court order.
This is a specialised regime applicable only to "commercial disputes" as defined under the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 — not to civil suits generally.
breakdown.how_to_read: In commercial suits, never treat verification as boilerplate — the Statement of Truth in the prescribed Appendix form is a substantive precondition to using the pleading as evidence at all, and a defectively verified commercial plaint or written statement risks being struck out outright under sub-rule (5), a far harsher consequence than under ordinary Rule 15.

sections.title: Order VI, Rule 16 — Striking out pleadings
sections.raw_text:
16. Striking out pleadings.—The Court may at any stage of the proceedings order to be struck out or amended any matter in any pleading—
(a) which may be unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, of
(b) which may tend to prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trail of the suit, or
(c) which is otherwise an abuse of the process of the Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: At any stage of a suit, the Court can order any matter in a pleading struck out or amended if it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous, or vexatious; if it would prejudice, embarrass, or delay a fair trial; or if it otherwise abuses the Court's process.
essential_elements: Available "at any stage of the proceedings" — not limited to a preliminary window.
Three independent grounds: (a) unnecessary/scandalous/frivolous/vexatious matter; (b) matter causing prejudice, embarrassment, or delay to a fair trial; (c) abuse of process.
Court may order the matter struck out, or simply amended, as appropriate.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a discretionary power ("may"), not a mandatory one — the Court weighs whether striking out is warranted rather than being compelled to act on every objectionable averment.
breakdown.how_to_read: A powerful defensive tool against padded, scandalous, or deliberately embarrassing pleadings (common in matrimonial-adjacent or personal civil disputes) — but courts use this power sparingly, so an application under Rule 16 should target clearly unnecessary or abusive content, not merely unfavourable factual allegations.

sections.title: Order VI, Rule 17 — Amendment of pleadings
sections.raw_text:
17. Amendment of pleadings.—The Court may at any stage of the proceedings allow either party to alter or amend his pleadings in such manner and on such terms as may be just, and all such amendments shall be made as may be necessary for the purpose of determining the real questions in controversy between the parties:
Provided that no application for amendment shall be allowed after the trial has commenced, unless the Court comes to the conclusion that in spite of due diligence, the party could not have raised the matter before the commencement of trial.

breakdown.plain_summary: The Court has broad power to let either party amend their pleadings, on just terms, at any stage — but the overriding purpose must be to determine the real questions in controversy between the parties. Once trial has commenced, amendment is barred unless the party shows that, despite due diligence, the matter could not have been raised before trial began.
essential_elements: General power: amendment allowed at any stage, on just terms, for determining the real questions in controversy.
Restored 2002-amendment proviso: post-trial-commencement amendment barred absent a due-diligence showing that the matter could not have been raised earlier.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The due-diligence proviso is the key exception/qualification on an otherwise liberal amendment power — courts apply it strictly once trial has genuinely commenced (as opposed to merely being listed).
breakdown.how_to_read: Courts of India have repeatedly emphasised (post-2002 amendment) that liberal amendment is the norm before trial begins, but the proviso bites hard afterward — so always seek amendment early, and if forced to seek it after trial commencement, build a specific due-diligence record (why the fact/ground could not have been known or pleaded earlier) rather than a bare request.

sections.title: Order VI, Rule 18 — Failure to amend after Order
sections.raw_text: 18. Failure to amend after Order.—If a party who has obtained an order for leave to amend does not amend accordingly within the time limited for that purpose by the order, or if no time is thereby limited then within fourteen days from the date of the order, he shall not be permitted to amend after the expiration of such limited time as aforesaid or of such fourteen days, as the case may be, unless the time is extended by the Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: Once a party obtains leave to amend a pleading, the amendment must actually be carried out within the time fixed by the order, or within 14 days if no time was fixed. Miss that deadline, and the party loses the right to amend unless the Court extends the time.
essential_elements: Deadline is whatever the amendment order specifies, defaulting to 14 days from the order if none is specified.
Missing the deadline forfeits the leave to amend.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Court retains discretion to extend the time even after the default period, preventing an automatic, irreversible forfeiture — but the party must apply for and obtain that extension.
breakdown.how_to_read: Once leave to amend is granted, calendar the deadline immediately and file the amended pleading well within time (or apply proactively for an extension before the deadline lapses) — letting leave to amend lapse is an avoidable, purely administrative failure that can cost a party a hard-won procedural opportunity.

sections.title: Order VII — Plaint (Overview)
sections.raw_text:
ORDER VII
Plaint

This Order is the complete code on the plaintiff's foundational pleading: the mandatory particulars every plaint must contain, special requirements for money suits, interest claims, immovable property, representative suits, limitation exemption, and specific relief; the procedure on admitting a plaint, returning it to the correct Court, and — most critically for practitioners — the grounds and procedure for rejecting a plaint under Rule 11; and the rules on producing documents relied on in the plaint.

breakdown.plain_summary: Order VII governs everything about drafting, filing, and testing a plaint. Rule 1 lists the mandatory particulars (parties, cause of action and when it arose, jurisdictional facts, relief claimed, valuation); Rules 2-8 add special requirements for money claims, interest claims (Rule 2A), immovable property suits, representative suits, limitation-exemption pleading, and specific relief. Rules 9-10B deal with Court procedure after a plaint is admitted, including the pivotal power to return a plaint to the proper Court (Rule 10) and the appellate-transfer mechanism (Rule 10B). Rule 11 — one of the most heavily litigated provisions in the entire Code — lists the exhaustive grounds on which a plaint must be rejected (no cause of action, undervaluation, insufficient stamping, statutory bar apparent from the plaint, non-filing in duplicate, non-compliance with Rule 9), with Rule 13 clarifying that rejection does not by itself bar a fresh plaint on the same cause of action. Rules 14-17 govern production of documents the plaintiff relies on, with Rule 14(3) excluding undisclosed documents from evidence absent leave of Court.
essential_elements: Rule 1 mandates specific particulars in every plaint: Court, parties' details, minority/unsoundness-of-mind status, cause of action facts and date, jurisdictional facts, relief claimed, any set-off/relinquishment, and valuation for jurisdiction/court-fees.

Rule 2A requires plaints seeking interest to specify whether it is claimed under Section 34, under a contract/statute, or otherwise, with the rate, start date, calculation date, total to date, and post-date daily accrual rate.

Rule 10 empowers the Court to return a plaint at any stage to the Court in which the suit should have been instituted (lack of jurisdiction), with Rule 10A letting the Court fix an appearance date in the transferee Court to streamline the transition, and Rule 10B governing appellate-level transfer.

Rule 11 is the core gatekeeping provision: a plaint MUST be rejected for no disclosed cause of action, undervaluation uncorrected after Court direction, insufficient stamping uncorrected after Court direction, a statutory bar apparent on the plaint's own statements, non-duplicate filing, or non-compliance with Rule 9 — tested ordinarily by reading the plaint's own averments as true, without looking at the written statement.

Rule 13 softens Rule 11's bite: rejection of a plaint does not, by its own force, bar the plaintiff from presenting a fresh plaint on the same cause of action (subject to limitation and other legal bars).

Rule 14 requires the plaintiff to produce and list, at the time of presenting the plaint, every document sued upon or relied on that is in the plaintiff's possession/power, with Rule 14(3) barring an undisclosed document from being received in evidence on the plaintiff's behalf without the Court's leave.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Rule 15 (statement where documents are not in the plaintiff's possession) was omitted by the 1999 amendment, and Rule 18 (inadmissibility of undisclosed documents) was omitted by the 2002 amendment — their substance now largely folded into Rule 14.

Rule 11's proviso bars extension of time to correct valuation/stamping unless the Court is satisfied, for recorded reasons, that an exceptional cause prevented timely compliance and that refusing extension would cause grave injustice.
Rule 14(4) exempts documents used only for cross-examining the plaintiff's witnesses or to refresh a witness's memory from the disclosure-and-list requirement.
Rule 17's shop-book production requirement yields to the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891 where that special Act applies.
breakdown.how_to_read: Order VII Rule 11 is the single most common pre-trial battleground in Indian civil litigation — as a defendant, scrutinise the plaint's own averments (not the merits) for a missing cause of action, an apparent limitation/jurisdictional bar, or undervaluation/stamping defects, and move promptly; as a plaintiff, draft the plaint defensively against exactly these six grounds, since an adverse Rule 11 order (though not an automatic bar to re-filing under Rule 13) can still cost time, limitation exposure, and costs.

sections.title: Order VII, Rule 1 — Particulars to be contained in plaint

breakdown.plain_summary: This Rule is the master checklist for every plaint: the Court's name, both parties' identifying details, any minority/unsoundness-of-mind status, the cause-of-action facts and when they arose, the facts establishing the Court's jurisdiction, the relief claimed, any set-off allowed or claim relinquished, and the suit's valuation for jurisdiction and court-fee purposes.
essential_elements: Clause (a): correct Court's name.
Clauses (b)-(c): parties' name, description, and residence (defendant's, so far as ascertainable).
Clause (d): minority/unsoundness-of-mind disclosure where applicable.
Clause (e): cause-of-action facts AND when the cause of action arose (critical for limitation).
Clause (f): jurisdictional facts (pecuniary and territorial).
Clause (g): relief claimed.
Clause (h): disclosure of any set-off allowed or portion of claim relinquished.
Clause (i): valuation for jurisdiction and court-fees.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (c)'s defendant-details requirement is qualified by "so far as they can be ascertained" — a plaintiff is not expected to supply details genuinely unknown despite reasonable effort.
breakdown.how_to_read: This Rule 1 checklist is the first thing to audit both when drafting a plaint and when attacking one under Order VII Rule 11 — a missing cause-of-action date (clause (e)) is often the entry point for a limitation-bar rejection argument, and missing jurisdictional facts (clause (f)) for a jurisdiction challenge.

sections.title: Order VII, Rule 2 — In money suits
sections.raw_text:
2. In money suits.—Where the plaintiff seeks the recovery of money, the plaint shall state the precise amount claimed:
But where the plaintiff sues for mesne profits, or for an amount which will be found due to him on taking unsettled accounts between him and the defendant, or for movables in the possession of the defendant, or for debts of which the value he cannot, after the exercise of reasonable diligence, estimate, the plaint shall state approximately the amount or value sued for.

breakdown.plain_summary: A plaint seeking recovery of money must state the exact amount claimed — except in specific situations (mesne profits, amounts to be ascertained from unsettled accounts, movables in the defendant's possession, or debts whose value cannot be estimated despite reasonable diligence), where an approximate amount or value suffices.
essential_elements: General rule: precise amount must be stated for money claims.
Exception: approximate amount/value suffices for mesne profits, unsettled-account claims, movables in defendant's possession, or genuinely inestimable debts.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The approximation exception is conditioned on "reasonable diligence" having been exercised first — a plaintiff cannot claim the exception merely for convenience without having tried to ascertain the precise figure.
breakdown.how_to_read: Court-fee calculation usually tracks the amount stated under this Rule, so getting the precise-vs-approximate characterisation right (and being able to justify an approximate figure if challenged) has direct cost and Rule 11(b) undervaluation-rejection consequences.

sections.title: Order VII, Rule 2A — Where interest is sought in the suit

breakdown.plain_summary: A plaint claiming interest must spell out the legal basis for the claim (commercial transaction under Section 34, a contract, a statute, or some other basis) and give full particulars: the rate, the start date, the date up to which it is calculated, the total interest to that date, and the daily rate accruing thereafter.
essential_elements: Sub-rule (2): must identify the basis of the interest claim (Section 34 commercial-transaction interest, contractual, statutory, or other).
Sub-rule (3): must state rate, start date, calculation-date cut-off, total interest to that date, and post-cut-off daily accrual rate.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Rule applies specifically where the plaintiff "seeks interest" — a plaint making no interest claim need not address it at all.
breakdown.how_to_read: Pleading interest with this level of particularity avoids later disputes over quantum at the decree stage — draft the interest paragraph as a worked calculation (principal, rate, period, running total, daily accrual) rather than a vague "interest at such rate as the Court deems fit" formula, which invites challenge under this Rule's specificity requirement.

sections.title: Order VII, Rule 3 — Where the subject-matter of the suit is immovable property
sections.raw_text: 3. Where the subject-matter of the suit is immovable property.—Where the subject-matter of the suit is immovable property, the plaint shall contain a description of the property sufficient to identify it, and, in case such property can be identified by boundaries or numbers in a record of settlement or survey, the plaint shall specify such boundaries or numbers.

breakdown.plain_summary: Suits concerning immovable property must describe the property precisely enough to identify it — and where settlement/survey records give it boundaries or numbers, those must be specified in the plaint.
essential_elements: Sufficient description to identify the property is mandatory.
Settlement/survey boundaries or numbers must be specified where they exist.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Where no settlement/survey record exists for the property, a general but sufficiently identifying description (metes and bounds, landmarks, etc.) will suffice in its place.
breakdown.how_to_read: Vague property descriptions in suits for possession, partition, or injunction are a recurring source of execution difficulty later — always attach survey numbers/boundaries and, where practical, a site plan or schedule of property to the plaint to pre-empt identification disputes at the decree-execution stage.

sections.title: Order VII, Rule 4 — When plaintiff sues as representative
sections.raw_text: 4. When plaintiff sues as representative.—Where the plaintiff sues in a representative character the plaint shall show not only that he has an actual existing interest in the subject-matter, but that he has taken the steps (if any) necessary to enable him to institute a suit concerning it.

breakdown.plain_summary: A plaintiff suing in a representative capacity (e.g., as trustee, next friend, or under Order I Rule 8) must show in the plaint both an actual existing interest in the subject-matter and compliance with any procedural steps required to be entitled to sue representatively.
essential_elements: Must show actual existing interest in the subject-matter.
Must show compliance with any preconditions/steps necessary to sue in that representative character.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Applies only where the plaintiff sues "in a representative character" — an ordinary plaintiff suing in his own right need not address this Rule.
breakdown.how_to_read: When suing as a representative (trustee, guardian, or under a representative-suit order), expressly plead both the source of the representative interest and compliance with any procedural precondition (e.g., Court permission under Order I Rule 8) — omitting this is a common ground for a maintainability challenge.

sections.title: Order VII, Rule 5 — Defendant's interest and liability to be shown
sections.raw_text: 5. Defendant's interest and liability to be shown.—The plaint shall show that the defendant is or claims to be interested in the subject-matter, and that he is liable to be called upon to answer the plaintiff's demand.

breakdown.plain_summary: The plaint must affirmatively show that the defendant has (or claims) an interest in the subject-matter of the suit and is liable to be called upon to answer the plaintiff's claim — tying the defendant into the dispute, not just naming them.
essential_elements: Must show the defendant's actual or claimed interest in the subject-matter.
Must show the defendant's liability to answer the plaintiff's demand.
breakdown.how_to_read: A plaint that merely names a party as defendant without pleading facts connecting them to the cause of action or showing their liability is vulnerable to a misjoinder or no-cause-of-action objection — always plead the specific nexus between each defendant and the relief sought against them.

sections.title: Order VII, Rule 6 — Grounds of exemption from limitation law
sections.raw_text:
6. Grounds of exemption from limitation law.—Where the suit is instituted after the expiration of the period prescribed by the law of limitation, the plaint shall show the ground upon which exemption from such law is claimed:
Provided that the Court may permit the plaintiff to claim exemption from the law of limitation on any ground not set out in the plaint, if such ground is not inconsistent with the grounds set out in the plaint.

breakdown.plain_summary: If a suit is filed after the normal limitation period, the plaint must plead the specific ground relied on to claim exemption from the bar of limitation. The Court may still permit reliance on an additional, unpleaded ground later — but only if it is consistent with (not contradictory to) the grounds already pleaded.
essential_elements: Mandatory pleading of the limitation-exemption ground where the suit is filed beyond the limitation period.
Proviso: Court may permit an additional unpleaded ground, but only if consistent with the pleaded grounds.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The proviso's consistency requirement prevents a plaintiff from pleading one exemption ground and later shifting to a factually contradictory one — a genuinely inconsistent new ground requires amendment, not mere Court permission under this proviso.
breakdown.how_to_read: A time-barred-looking plaint that fails to plead a limitation-exemption ground at all is a direct, often fatal, target for Rule 11(d) rejection (suit barred by law apparent from the plaint) — always address limitation head-on in the plaint if the suit is filed anywhere near or past the ordinary limitation period.

sections.title: Order VII, Rule 7 — Relief to be specifically stated
sections.raw_text: 7. Relief to be specifically stated.—Every plaint shall state specifically the relief which the plaintiff claims either simply or in the alternative, and it shall not be necessary to ask for general or other relief which may always be given as the Court may think just to the same extent as if it had been asked for. And the same rule shall apply to any relief claimed by the defendant in his written statement.

breakdown.plain_summary: The plaint must specifically state the relief claimed, whether as a simple claim or in the alternative. There is no need to separately ask for "general or other relief" — the Court can always grant such relief as it thinks just, to the same extent as if it had been expressly asked for. The same principle applies to relief a defendant claims in a written statement (e.g., counter-claim).
essential_elements: Specific relief (simple or alternative) must be stated.
No separate "general relief" prayer is necessary — the Court's power to grant just relief is not limited to what is expressly prayed.
Applies equally to defendant's relief claims in a written statement.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Court's power to grant unprayed "general relief" is not unlimited — it operates within the bounds of what is just on the facts and cause of action actually pleaded, not as a licence to grant an entirely different, unpleaded relief.
breakdown.how_to_read: Always plead relief in the alternative wherever the facts support more than one possible outcome (e.g., specific performance, or alternatively damages) — this Rule expressly sanctions alternative prayers, and failing to do so can needlessly narrow what the Court can grant even though general-relief power exists as a backstop.

sections.title: Order VII, Rule 8 — Relief founded on separate grounds
sections.raw_text: 8. Relief founded on separate grounds.—Where the plaintiff seeks relief in respect of several distinct claims or causes of action founded upon separate and distinct grounds, they shall be stated as far as may be separately and distinctly.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where a plaintiff claims relief on multiple distinct claims or causes of action, each founded on separate grounds, those claims/grounds must be pleaded separately and distinctly, as far as practicable — not blended together.
essential_elements: Requires separate and distinct pleading of each distinct claim/cause of action founded on separate grounds.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Qualified by "as far as may be" — practical blending is tolerated where genuinely necessary, but the default expectation is separation.
breakdown.how_to_read: In a plaint combining multiple causes of action (e.g., breach of contract and a separate tortious claim against the same defendant), structure the plaint with clearly separated sections/headings for each — this Rule reflects the same discipline Order II Rule 3 encourages for joinder of causes of action.

sections.title: Order VII, Rule 9 — Procedure on admitting plaint
sections.raw_text: 9. Procedure on admitting plaint.—Where the Court orders that the summons be served on the defendants in the manner provided in rule 9 of Order V, it will direct the plaintiff to present as many copies of the plaint on plain paper as there are defendants within seven days from the date of such order along with requisite fee for service of summons on the defendants.

breakdown.plain_summary: Once the Court admits the plaint and orders summons to be served under Order V Rule 9's modern service modes, it directs the plaintiff to file one copy of the plaint on plain paper for each defendant, within seven days, along with the fee needed for serving summons.
essential_elements: Triggered once the Court orders Order V Rule 9 service.
Plaintiff must supply one plain-paper copy per defendant within seven days of the order.
Plaintiff must also pay the requisite service fee within that window.
breakdown.how_to_read: Non-compliance with this Rule is itself a ground for rejection of the plaint under Rule 11(f) — calendar the seven-day deadline for supplying copies and fees the moment the Court admits the plaint, since missing it can unravel an otherwise sound suit on a purely administrative default.

sections.title: Order VII, Rule 10 — Return of plaint
sections.raw_text:
10. Return of plaint.—(1) Subject to the provisions of rule 10A, the plaint shall at any stage of the suit be returned to be presented to the Court in which the suit should have been instituted.
Explanation.— For the removal of doubts, it is hereby declared that a Court of appeal or revision may direct after setting aside the decree passed in a suit, the return of the plaint under this sub-rule.
(2) Procedure on returning plaint.—On returning a plaint, the Judge shall endorse thereon the date of its presentation and return, the name of the party presenting it, and a brief statement of the reasons for returning it.

breakdown.plain_summary: If a suit was instituted in the wrong Court, the plaint must be returned (at any stage of the suit) for presentation to the correct Court — even an appellate or revisional Court can order this after setting aside a decree. On return, the Judge endorses the presentation date, return date, presenter's name, and brief reasons for return.
essential_elements: Return is available "at any stage of the suit" once the wrong-Court problem is identified.
Explanation confirms appellate/revisional Courts can direct return of plaint after setting aside a decree.
Mandatory judicial endorsement: dates of presentation and return, presenter's name, and reasons.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Rule 10 operates "subject to the provisions of rule 10A" — where the defendant has already appeared, the Court must follow Rule 10A's intimation-and-appearance-date procedure before (or as part of) returning the plaint.
breakdown.how_to_read: A plaint return for want of jurisdiction is not the end of the suit — the plaintiff can represent it to the correct Court, and under the Limitation Act the time spent in the wrong Court in good faith is typically excludable, so always check the endorsed return order and reasons carefully before refiling.

sections.title: Order VII, Rule 10A — Power of Court to fix a date of appearance in the Court where plaint is to be filed after its return
sections.raw_text:
10A. Power of Court to fix a date of appearance in the Court where plaint is to be filed after its return.—(1) Where, in any suit, after the defendant has appeared, the Court is of opinion that the plaint should be returned, it shall, before doing so, intimate its decision to the plaintiff.
(2) Where an intimation is given to the plaintiff under sub-rule (1), the plaintiff may make an application to the Court—
(a) specifying the Court in which he proposes to present the plaint after its return,
(b) praying that the Court may fix a date for the appearance of the parties in the said Court, and
(c) requesting that the notice of the date so fixed may be given to him and to the defendant.
(3) Where an application is made by the plaintiff under sub-rule (2), the Court shall, before returning the plaint and notwithstanding that the order for return of plaint was made by it on the ground that it has no jurisdiction to try the suit,—
(a) fix a date for the appearance of the parties in the Court in which the plaint is proposed to be presented, and
(b) give to the plaintiff and to the defendant notice of such date for appearance.
(4) Where the notice of the date for appearance is given under sub-rule (3),—
(a) it shall not be necessary for the Court in which the plaint is presented after its return, to serve the defendant with a summons for appearance in the suit, unless that Court, for reasons to be recorded, otherwise directs, and
(b) the said notice shall be deemed to be a summons for the appearance of the defendant in the Court in which the plaint is presented on the date so fixed by the Court by which the plaint was returned.
(5) Where the application made by the plaintiff under sub-rule (2) is allowed by the Court, the plaintiff shall not be entitled to appeal against the order returning the plaint.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where the defendant has already appeared and the Court decides the plaint must be returned for want of jurisdiction, it must first intimate the plaintiff. The plaintiff can then apply for the Court to fix a date of appearance in the proposed correct Court and notify both sides — which, if granted, dispenses with a fresh summons in the new Court (the notice itself counts as the summons) and smooths the transition. But opting for this streamlined route costs the plaintiff the right to appeal the return order.
essential_elements: Sub-rule (1): mandatory prior intimation to the plaintiff once the Court is minded to return the plaint after the defendant's appearance.
Sub-rule (2): plaintiff's application specifying the proposed Court and requesting a fixed appearance date with notice to both parties.
Sub-rule (3): Court must fix the date and give notice before actually returning the plaint, despite the jurisdictional defect.
Sub-rule (4): the notice doubles as a deemed summons in the new Court, ordinarily dispensing with fresh service.
Sub-rule (5): the trade-off — if the plaintiff's application is allowed, no appeal lies against the order returning the plaint.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Sub-rule (4)(a)'s dispensation from fresh summons yields if the new Court, for recorded reasons, directs otherwise.
breakdown.how_to_read: This Rule offers real efficiency (no fresh summons, immediate continuity in the correct Court) but at the explicit cost of appeal rights over the jurisdiction finding — weigh that trade-off carefully before invoking sub-rule (2), especially if the jurisdictional ruling itself is arguably wrong and worth appealing.

sections.title: Order VII, Rule 10B — Power of appellate Court to transfer suit to the proper Court
sections.raw_text:
10B. Power of appellate Court to transfer suit to the proper Court.—(1) Where, on an appeal against an order for the return of plaint, the Court hearing the appeal confirms such order, the Court of appeal may, if the plaintiff by an application so desires, while returning the plaint, direct plaintiff to file the plaint, subject to the provisions of the Limitation Act, 1963 (36 of 1963), in the Court in which the suit should have been instituted, (whether such Court is within or without the State in which the Court hearing the appeal is situated), and fix a date for the appearance of the parties in the Court in which the plaint is directed to be filed and when the date is so fixed it shall not be necessary for the Court in which the plaint is filed to serve the defendant with the summons for appearance in the suit, unless that Court in which the plaint is filed, for reasons to be recorded, otherwise directs.
(2) The direction made by the Court under sub-rule (1) shall be without any prejudice to the rights of the parties to question the jurisdiction of the Court, in which the plaint is filed, to try the suit.

breakdown.plain_summary: When an appeal against a plaint-return order is dismissed (the return order is confirmed), the appellate Court can, on the plaintiff's application, direct the plaintiff to file the plaint in the correct Court (even in another State), fix an appearance date there, and dispense with fresh summons — all without prejudicing either party's right to later contest that new Court's jurisdiction.
essential_elements: Available only after an appeal against a return-of-plaint order is dismissed (order confirmed).
Requires a plaintiff application.
Can direct filing in a Court outside the State, subject to the Limitation Act.
Fixes an appearance date and (ordinarily) dispenses with fresh summons.
Sub-rule (2): expressly preserves both parties' right to still contest the new Court's jurisdiction.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The fresh-summons dispensation again yields if the new Court records reasons to require fresh service.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the appellate-stage counterpart to Rule 10A — useful for cross-State jurisdictional disputes where re-institution from scratch would be costly, but note it operates subject to the Limitation Act, so a plaintiff should not assume indefinite protection from limitation merely by invoking this transfer mechanism.

sections.title: Order VII, Rule 11 — Rejection of plaint

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the Code's exhaustive list of grounds requiring a plaint's rejection: no disclosed cause of action; uncorrected undervaluation after a Court direction; uncorrected insufficient stamping after a Court direction; a statutory bar apparent from the plaint's own statements; non-duplicate filing; or non-compliance with Rule 9's post-admission procedure. The proviso makes time extensions for valuation/stamping defects hard to get — only for exceptional, recorded reasons where refusal would cause grave injustice.
essential_elements: Clause (a): tested on the plaint's own averments — does it disclose a cause of action at all, taken as true?
Clause (b): undervaluation, but only rejectable after the plaintiff is given a Court-fixed time to correct and fails to do so.
Clause (c): insufficient stamping, again only rejectable after a similar correction opportunity and failure.
Clause (d): a legal bar (e.g., limitation, res judicata, lack of jurisdiction) apparent from the plaint's own statements — not requiring evidence outside the plaint.
Clause (e): failure to file in duplicate (procedural, tied to Order IV).
Clause (f): failure to comply with Rule 9 (supplying plain-paper copies and service fees after admission).
Proviso: strict limits on extending the valuation/stamping correction time — exceptional cause, recorded reasons, and grave injustice if refused.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Rejection is tested ONLY on the plaint's own statements (and, per settled jurisprudence, documents filed with it) — the Court does not look at the written statement or weigh evidence at this stage.
The proviso is itself a tight exception on an exception — ordinarily the Court-fixed correction time is firm, and extension is the rare case, not the default.
breakdown.how_to_read: Order VII Rule 11 applications are won or lost entirely on the four corners of the plaint — never try to rely on the written statement or extraneous facts to support a Rule 11(a)/(d) application, and conversely, as plaintiff's counsel, always plead cause-of-action facts and limitation/jurisdiction facts defensively enough that no clause of this Rule can be triggered by a plain reading of the plaint alone.

sections.title: Order VII, Rule 12 — Procedure on rejecting plaint
sections.raw_text: 12. Procedure on rejecting plaint.—Where a plaint is rejected the Judge shall record an order to that effect with the reasons for such order.

breakdown.plain_summary: When a plaint is rejected under Rule 11, the Judge must record a formal order to that effect, stating the reasons for rejection.
essential_elements: Mandatory recorded order.
Mandatory recorded reasons.
breakdown.how_to_read: A reasoned rejection order is essential for any appeal against it (rejection of a plaint is treated as a decree, appealable under Section 96) — always obtain and carefully analyse the recorded reasons before deciding whether and how to challenge a Rule 11 rejection.

sections.title: Order VII, Rule 13 — Where rejection of plaint does not preclude presentation of fresh plaint
sections.raw_text: 13. Where rejection of plaint does not preclude presentation of fresh plaint.—The rejection of the plaint on any of the grounds hereinbefore mentioned shall not of its own force preclude the plaintiff from presenting a fresh plaint in respect of the same cause of action.

breakdown.plain_summary: Rejection of a plaint under Rule 11 does not, by itself, stop the plaintiff from filing a fresh plaint on the same cause of action — rejection is a curable, non-final-on-the-merits disposal, not an adjudication barring re-litigation.
essential_elements: Rejection alone does not operate as res judicata or any automatic bar to a fresh plaint on the same cause of action.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This protection is "of its own force" only — other legal bars (limitation having since expired, a fresh and independent statutory bar, etc.) can still prevent a fresh plaint from succeeding even though Rule 11 rejection itself does not bar it.
breakdown.how_to_read: A Rule 11 rejection is rarely the end of the road for the plaintiff — but don't treat Rule 13 as a safety net that removes all urgency: limitation keeps running, so refile the corrected plaint promptly rather than relying on this Rule to indefinitely preserve the claim.

sections.title: Order VII, Rule 14 — Production of document on which plaintiff sues or relies
sections.raw_text:
14. Production of document on which plaintiff sues or relies.—(1) Where a plaintiff sues upon a document or relies upon document in his possession or power in support of his claim, he shall enter such documents in a list, and shall produce it in Court when the plaint is presented by him and shall, at the same time deliver the document and a copy thereof, to be filed with the plaint.
(2) Where any such document is not in the possession or power of the plaintiff, he shall, wherever possible, state in whose possession or power it is.
(3) A document which ought to be produced in Court by the plaintiff when the plaint is presented, or to be entered in the list to be added or annexed to the plaint but is not produced or entered accordingly, shall not, without the leave of the Court, be received in evidence on his behalf at the hearing of the suit.
(4) Nothing in this rule shall apply to document produced for the cross-examination of the plaintiff's witnesses, or handed over to a witness merely to refresh his memory.

breakdown.plain_summary: Every document the plaintiff sues upon or relies on, if in the plaintiff's possession or power, must be listed, produced in Court, and filed (with a copy) along with the plaint. If a relied-on document is not in the plaintiff's possession, the plaint should state who has it, where possible. Failing to produce/list a document this way bars it from being used in evidence for the plaintiff later, unless the Court grants leave. Documents used only for cross-examining the plaintiff's own witnesses, or to refresh a witness's memory, are exempt from this entire discipline.
essential_elements: Sub-rule (1): mandatory listing, production, and filing of documents in the plaintiff's possession/power at the time of presenting the plaint.
Sub-rule (2): where not in possession/power, state (where possible) who holds it.
Sub-rule (3): non-compliance bars the document from evidence on the plaintiff's behalf absent Court leave.
Sub-rule (4): cross-examination and memory-refreshing documents are outside this Rule's scope entirely.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Sub-rule (3)'s evidentiary bar is not absolute — the Court retains discretion to grant leave allowing a late or undisclosed document into evidence.
breakdown.how_to_read: Build a document list as a standing checklist alongside every plaint: every document the plaint relies on must be filed with it, or expressly explained as held by a named third party — a document surfacing for the first time at trial without having been disclosed risks exclusion under sub-rule (3), and obtaining leave to cure that is never guaranteed.

sections.title: Order VII, Rule 16 — Suits on lost negotiable instruments
sections.raw_text: 16. Suits on lost negotiable instruments.—Where the suit is founded upon a negotiable instrument, and it is proved that the instrument is lost, and an indemnity is given by the plaintiff, to the satisfaction of the Court, against the claims of any other person upon such instrument, the Court may pass such decree as it would have passed if the plaintiff had produced the instrument in Court when the plaint was presented, and had at the same time delivered a copy of the instrument to be filed with the plaint.

breakdown.plain_summary: If a suit is based on a negotiable instrument (promissory note, bill of exchange, cheque) that has been lost, the plaintiff can still get a decree exactly as if the instrument had been produced — provided the loss is proved and the plaintiff gives the Court a satisfactory indemnity against anyone else later claiming on that same instrument.
essential_elements: Loss of the instrument must be proved.
Plaintiff must give an indemnity, to the Court's satisfaction, against third-party claims on the lost instrument.
On satisfying both, the Court may decree the suit as if the instrument had been produced per Rule 14.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This Rule is a specific carve-out from Rule 14's production requirement, available only for negotiable instruments and only on proof of loss plus adequate indemnity — it does not excuse non-production of any other type of document.
breakdown.how_to_read: In a suit on a lost cheque or promissory note, plead the loss explicitly and come prepared to offer a concrete indemnity (bond, undertaking, or security) rather than merely asserting the instrument is lost — Court satisfaction on the indemnity is a real precondition, not a formality.

sections.title: Order VII, Rule 17 — Production of shop-book
sections.raw_text:
17. Production of shop-book.—(1) Save in so far as is otherwise provided by the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891 (XVIII of 1891), where the document on which the plaintiff sues is an entry in a shop-book or other account in his possession or power, the plaintiff shall produce the book or account at the time of filing the plaint, together with a copy of the entry on which he relies.
(2) Original entry to be marked and returned.—The Court or such officer as it appoints in this behalf, shall forthwith mark the document for the purpose of identification; and, after examining and comparing the copy with the original, shall, if it is found correct, certify it to be so and return the book to the plaintiff and cause the copy to be filed.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where a plaintiff sues on an entry in a shop-book or other account, the original book/account must be produced at the time of filing the plaint along with a copy of the relevant entry (subject to the special regime under the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891, for banking records). The Court marks the original for identification, compares it with the copy, certifies the copy correct if it matches, and returns the original book to the plaintiff while retaining the certified copy on file.
essential_elements: Production of the original shop-book/account at plaint-filing, with a copy of the relevant entry.
Court identification-marking, comparison, and certification procedure, followed by return of the original and filing of the certified copy.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Yields to the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891 where that special statute governs the document (i.e., banking records generally follow that Act's certified-copy regime instead).
breakdown.how_to_read: For suits founded on ledger or account-book entries (not bank records), this Rule lets the plaintiff retain the original book for ongoing business use by substituting a Court-certified copy on the record — invoke it proactively rather than leaving an original business record tied up in Court files indefinitely.

sections.title: Order VIII — Written Statement, Set-off and Counter-claim (Overview)
sections.raw_text:
ORDER VIII
Written statement, set-off and counter-claim

This Order is the defendant's mirror of Order VI/VII: it governs the written statement's timeline and content, the duty to produce documents relied on, the rules of specific denial (including the heightened Commercial Division/Commercial Court denial regime), the drastic consequence of deemed admission for unspecific denials, and the complete code on set-off and counter-claim — the defendant's offensive tools within the same suit.

breakdown.plain_summary: Order VIII is the Code's full regulation of the defendant's response. Rule 1 fixes the 30-day (extendable to 90, or 120 with forfeiture for commercial disputes) written-statement deadline. Rule 1A mirrors Order VII Rule 14's document-production duty for the defence. Rules 2-5 are the law of denial: new facts (fraud, limitation, illegality) must be specially pleaded (Rule 2); denials must be specific, not general (Rule 3), with a heightened Commercial Courts regime (Rule 3A); evasive denials are treated as admissions (Rule 4); and — critically — any allegation not specifically denied is deemed admitted (Rule 5), with a drastic further consequence under Rule 5(2) and Rule 10 allowing the Court to pronounce judgment where no written statement is filed at all. Rules 6-6G codify set-off (a defendant's ascertained money cross-claim, treated as a plaint in a cross-suit) and counter-claim (a broader cross-claim mechanism, also treated as a plaint, that survives even if the plaintiff's suit is stayed/discontinued/dismissed). Rules 7-10 round out separate-grounds pleading, new post-institution defence grounds, subsequent pleadings requiring leave of Court, and the consequence of failing to file a called-for written statement.
essential_elements: Rule 1's 30/90/120-day written statement timeline (with the commercial-dispute 120-day hard forfeiture) is the written-statement counterpart to Order V Rule 1's summons timeline — and the second, specifically commercial-dispute, proviso forbids any further extension beyond 120 days at all (reinforced by Rule 10's own proviso).

Rule 3's specific-denial requirement, combined with Rule 5's deeming provision, means silence or vague denial of a plaint allegation is treated as an admission — one of the most consequential defaults in Indian pleading practice.

Rule 3A imposes, for Commercial Division/Commercial Court suits, a structured denial format: identify what is denied (with reasons and the defendant's own version), what is not admitted but put to proof, what is admitted, and specific statements on jurisdiction and valuation disputes.

Rule 6 lets a defendant set off an ascertained, legally recoverable sum against the plaintiff's money claim (within pecuniary jurisdiction, same character on both sides), with the set-off written statement operating exactly like a plaint in a cross-suit.

Rule 6A broadens this into counter-claim — any right or claim (not limited to ascertained money or same-character cross-claims) accruing before the defence is delivered, treated as a cross-suit plaint and surviving even if the plaintiff's own suit is stayed, discontinued, or dismissed (Rule 6D).

Rule 10 (with its added proviso) is the ultimate sanction for non-filing: the Court can pronounce judgment against a defaulting party, and no Court may extend the Rule 1 written-statement deadline at all.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Rule 5(1)'s proviso lets the Court, in its discretion, still require proof of an admitted fact rather than acting purely on the deemed admission; a second proviso ties the deeming effect specifically to Rule 3A's denial format for commercial disputes.
Rule 5's deeming provision does not operate "against a person under disability" — a protected category exempt from the admission-by-silence consequence.
Rule 8A (duty to produce documents supporting a defendant's claimed relief) was omitted by the 1999 amendment — its substance is now covered by Rule 1A.

Rule 9 requires leave of Court for any pleading subsequent to the written statement other than a reply to set-off/counter-claim, though the Court can itself call for a further written statement with up to 30 days to file it.
breakdown.how_to_read: Draft every written statement as a paragraph-by-paragraph response to the plaint using Rule 3/3A's specific-denial discipline — treat every unaddressed plaint allegation as a potential admission under Rule 5, and in commercial suits follow Rule 3A's four-way classification (deny-with-reasons / don't-admit-and-require-proof / admit / dispute-jurisdiction-or-valuation) precisely, since Commercial Courts enforce this format strictly.

sections.title: Order VIII, Rule 1 — Written Statement
sections.raw_text:
1. Written Statement.—The Defendant shall, within thirty days from the date of service of summons on him, present a written statement of his defence:
Provided that where the defendant fails to file the written statement within the said period of thirty days, he shall be allowed to file the same on such other day, as may be specified by the Court, for reasons to be recorded in writing, but which shall not be later than ninety days from the date of service of summons.
Provided that where the defendant fails to file the written statement within the said period of thirty days, he shall be allowed to file the written statement on such other day, as may be specified by the Court, for reasons to be recorded in writing and on payment of such costs as the Court deems fit, but which shall not be later than one hundred twenty days from the date of service of summons and on expiry of one hundred twenty days from the date of service of summons, the defendant shall forfeit the right to file the written statement and the Court shall not allow the written statement to be taken on record.

breakdown.plain_summary: A defendant must file his written statement within 30 days of service of summons. For ordinary suits, the Court can extend this (for recorded reasons) up to 90 days. For commercial disputes, a separate, harder regime applies: extension up to 120 days is possible (with costs), but beyond 120 days the defendant permanently forfeits the right to file a written statement at all, and the Court cannot take a late one on record.
essential_elements: Default deadline: 30 days from service of summons.
General extension: up to 90 days, for reasons recorded in writing.
Commercial-dispute extension: up to 120 days, for reasons recorded in writing and on payment of costs as the Court deems fit.
Commercial-dispute hard stop: forfeiture of the right to file beyond 120 days — the Court cannot accept a written statement filed after that.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 120-day forfeiture rule applies specifically to commercial disputes of specified value under the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 — ordinary civil suits remain governed by the 90-day extension ceiling.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is one of the most rigorously enforced timelines in Indian commercial litigation post-2015/2018 amendments — in a commercial suit, treat day 120 as an absolute, non-negotiable deadline (the Supreme Court in SCG Contracts India Pvt. Ltd. v. K.S. Chamankar Infrastructure, (2019) 12 SCC 210, held the 120-day forfeiture is mandatory and courts have no power to condone delay beyond it), so file protectively well before the outer limit rather than relying on any extension application succeeding.

sections.title: Order VIII, Rule 1A — Duty of defendant to produce documents upon which relief is claimed or relied upon by him
sections.raw_text:
1A. Duty of defendant to produce documents upon which relief is claimed or relied upon by him.—(1) Where the defendant bases his defence upon a document or relies upon any document in his possession or power, in support of his defence or claim for set-off or counter-claim, he shall enter such document in a list, and shall produce it in Court when the written statement is presented by him and shall, at the same time, deliver the document and a copy thereof, to be filed with the written statement.
(2) Where any such document is not in the possession or power of the defendant, he shall, wherever possible, state in whose possession or power it is.
(3) A document which ought to be produced in Court by the defendant under this rule, but, is not so produced shall not, without the leave of the Court, be received in evidence on his behalf at the hearing of the suit.
(4) Nothing in this rule shall apply to documents—
(a) produced for the cross-examination of the plaintiff's witnesses, or
(b) handed over to a witness merely to refresh his memory.

breakdown.plain_summary: The defendant's mirror of Order VII Rule 14: any document the defence, set-off, or counter-claim relies on, if in the defendant's possession or power, must be listed, produced, and filed (with a copy) along with the written statement. Non-disclosure bars the document from evidence absent Court leave. Cross-examination and memory-refreshing documents are exempt.
essential_elements: Sub-rule (1): mandatory listing, production, and filing of defence/set-off/counter-claim documents in the defendant's possession/power.
Sub-rule (2): where not in possession/power, state who holds it, where possible.
Sub-rule (3): non-compliance bars evidentiary use absent Court leave.
Sub-rule (4): cross-examination and memory-refreshing documents are excluded from this discipline.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The evidentiary bar in sub-rule (3) is curable with the Court's leave, not an absolute, permanent exclusion.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat document disclosure in the written statement with the same rigour as the plaint — a defence or counter-claim resting on an undisclosed document risks exclusion at trial, so build the document list simultaneously with drafting the written statement, not as an afterthought.

sections.title: Order VIII, Rule 2 — New facts must be specially pleaded
sections.raw_text: 2. New facts must be specially pleaded.—The defendant must raise by his pleading all matters which show the suit not be maintainable, or that the transaction is either void or voidable in point of law, and all such grounds of defence as, if not raised, would be likely to take the opposite party by surprise, or would raise issues of fact not arising out of the plaint, as, for instance, fraud, limitation, release, payment, performance, or facts showing illegality.

breakdown.plain_summary: Certain categories of defence cannot simply be argued at trial out of nowhere — they must be expressly pleaded in the written statement: maintainability objections, void/voidable transactions, and any defence that would otherwise ambush the plaintiff or introduce facts outside the plaint, such as fraud, limitation, release, payment, performance, or illegality.
essential_elements: Maintainability-defeating matters must be specially pleaded.
Void/voidable-in-law transaction defences must be specially pleaded.
Any surprise-risking or outside-the-plaint-facts defence (illustratively: fraud, limitation, release, payment, performance, illegality) must be specially pleaded.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The listed examples (fraud, limitation, etc.) are illustrative ("as, for instance"), not exhaustive — any defence fitting the general test of surprise or new-fact-introduction falls within this Rule even if not named.
breakdown.how_to_read: Never assume a limitation or fraud defence can be raised for the first time in arguments or evidence — if it is not specially pleaded in the written statement under this Rule, the defendant risks being barred from relying on it at all; always audit the written statement against this Rule's checklist before filing.

sections.title: Order VIII, Rule 3 — Denial to be specific
sections.raw_text: 3. Denial to be specific.—It shall not be sufficient for a defendant in his written statement to deny generally the grounds alleged by the plaintiff, but the defendant must deal specifically with each allegation of fact of which he does not admit the truth, except damages.

breakdown.plain_summary: A defendant cannot get away with a blanket, general denial of the plaint's allegations — each factual allegation not admitted must be specifically addressed and denied, one by one. The only exception is damages, which need not be specifically denied.
essential_elements: General/blanket denial is insufficient.
Each non-admitted factual allegation must be specifically dealt with.
Exception: damages need not be specifically denied.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Damages are expressly carved out — a defendant need not specifically deny the quantum of damages claimed even while specifically denying liability.
