breakdown.how_to_read: Draft the written statement paragraph-by-paragraph mirroring the plaint's own paragraph numbering, specifically admitting or denying each one — a lazily drafted "save as expressly admitted, all averments are denied" style written statement is vulnerable to the deemed-admission consequence under Rule 5.

sections.title: Order VIII, Rule 3A — Denial by the defendant in suits before the Commercial Division of the High Court or the Commercial Court
sections.raw_text:
*3A. Denial by the defendant in suits before the Commercial Division of the High Court or the Commercial Court.— (1) Denial shall be in the manner provided in sub-rules (2), (3), (4) and (5) of this Rule.
(2) The defendant in his written statement shall state which of the allegations in the particulars of plaint he denies, which allegations he is unable to admit or deny, but which he requires the plaintiff to prove, and which allegations he admits.
(3) Where the defendant denies an allegation of fact in a plaint, he must state his reasons for doing so and if he intends to put forward a different version of events from that given by the plaintiff, he must state his own version.
(4) If the defendant disputes the jurisdiction of the Court he must state the reasons for doing so, and if he is able, give his own statement as to which Court ought to have jurisdiction.
(5) If the defendant disputes the plaintiff's valuation of the suit, he must state his reasons for doing so, and if he is able, give his own statement of the value of the suit.

breakdown.plain_summary: For suits before the Commercial Division of a High Court or a Commercial Court, denial must follow a structured, four-part format: classify every plaint allegation as denied, not-admitted-and-put-to-proof, or admitted; give reasons and a counter-version for every denial; give reasons (and, if possible, the defendant's own view of the correct Court) for any jurisdiction dispute; and give reasons (and, if possible, the defendant's own valuation) for any valuation dispute.
essential_elements: Sub-rule (2): three-way classification of every plaint allegation (deny / can't admit-or-deny, require proof / admit).
Sub-rule (3): every denial needs reasons, plus the defendant's own version of events if a different account is intended.
Sub-rule (4): jurisdiction disputes need reasons and, where possible, the defendant's proposed correct Court.
Sub-rule (5): valuation disputes need reasons and, where possible, the defendant's own valuation.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This heightened regime applies only to commercial disputes of specified value under the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 — ordinary suits remain governed by Rule 3's simpler specific-denial standard.
breakdown.how_to_read: Commercial Courts enforce Rule 3A strictly as a case-management tool — draft the written statement with an explicit three-column mental model (denied-with-reasons / not-admitted-requiring-proof / admitted) for every plaint paragraph, since a written statement that merely tracks Rule 3's general specific-denial style without Rule 3A's structure risks adverse procedural treatment in a commercial suit.

sections.title: Order VIII, Rule 4 — Evasive denial
sections.raw_text: 4. Evasive-denial.—Where a defendant denies an allegation of fact in the plaint, he must not do so evasively, but answer the point of substance. Thus, if it is alleged that he received a certain sum of money, it shall not be sufficient to deny that he received that particular amount, but he must deny that he received that sum or any part thereof, or else set out how much he received. And if an allegation is made with diverse circumstances, it shall not be sufficient to deny it along with those circumstances.

breakdown.plain_summary: A denial must answer the real substance of the allegation, not dodge around it. The Code's own example: if the plaint alleges receipt of a specific sum, merely denying receipt of that exact figure is evasive — the defendant must deny receiving that sum or any part of it, or state exactly how much was received. Similarly, denying an allegation only along with its surrounding circumstantial detail, without addressing the core allegation, is insufficient.
essential_elements: Denials must address the substantive point, not just its precise technical framing.
The illustrative money example: deny the sum or any part thereof, or state the actual amount received.
Denying surrounding circumstances without denying the core allegation itself is insufficient.
breakdown.how_to_read: A classic drafting trap: denying "receipt of Rs. 10,00,000 on 1 January" without denying receipt of any lesser sum or on any other date is an evasive, Rule-4-violating denial that courts (and Rule 5's deeming provision) will likely treat as an effective admission of the substance — always deny the substance, not just the precise particulars pleaded.

sections.title: Order VIII, Rule 5 — Specific denial
sections.raw_text:
5. Specific denial.—(1) Every allegation of fact in the plaint, if not denied specifically or by necessary implication, or stated to be not admitted in the pleading of the defendant, shall be taken to be admitted except as against a person under disability:
Provided that the Court may in its discretion require any fact so admitted to be proved otherwise than by such admission:
Provided further that every allegation of fact in the plaint, if not denied in the manner provided under Rule 3A of this Order, shall be taken to be admitted except as against a person under disability.
(2) Where the defendant has not filed a pleading, it shall be lawful for the court to pronounce judgment on the basis of the facts contained in the plaint, except as against a person under a disability, but the Court may, in its discretion, require any such fact to be proved.
(3) In exercising its discretion under the proviso to sub-rule (1) or under sub-rule (2), the Court shall have due regard to the fact whether the defendant could have, or has, engaged a pleader.
(4) Whenever a judgment is pronounced under this rule, a decree shall be drawn up in accordance with such judgment and such decree shall bear the date on which the judgment was pronounced.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the sharp edge behind Rules 3-4: any plaint allegation not specifically denied (or denied by necessary implication, or stated as not admitted) is treated as admitted — except against a person under a legal disability. For commercial suits, the second proviso ties this deeming effect to Rule 3A's structured denial format specifically. If the defendant files no written statement at all, the Court can straight away pronounce judgment on the plaint's facts (again, except against a disabled person), though it retains discretion to still require proof — a discretion exercised with an eye to whether the defendant could have, or did, engage a lawyer. Any judgment under this Rule results in a decree dated the day of pronouncement.
essential_elements: Sub-rule (1): deemed admission of any non-specifically-denied, non-necessary-implication-denied, non-not-admitted allegation, except against a disabled person.
First proviso: Court discretion to still require independent proof of a deemed-admitted fact.
Second proviso: ties deemed admission to Rule 3A's format specifically for commercial-dispute written statements.
Sub-rule (2): total non-filing of a written statement lets the Court pronounce judgment on the plaint's facts, subject to the same disability exception and proof discretion.
Sub-rule (3): the Court must consider the defendant's access to/engagement of legal representation when exercising its proof-requiring discretion.
Sub-rule (4): a decree dated the pronouncement date follows automatically from a judgment under this Rule.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The entire deeming mechanism (sub-rules (1) and (2)) is expressly disapplied "against a person under disability" — minors, persons of unsound mind, and similar protected categories cannot be bound by deemed admissions from a defective or absent written statement.
breakdown.how_to_read: Rule 5 is the real teeth behind the specific-denial discipline of Rules 3-4: before filing, cross-check the written statement paragraph-by-paragraph against the plaint to ensure no allegation is left unaddressed, because an inadvertently un-denied allegation becomes a binding admission, not a mere procedural lapse — and if representing a defendant who could not afford/engage counsel, flag that explicitly, since sub-rule (3) makes it relevant to the Court's proof-discretion.

sections.title: Order VIII, Rule 6 — Particulars of set-off to be given in written statement
sections.raw_text:
6. Particulars of set-off to be given in written statement.—(1) Where in a suit for the recovery of money the defendant claims to set-off against the plaintiff's demand any ascertained sum of money legally recoverable by him from the plaintiff, not exceeding the pecuniary limits of the jurisdiction of the Court, and both parties fill the same character as they fill in the plaintiff's suit, the defendant may, at the first hearing of the suit, but not afterwards unless permitted by the Court, presents a written statement containing the particulars of the debt sought to be set-off.
(2) Effect of set-off.—The written statement shall have the same effect as a plaint in a cross-suit so as to enable the court to pronounce a final judgment in respect both of the original claim and of the set-off: but this shall not affect the lien, upon the amount decreed, of any pleader in respect of the costs payable to him under the decree.
(3) The rules relating to a written statement by a defendant apply to a written statement in answer to a claim of set-off.

Illustrations
(a) A bequeaths Rs. 2,000 to B and appoints C his executor and residuary legatee. B dies and D takes out administration to B's effects, C pays Rs, 1,000 as surety for D; then D sues C for the legacy. C cannot set-off the debt of Rs. 1,000 against the legacy, for neither C nor D fills the same character with respect to the legacy as they fill with respect to the payment of the Rs. 1,000.
(b) A dies intestate and in debt to B. C takes out administration to A's effects and B buys part of the effects from C. In a suit for the purchase-money by C against B, the latter cannot set-off the debt against the price, for C fills two different characters, one as the vendor to B, in which he sues B, and the other as representative to A.
(c) A sues B on a bill of exchange. B alleges that A has wrongfully neglected to insure B's goods and is liable to him in compensation which he claims to set-off. The amount not being ascertained cannot be set-off.
(d) A sues B on a bill of exchange for Rs. 500. B holds a judgment against A for Rs. 1,000. The two claims being both definite pecuniary demands may be set-off.
(e) A sues B for compensation on account of trespass. B hold a promissory note for Rs. 1,000 from A and claims to set-off that amount against any sum that A may recover in the suit. B may do so, for, as soon as A recovers, both sums are definite pecuniary demands.
(f) A and B sue C for Rs. 1,000. C cannot set-off a debt due to him by A alone.
(g) A sues B and C for Rs. 1,000. B cannot set-off a debt due to him alone by A.
(h) A owes the partnership firm of B and C Rs. 1,000. B dies, leaving C surviving. A sues C for a debt for Rs. 1,500 due in his separate character. C may set-off the debt of Rs. 1,000.

breakdown.plain_summary: In a money suit, a defendant can set off against the plaintiff's claim any ascertained, legally recoverable sum owed to him by the plaintiff — but only if it is within the Court's pecuniary jurisdiction and both parties occupy the same legal character in both claims. This must be pleaded at the first hearing (absent Court permission for later filing). The set-off written statement is treated exactly as a plaint in a cross-suit, letting the Court give one final judgment covering both the original claim and the set-off — without affecting any pleader's lien for costs on the decreed amount. The Illustrations work through when the "same character" requirement is (and isn't) met, and confirm set-off requires a definite, ascertained sum on both sides.
essential_elements: Must be a money suit, with the set-off being an ascertained sum (not an unliquidated/uncertain claim).
The set-off sum must be legally recoverable by the defendant from the plaintiff.
Must not exceed the Court's pecuniary jurisdiction.
Both parties must occupy the same character in both the original claim and the set-off claim.
Must ordinarily be pleaded at the first hearing, not later, absent Court permission.
Operates as a cross-suit plaint, enabling one combined final judgment.
exceptions_and_qualifications: "Legal set-off" under this Rule is distinct from "equitable set-off," which Indian courts recognise independently even for unascertained sums arising from the same transaction, outside this Rule's strict ascertained-sum/same-character/first-hearing conditions.
The set-off written statement's cross-suit effect does not disturb a pleader's lien on the decreed amount for costs owed to him.
breakdown.how_to_read: Before pleading set-off, run through all four conditions (ascertained sum, legal recoverability, pecuniary jurisdiction, same character) using the Illustrations as a template — a set-off that fails the "same character" test (as in Illustrations (a)-(b), (f)-(g)) is not salvageable under Rule 6 and may instead need to be pursued as equitable set-off or a separate suit/counter-claim.

sections.title: Order VIII, Rule 6A — Counter-claim by defendant
sections.raw_text:
6A. Counter-claim by defendant.—(1) A defendant in a suit may, in addition to his right of pleading a set-off under rule 6, set up, by way of counter-claim against the claim of the plaintiff, any right or claim in respect of a cause of action accruing to the defendant against the plaintiff either before or after the filing of the suit but before the defendant has delivered his defence or before the time limited for delivering his defence has expired, whether such counter-claim is in the nature of a claim for damages or not:
Provided that such counter-claim shall not exceed the pecuniary limits of the jurisdiction of the court.
(2) Such counter-claim shall have the same effect as a cross-suit so as to enable the Court to pronounce a final judgment in the same suit, both on the original claim and on the counter-claim.
(3) The plaintiff shall be at liberty to file a written statement in answer to the counter-claim of the defendant within such period as may be fixed by the court.
(4) The counter-claim shall be treated as a plaint and governed by the rules applicable to plaints.

breakdown.plain_summary: Beyond set-off, a defendant can bring a broader counter-claim — any right or claim against the plaintiff (damages or otherwise), arising before or after the suit was filed but before the defence was delivered (or the time for delivering it expired), as long as it stays within the Court's pecuniary jurisdiction. The counter-claim operates as a cross-suit, letting the Court decide both the original claim and the counter-claim in one final judgment; the plaintiff gets a Court-fixed period to answer it; and the counter-claim itself is treated exactly as a plaint, governed by all the ordinary plaint rules.
essential_elements: Available in addition to (not instead of) set-off under Rule 6.
Covers any right or claim, not limited to ascertained money sums (unlike set-off) — can include unliquidated damages claims.
Timing: cause of action must accrue before or after suit-filing, but before the defence is delivered or the time for delivering it expires.
Must not exceed the Court's pecuniary jurisdiction (proviso).
Operates as a cross-suit for a combined final judgment; treated as a plaint for all procedural purposes.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The timing window is tied to delivery of the defence, not merely to filing of the suit — a cause of action accruing after the written statement is filed falls outside Rule 6A and would need a separate suit instead.
breakdown.how_to_read: Counter-claim is strategically broader and more flexible than set-off (no "same character" or "ascertained sum" restriction) and is often the better route where the defendant has an independent, even unliquidated, claim against the plaintiff — but always check the accrual-timing window against the defence-delivery deadline before relying on it, since a late-accruing claim cannot be shoehorned into an already-filed written statement as a Rule 6A counter-claim.

sections.title: Order VIII, Rule 6B — Counter-claim to be stated
sections.raw_text: 6B. Counter-claim to be stated.—Where any defendant seeks to rely upon any ground as supporting a right of counter-claim, he shall, in his written statement, state specifically that he does so by way of counter-claim.

breakdown.plain_summary: A defendant relying on a ground as a counter-claim must say so explicitly in the written statement — it must be clearly flagged as a counter-claim, not left to be inferred from the general defence narrative.
essential_elements: Mandatory explicit labelling of a ground as a counter-claim in the written statement.
breakdown.how_to_read: Draft a distinct, clearly headed "Counter-claim" section in the written statement (with its own cause-of-action narrative and prayer) rather than burying counter-claim allegations within the general defence — ambiguity here risks the claim not being recognised or processed as a counter-claim at all.

sections.title: Order VIII, Rule 6C — Exclusion of counter-claim
sections.raw_text: 6C. Exclusion of counter-claim.—Where a defendant sets up a counter-claim and the plaintiff contends that the claim thereby raised ought not to be disposed of by way of counter-claim but in an independent suit, the plaintiff may, at any time before issues are settled in relation to the counter-claim, apply to the Court for an order that such counter-claim may be excluded, and the Court may, on the hearing of such application make such order as it thinks fit.

breakdown.plain_summary: If the plaintiff believes a defendant's counter-claim shouldn't be tried along with the main suit and should instead be pursued as a separate, independent suit, the plaintiff can apply to exclude it — but only before issues are settled on the counter-claim. The Court then has full discretion on how to dispose of that application.
essential_elements: Available only to the plaintiff.
Must be applied for before issues are settled on the counter-claim.
Court's order on the application is discretionary ("as it thinks fit").
exceptions_and_qualifications: The window closes once issues are settled on the counter-claim — a plaintiff who delays past that point loses the ability to seek exclusion under this specific Rule.
breakdown.how_to_read: If a counter-claim genuinely raises an unrelated, complex, or inconvenient set of issues that would derail the main suit, move promptly under Rule 6C before issues are framed — waiting past the issue-settlement stage forecloses this particular remedy.

sections.title: Order VIII, Rule 6D — Effect of discontinuance of suit
sections.raw_text: 6D. Effect of discontinuance of suit.—If in any case in which the defendant sets up a counterclaim, the suit of the plaintiff is stayed, discontinued or dismissed, the counter-claim may nevertheless be proceeded with.

breakdown.plain_summary: A counter-claim has independent life: even if the plaintiff's own suit is stayed, discontinued, or dismissed, the defendant's counter-claim can still proceed to its own conclusion.
essential_elements: Counter-claim survives stay, discontinuance, or dismissal of the plaintiff's suit.
breakdown.how_to_read: This independence is a key strategic advantage of counter-claim over set-off — a defendant with a strong independent claim should consider pleading it as a counter-claim specifically because it will survive even if the plaintiff later abandons or loses the main suit, unlike a purely defensive set-off which is more tightly tied to the original claim's survival.

sections.title: Order VIII, Rule 6E — Default of plaintiff to reply to counter-claim
sections.raw_text: 6E. Default of plaintiff to reply to counter-claim.—If the plaintiff makes default in putting in a reply to the counter-claim made by the defendant, the Court may pronounce judgment against the plaintiff in relation to the counter-claim made against him, or make such order in relation to the counter-claim as it thinks fit.

breakdown.plain_summary: If the plaintiff fails to file a reply to the defendant's counter-claim, the Court can pronounce judgment against the plaintiff on the counter-claim, or make whatever other order it considers appropriate.
essential_elements: Plaintiff's default in replying to a counter-claim can lead to judgment against the plaintiff on that counter-claim.
Court retains discretion to make any other appropriate order instead.
breakdown.how_to_read: A plaintiff facing a counter-claim must treat the Court-fixed reply deadline (under Rule 6A(3)) with the same seriousness as a defendant treats the original written-statement deadline — default here mirrors the Rule 5/Rule 10 consequences on the other side of the suit.

sections.title: Order VIII, Rule 6F — Relief to defendant where counter-claim succeeds
sections.raw_text: 6F. Relief to defendant where counter-claim succeeds.—Where in any suit a set-off or counter-claim is established as a defence against the plaintiff's claim and any balance is found due to the plaintiff or the defendant, as the case may be, the Court may give judgment to the party entitled to such balance.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where a set-off or counter-claim succeeds as a defence and, after netting the original claim against it, a balance is found owing to either side, the Court can give judgment in favour of whichever party is actually entitled to that net balance — including the defendant, if the balance tips in his favour.
essential_elements: Applies once a set-off or counter-claim is established as a defence.
The Court nets the original claim against the set-off/counter-claim to find the balance.
Judgment follows the balance, in favour of plaintiff or defendant as the net result dictates.
breakdown.how_to_read: A successful counter-claim or set-off is not just a shield that defeats the plaintiff's claim — it can be a sword that produces an affirmative money decree in the defendant's favour if the net balance favours the defendant; frame the written statement's prayer clause to expressly seek this affirmative relief, not just dismissal of the suit.

sections.title: Order VIII, Rule 6G — Rules relating to written statement to apply
sections.raw_text: 6G. Rules relating to written statement to apply.—The rules relating to a written statement by a defendant shall apply to a written statement filed in answer to a counter-claim.

breakdown.plain_summary: The plaintiff's written statement in reply to a defendant's counter-claim is itself governed by all the same Order VIII rules that apply to an ordinary written statement (specific denial, document production, etc.).
essential_elements: Applies the entire Order VIII framework (specific denial, Rule 1A document duties, etc.) to the plaintiff's reply to a counter-claim.
breakdown.how_to_read: When drafting a plaintiff's reply to a counter-claim, apply the exact same specific-denial and document-disclosure discipline (Rules 1A, 3, 3A, 4, 5) used in an ordinary written statement — treating the reply casually risks the same deemed-admission consequences under Rule 5 that a defendant would face.

sections.title: Order VIII, Rule 7 — Defence or set-off founded upon separate grounds
sections.raw_text: 7. Defence or set-off founded upon separate grounds.—Where the defendant relies upon several distinct grounds of defence or set-off or counter-claim founded upon separate and distinct facts, they shall be stated, as far as may be, separately and distinctly.

breakdown.plain_summary: Just as Order VII Rule 8 requires a plaintiff to separate distinct causes of action, this Rule requires a defendant relying on multiple distinct grounds of defence, set-off, or counter-claim founded on separate facts to state each ground separately and distinctly, as far as practicable.
essential_elements: Requires separate, distinct pleading of each distinct ground of defence/set-off/counter-claim founded on separate facts.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Qualified by "as far as may be" — the same practical flexibility as Order VII Rule 8.
breakdown.how_to_read: Structure a written statement raising multiple independent defences (e.g., limitation AND no cause of action AND a counter-claim) with clearly separated, labelled sections for each — a muddled, undifferentiated written statement invites confusion in framing issues later.

sections.title: Order VIII, Rule 8 — New ground of defence
sections.raw_text: 8. New ground of defence.—Any ground of defence which has arisen after the institution of the suit or the presentation of a written statement claiming a set-off or counter-claim may be raised by the defendant or plaintiff, as the case may be, in his written statement.

breakdown.plain_summary: A ground of defence that arises only after the suit was filed, or after a set-off/counter-claim written statement was presented, can still be raised — by either the defendant (in defence) or the plaintiff (replying to a set-off/counter-claim) — in their written statement.
essential_elements: Covers grounds arising after suit institution.
Covers grounds arising after presentation of a set-off/counter-claim written statement.
Available to both defendant and plaintiff (reciprocally, depending on who is responding to what).
breakdown.how_to_read: If a defence-relevant event occurs mid-suit (e.g., a subsequent payment, a later-arising limitation point, a post-filing settlement), this Rule confirms there is no need for a wholly separate proceeding — plead it via an appropriate written statement, subject to the Court's leave requirements under Rule 9 for subsequent pleadings where applicable.

sections.title: Order VIII, Rule 9 — Subsequent pleadings
sections.raw_text: 9. Subsequent pleadings.—No pleading subsequent to the written statement of a defendant other than by way of defence to set-off or counter-claim shall be presented except by the leave of the Court and upon such terms as the Court thinks fit; but the Court may at any time require a written statement or additional written statement from any of the parties and fix a time of not more than thirty days for presenting the same.

breakdown.plain_summary: Beyond the plaint and written statement (and a reply to set-off/counter-claim), no further pleading can be filed without the Court's leave and on whatever terms the Court sets. But the Court itself retains the power to call for a written statement or additional written statement from any party at any time, giving up to 30 days to file it.
essential_elements: Default bar: no further pleadings beyond plaint/written statement/set-off-counter-claim reply, without leave.
Leave is discretionary and can come with terms the Court thinks fit.
Court's own power to call for (additional) written statements at any time, with a maximum 30-day window.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The leave requirement does not apply to a defence to set-off or counter-claim — that reply is treated as part of the ordinary pleading sequence, not a "subsequent pleading" needing special leave.
breakdown.how_to_read: Resist the temptation to file a replication or rejoinder as of right — under this Rule it requires the Court's leave, so any additional pleading beyond the basic plaint/written statement/counter-claim-reply sequence should be sought by a specific, justified application rather than filed unilaterally.

sections.title: Order VIII, Rule 10 — Procedure when party fails to present written statement called for by Court
sections.raw_text:
10. Procedure when party fails to present written statement called for by Court.—Where any party from whom a written statement is required under rule 1 or rule 9 fails to present the same within the time permitted or fixed by the Court, as the case may be, the Court shall pronounce judgment against him, or make such order in relation to the suit as it thinks fit and on the pronouncement of such judgment a decree shall be drawn up:
Provided further that no Court shall make an order to extend the time provided under Rule 1 of this Order for filing of the written statement.

breakdown.plain_summary: If a party required to file a written statement under Rule 1 or Rule 9 misses the permitted/fixed deadline, the Court can pronounce judgment against that party (with a resulting decree) or make any other order it considers fit for the suit. The added proviso makes clear that, once Rule 1's deadlines are exhausted, no Court can grant any further extension of time to file the written statement.
essential_elements: Applies to both the initial written statement (Rule 1) and any Court-called-for (additional) written statement (Rule 9).
Consequence of default: judgment against the defaulting party, or any other order the Court thinks fit, with a decree following any such judgment.
Proviso: an absolute bar on further extending Rule 1's written-statement filing time.
exceptions_and_qualifications: "Make such order... as it thinks fit" preserves some judicial flexibility short of outright judgment — not every default automatically ends in adverse judgment, though that is the headline consequence.
breakdown.how_to_read: Rule 10's proviso is the final enforcement mechanism behind Rule 1's 30/90/120-day scheme — once the applicable outer limit passes, there is no further room to argue for an extension, so defendants (and their counsel) should treat these deadlines as genuinely final rather than negotiable, particularly in commercial disputes where the Supreme Court has confirmed the 120-day limit is mandatory.

sections.title: Order IX — Appearance of Parties and Consequence of Non-appearance (Overview)
sections.raw_text:
ORDER IX
Appearance of parties and consequence of non-appearance

This Order governs what happens on the first and subsequent hearing dates depending on who shows up: dismissal where neither party appears, ex-parte hearing where only the plaintiff appears, dismissal (with a bar on fresh suit) where only the defendant appears, the procedure for multiple plaintiffs/defendants with partial non-appearance, and — in its final, heavily litigated segment — the grounds and procedure for setting aside an ex-parte decree.

breakdown.plain_summary: Order IX is the Code's complete regime for hearing-date attendance consequences. Rule 1 requires both parties' attendance on the fixed date. Rules 2-5 deal with dismissal: for the plaintiff's failure to pay service costs or supply plaint copies (Rule 2), for both parties' non-appearance (Rule 3, with a fresh-suit/restoration remedy under Rule 4), and for the plaintiff's failure to apply for fresh summons within seven days of an unserved summons being returned (Rule 5). Rules 6-8 cover one-sided appearance: if only the plaintiff appears, the suit may proceed ex parte (duly served), get a second summons issued (not duly served), or be postponed (served late) under Rule 6, with Rule 7 letting a defendant who shows good cause for earlier non-appearance be heard as if he had appeared originally; if only the defendant appears, the suit is dismissed (Rule 8) — and, critically, Rule 9 bars a fresh suit on that dismissal (subject to a restoration application on sufficient cause, unlike Rule 4's dismissal under Rules 2/3). Rules 10-12 handle multiple parties and personal-appearance defaults. Rules 13-14 are the ex-parte-decree-setting-aside code: Rule 13 lets a defendant apply to set aside an ex-parte decree on proof of improper summons service or sufficient cause for non-appearance, subject to a proviso barring relief for mere service irregularity where the defendant had actual notice and time to appear, and an Explanation barring a fresh Rule 13 application once an appeal against the ex-parte decree has been decided on merits.
essential_elements: Rule 3/4: dismissal for both-parties non-appearance is freely reversible — the plaintiff may either bring a fresh suit (subject to limitation) or apply to restore the dismissed suit on sufficient cause.

Rule 5: an unserved summons returned to Court starts a seven-day clock for the plaintiff to apply for fresh summons, with dismissal against that defendant as the default consequence, extendable only on best-endeavours-to-discover-residence, evasion-of-service, or other sufficient cause.

Rule 6(1)(a)-(c): the three-way fork when only the plaintiff appears — ex-parte hearing if duly served, fresh summons if not duly served, and postponement with notice if served but not in time — with Rule 6(2) shifting postponement costs onto a defaulting plaintiff.

Rule 8/9: dismissal for the plaintiff's own non-appearance (defendant alone appears) is harsher than Rules 2/3/4 — it bars a fresh suit on the same cause of action outright, leaving only a restoration application (on notice to the defendant and proof of sufficient cause) as the remedy, not a free choice of fresh suit.

Rule 13 is the master ex-parte-decree-setting-aside provision: grounds are (i) summons not duly served, or (ii) sufficient cause prevented appearance at the hearing — but the second proviso bars relief for a mere service irregularity if the defendant in fact had notice of the hearing date and sufficient time to appear.

Rule 13's Explanation: once an appeal against the ex-parte decree has been disposed of on a ground other than withdrawal, no Rule 13 application to set aside that same decree lies at all — the appellate remedy and the Rule 13 remedy are mutually exclusive once the appeal is decided on merits.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Rule 2's dismissal (for plaintiff's cost/copy default) does not apply if the defendant nonetheless attends in person or by agent on the fixed day, despite the plaintiff's default.

Rule 9(1)'s fresh-suit bar for plaintiff-non-appearance dismissal has its own carve-out: if the defendant had admitted the claim (in whole or part) before the plaintiff's non-appearance, the Court decrees on that admission instead of dismissing (back-reference to Rule 8 itself).

Rule 13's proviso on multi-defendant decrees: where an ex-parte decree's nature prevents setting it aside against only the applicant-defendant, it may be set aside against all or any of the other defendants too.
breakdown.how_to_read: The single most consequential distinction in this Order is between a Rule 3/4 dismissal (freely curable by fresh suit or restoration) and a Rule 8/9 dismissal (fresh suit barred, restoration-only) — always check which Rule a dismissal order was actually passed under before advising a client on next steps, and for ex-parte decree applications under Rule 13, build the application around either a genuine service defect or a concrete, evidenced sufficient-cause narrative for non-appearance, since the second proviso has hardened courts' willingness to excuse mere technical service irregularities where actual notice is shown.

sections.title: Order IX, Rule 1 — Parties to appear on day fixed in summons for defendant to appear and answer
sections.raw_text: 1. Parties to appear on day fixed in summons for defendant to appear and answer.—On the day fixed in the summons for the defendant to appear and answer, the parties shall be in attendance at the Court-house in person or by their respective pleaders, and the suit shall then be heard unless the hearing is adjourned to a future day fixed by the Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: On the date fixed by the summons, both parties (personally or through their pleaders/advocates) must attend Court, and the suit proceeds to hearing that day unless the Court adjourns it to a future date.
essential_elements: Mandatory attendance (in person or through a pleader) on the summons-fixed date.
Default is that the suit is heard that day, subject to the Court's adjournment power.
breakdown.how_to_read: This Rule sets the baseline expectation — the rest of Order IX is essentially a catalogue of what happens when one or both parties fail to meet this basic attendance requirement.

sections.title: Order IX, Rule 2 — Dismissal of suit where summons not served in consequence of plaintiff's failure to pay costs
sections.raw_text:
2. Dismissal of suit where summons not served in consequence of plaintiff's failure to pay costs.—Where on the day so fixed it is found that summons has not been served upon the defendant in consequence of the failure of the plaintiff to pay the court-fee or postal charges, if any, chargeable for such service, or failure to present copies of the plaint as required by rule 9 of Order VII, the Court may make an order that the suit be dismissed:
Provided that no such order shall be made, if notwithstanding such failure, the defendant attends in person or by agent when he is allowed to appear by agent on the day fixed for him to appear and answer.

breakdown.plain_summary: If, on the fixed date, summons was never served on the defendant purely because the plaintiff failed to pay the required court-fee/postal charges or failed to supply plaint copies under Order VII Rule 9, the Court can dismiss the suit — unless the defendant shows up anyway (in person or, where permitted, by agent) on that date despite the plaintiff's default.
essential_elements: Triggered by plaintiff's own default in payment or supplying copies, causing non-service.
Dismissal is discretionary ("may"), not automatic.
Proviso bars dismissal if the defendant attends anyway despite the service failure.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The proviso is a complete bar on dismissal where the defendant's actual attendance has cured any prejudice from the plaintiff's default.
breakdown.how_to_read: A plaintiff's own administrative lapse (unpaid service costs, missing plaint copies) can doom the suit at the very first hearing — make payment of court-fees/postal charges and timely supply of plaint copies under Order VII Rule 9 a tracked compliance item immediately after the plaint is admitted.

sections.title: Order IX, Rule 3 — Where neither party appears suit to be dismissed
sections.raw_text: 3. Where neither party appears suit to be dismissed.—Where neither party appears when the suit is called on for hearing, the court may make an order that the suit be dismissed.

breakdown.plain_summary: If, when the suit is called for hearing, neither the plaintiff nor the defendant appears, the Court can dismiss the suit.
essential_elements: Both parties' non-appearance triggers discretionary dismissal.
breakdown.how_to_read: A dismissal under this Rule is curable under Rule 4 (fresh suit or restoration) — if this happens, advise the client promptly on which route (fresh suit, subject to limitation, or a restoration application on sufficient cause) is more advantageous.

sections.title: Order IX, Rule 4 — Plaintiff may bring fresh suit or Court may restore suit to file
sections.raw_text: 4. Plaintiff may bring fresh suit or Court may restore suit to file.—Where a suit is dismissed under rule 2 or rule 3, the plaintiff may (subject to the law of limitation) bring a fresh suit; or he may apply for an order to set the dismissal aside, and if he satisfies the Court that there was sufficient cause for such failure as is referred to in rule 2, or for his non-appearance, as the case may be, the Court shall make an order setting aside the dismissal and shall appoint a day for proceeding with the suit.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where a suit was dismissed under Rule 2 (plaintiff's payment/copy default) or Rule 3 (neither party appeared), the plaintiff has a choice: file a fresh suit (subject to limitation), or apply to restore the dismissed suit by showing sufficient cause for the original default or non-appearance — restoration is mandatory ("shall") once sufficient cause is shown.
essential_elements: Available only for Rule 2/Rule 3 dismissals (not Rule 8/9 dismissals).
Plaintiff's choice: fresh suit (subject to limitation) OR restoration application.
Restoration is mandatory once sufficient cause is shown to the Court's satisfaction.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Restoration is conditional on proving sufficient cause — not an automatic right merely by applying.
breakdown.how_to_read: A Rule 2/3 dismissal is genuinely low-stakes compared to a Rule 8/9 dismissal — the plaintiff retains a real choice of remedies, so weigh limitation exposure (favouring restoration, which relates back) against the practical ease of simply refiling where limitation is not a concern.

sections.title: Order IX, Rule 5 — Dismissal of suit where plaintiff, after summons returned unserved, fails for seven days to apply for fresh summons
sections.raw_text:
5. Dismissal of suit where plaintiff after summons returned unserved, fails for seven days to apply for fresh summons.—(1) Where after a summons has been issued to the defendant, or to one of several defendants, and returned unserved, the plaintiff fails, for a period of seven days from the date of the return made to the Court by the officer ordinarily certifying to the Court returns made by the serving officers, to apply for the issue of a fresh summons the Court shall make an order that the suit be dismissed as against such defendant, unless the plaintiff has within the said period satisfied the Court that—
(a) he has failed after using his best endeavours to discover the residence of the defendant, who has not been served, or
(b) such defendant is avoiding service of process, or
(c) there is any other sufficient cause for extending the time,
in which case the Court may extend the time for making such application for such period as it thinks fit.
(2) In such case the plaintiff may (subject to the law of limitation) bring a fresh suit.

breakdown.plain_summary: If a summons returns unserved and the plaintiff doesn't apply for a fresh summons within seven days of the return being certified to the Court, the suit is dismissed against that defendant — unless the plaintiff satisfies the Court, within that seven-day window, that he made best efforts to find the defendant's residence, that the defendant is evading service, or that some other sufficient cause justifies more time, in which case the Court can extend the time as it sees fit. A plaintiff whose suit is dismissed this way can still bring a fresh suit, subject to limitation.
essential_elements: Seven-day clock runs from the officer's certified return of the unserved summons.
Default consequence: dismissal against that defendant for the plaintiff's inaction.
Three alternative escape routes within the seven days: best-endeavours-but-couldn't-find-residence; defendant evading service; or other sufficient cause — any of which lets the Court extend time.
Sub-rule (2): dismissal under this Rule leaves fresh suit open, subject to limitation.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The time extension itself is discretionary ("may") even once one of the three grounds is shown — it is not an automatic entitlement.
breakdown.how_to_read: Diary the seven-day deadline the moment a summons return report shows non-service — a plaintiff's counsel should proactively seek an extension (documenting best-efforts-to-locate or evasion evidence) well within the window rather than waiting for dismissal and then relying on the fresh-suit fallback, which restarts cost and delay.

sections.title: Order IX, Rule 6 — Procedure when only plaintiff appears

breakdown.plain_summary: If only the plaintiff appears at the hearing, the outcome turns entirely on the state of service: duly served summons lets the Court proceed ex parte against the defendant; summons not proved duly served requires a second summons; and summons served but too late to allow the defendant time to prepare requires postponement with fresh notice to the defendant. If the plaintiff's own default caused the bad/late service, the plaintiff bears the postponement costs.
essential_elements: Three-way fork based purely on proof of service status: duly served -> ex parte order possible; not duly served -> second summons mandatory; served but too late -> postponement mandatory, with notice to defendant.
Ex-parte order under (a) is discretionary ("may"); the other two outcomes are mandatory ("shall").
Sub-rule (2): plaintiff-caused service defects shift the postponement costs onto the plaintiff.
breakdown.how_to_read: Before seeking an ex-parte order under Rule 6(1)(a), be ready to affirmatively prove due service (the process-server's report, affidavit of service, or equivalent) — an ex-parte decree built on service that later turns out not to have been "duly" proved is exactly the fact pattern Rule 13 applications are built to unwind.

sections.title: Order IX, Rule 7 — Procedure where defendant appears on day of adjourned hearing and assigns good cause for previous non-appearance
sections.raw_text: 7. Procedure where defendant appears on day of adjourned hearing and assigns good cause for previous non-appearance.—Where the Court has adjourned the hearing of the suit, ex parte, and the defendant, at or before such hearing appears and assigns good cause for his previous non-appearance, he may, upon such terms as the Court directs as to costs or otherwise, be heard in answer to the suit as if he had appeared on the day fixed for his appearance.

breakdown.plain_summary: If a suit has been proceeding ex parte and, before or at the adjourned hearing, the defendant shows up and gives good cause for his earlier absence, the Court can let him back into the suit — to answer as though he had appeared on the original date — on whatever terms (usually costs) the Court sets.
essential_elements: Available where the suit is already proceeding ex parte, before or at an adjourned hearing.
Requires the defendant to assign good cause for the earlier non-appearance.
Re-entry is on terms the Court directs (typically costs).
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a cheaper, faster route back into the suit than a full Rule 13 ex-parte-decree-setting-aside application — a defendant who realises he missed a hearing should move under Rule 7 immediately, before any ex-parte decree is actually passed, rather than waiting and later needing the heavier Rule 13 machinery.

sections.title: Order IX, Rule 8 — Procedure where defendant only appears
sections.raw_text: 8. Procedure where defendant only appears.—Where the defendant appears and the plaintiff does not appear when the suit is called on for hearing, the Court shall make an order that the suit be dismissed, unless the defendant admits the claim, or part thereof, in which case the Court shall pass a decree against the defendant upon such admission, and where part only of the claim has been admitted, shall dismiss the suit so far as it relates to the remainder.

breakdown.plain_summary: If only the defendant appears (plaintiff absent) at the hearing, the suit is dismissed — unless the defendant admits the claim (wholly or partly), in which case the Court decrees on the admitted portion and dismisses the rest.
essential_elements: Default consequence: mandatory dismissal of the suit for plaintiff's non-appearance.
Exception: defendant's admission (full or partial) converts the outcome to a decree on the admitted part, with dismissal only of the un-admitted remainder.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The defendant's voluntary admission is the sole escape from outright dismissal — absent an admission, dismissal under this Rule is mandatory ("shall"), not discretionary.
breakdown.how_to_read: Unlike Rule 3's discretionary dismissal for both-parties absence, Rule 8's dismissal for plaintiff-only-absence is mandatory and — per Rule 9 — much harder to undo, so plaintiffs and their counsel must treat hearing-date attendance (personally or through a diligent pleader) as non-negotiable.

sections.title: Order IX, Rule 9 — Decree against plaintiff by default bars fresh suit
sections.raw_text:
9. Decree against plaintiff by default bars fresh suit.—(1) Where a suit is wholly or partly dismissed under rule 8, the plaintiff shall be precluded from bringing a fresh suit in respect of the same cause of action. But he may apply for an order to set the dismissal aside, and if he satisfies the Court that there was sufficient cause for his non-appearance when the suit was called on for hearing, the Court shall make an order setting aside the dismissal upon such terms as to costs or otherwise as it thinks fit, and shall appoint a day for proceeding with the suit.
(2) No order shall be made under this rule unless notice of the application has been served on the opposite party.

breakdown.plain_summary: A Rule 8 dismissal (for the plaintiff's own non-appearance) is harsher than a Rule 2/3 dismissal: the plaintiff is barred outright from filing a fresh suit on the same cause of action. The only remedy is a restoration application, which succeeds (mandatorily) if the plaintiff proves sufficient cause for the non-appearance — but no restoration order can be made without notice to the defendant.
essential_elements: Fresh suit on the same cause of action is barred outright — no fallback option as under Rule 4.
Sole remedy: restoration application, granted mandatorily ("shall") on proof of sufficient cause.
Restoration comes on such terms as to costs or otherwise as the Court thinks fit.
Sub-rule (2): mandatory notice to the opposite party before any restoration order — no ex-parte restoration.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Unlike Rule 4 (which gives a genuine fresh-suit choice for Rule 2/3 dismissals), Rule 9's bar is absolute for the cause of action — restoration is the only door back in.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the single biggest practical reason plaintiffs' counsel must never skip a hearing date without an adjournment on record — a Rule 8 dismissal converts a procedural lapse into a potential complete loss of the cause of action if a sufficient-cause restoration application later fails, which Rule 4's more forgiving regime does not risk.

sections.title: Order IX, Rule 10 — Procedure in case of non-attendance of one or more of several plaintiffs
sections.raw_text: 10. Procedure in case of non-attendance of one or more of several plaintiffs.—Where there are more plaintiffs than one, and one or more of them appear, and the others do not appear, the Court may, at the instance of the plaintiff or plaintiffs appearing, permit the suit to proceed in the same way as if all the plaintiffs had appeared, or make such order as it thinks fit.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where there are several plaintiffs and only some appear, the Court can — at the request of the appearing plaintiff(s) — let the suit proceed as though everyone had appeared, or make whatever other order it thinks appropriate.
essential_elements: Applies specifically to multi-plaintiff suits with partial attendance.
Court has discretion to let the suit proceed as if all appeared, or make any other suitable order, at the appearing plaintiffs' instance.
breakdown.how_to_read: In multi-plaintiff suits, the appearing plaintiffs should proactively seek an order under this Rule to keep the suit moving rather than risk the suit's progress being held hostage by one absent co-plaintiff.

sections.title: Order IX, Rule 11 — Procedure in case of non-attendance of one or more of several defendants
sections.raw_text: 11. Procedure in case of non-attendance of one or more of several defendants.—Where there are more defendants than one, and one or more of them appear, and the others do not appear, the suit shall proceed, and the Court shall, at the time of pronouncing judgment, make such order as it thinks fit with respect to the defendants who do not appear.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where there are several defendants and only some appear, the suit simply proceeds regardless — the Court deals with the consequences for the non-appearing defendants only later, at the time of pronouncing judgment, in whatever manner it thinks fit.
essential_elements: Suit proceeds automatically despite partial defendant non-appearance (no separate order needed to continue, unlike Rule 10's plaintiff-side mechanism).
Consequences for absent defendants are deferred to judgment, decided as the Court thinks fit at that stage.
breakdown.how_to_read: Unlike the plaintiff-side Rule 10 (which requires an affirmative order to proceed), Rule 11 makes continuation automatic on the defendant side — but this means the practical consequences for an absent co-defendant remain genuinely open until judgment, so an absent defendant should not assume inaction is risk-free merely because the suit didn't immediately get dismissed or proceed ex parte against him specifically.

sections.title: Order IX, Rule 12 — Consequence of non-attendance, without sufficient cause shown, of party ordered to appear in person
sections.raw_text: 12. Consequence of non-attendance, without sufficient cause shown, of party ordered to appear in person.—Where a plaintiff or defendant, who has been ordered to appear in person, does not appear in person, or show sufficient cause to the satisfaction of the court for failing so to appear, he shall be subject to all provisions of the foregoing rules applicable to plaintiffs and defendants, respectively who do not appear.

breakdown.plain_summary: If a party was specifically ordered to appear in person (under Order V Rules 3-4, for instance) and fails to do so without showing sufficient cause, that party is treated exactly as if they hadn't appeared at all — subjecting them to all the ordinary non-appearance consequences of this Order.
essential_elements: Applies specifically where a personal-appearance order was made.
Failure to comply (without sufficient cause) triggers the full range of ordinary non-appearance consequences under this Order.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Showing sufficient cause for the personal non-appearance is the escape valve — a party who can justify it is not automatically treated as a non-appearing party.
breakdown.how_to_read: A personal-appearance order should never be treated as optional merely because the party's pleader is present — appearing only through counsel when personal appearance was specifically ordered risks the same dismissal/ex-parte consequences as not appearing at all.

sections.title: Order IX, Rule 13 — Setting aside decree ex parte against defendant
sections.raw_text:
13. Setting aside decree ex parte against defendant.—In any case in which a decree is passed ex parte against a defendant, he may apply to the Court by which the decree was passed for an order to set it aside; and if he satisfies the Court that the summons was not duly served, or that he was prevented by any sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing, the Court shall make an order setting aside the decree as against him upon such terms as to costs, payment into Court or otherwise as it thinks fit, and shall appoint a day for proceeding with the suit:
Provided that where the decree is of such a nature that it cannot be set aside as against such defendant only it may be set aside as against all or any of the other defendants also:
Provided further than no Court shall set aside a decree passed ex parte merely on the ground that there has been an irregularity in the service of summons, if it is satisfied that the defendant had notice of the date of hearing and had sufficient time to appear and answer the plaintiff's claim.
Explanation.—Where there has been an appeal against a decree passed ex parte under this rule, and the appeal has been disposed of on any ground other than the ground that the appellant has withdrawn the appeal, no application shall lie under this rule for setting aside that ex parte decree.

breakdown.plain_summary: A defendant against whom an ex-parte decree has been passed can apply to the very same Court to set it aside, on one of two grounds: the summons was not duly served, or sufficient cause prevented appearance at the hearing. If satisfied, the Court must set the decree aside (on whatever terms as to costs/payment into Court it thinks fit) and fix a new hearing date — and if the decree can't be set aside against just this defendant alone (because of its nature), it can be set aside against all or any co-defendants too. But the second proviso hardens this: a mere service irregularity is not enough to set aside the decree if the defendant actually had notice of the hearing date and sufficient time to appear and answer. And the Explanation closes the door entirely once an appeal against the same ex-parte decree has been decided on any ground other than withdrawal — no Rule 13 application can then be filed.
essential_elements: Two independent grounds: (i) summons not duly served; (ii) sufficient cause prevented appearance at the hearing.
Relief is mandatory ("shall") once either ground is satisfactorily shown — subject to the two provisos.
First proviso: multi-defendant decrees of an inseverable nature can be set aside against all/any defendants, not just the applicant.
Second proviso: bars relief for a mere service irregularity where the defendant actually had notice of the hearing date and sufficient time to respond.
Explanation: once an appeal against the same ex-parte decree is disposed of on merits (any ground other than withdrawal), no Rule 13 application lies at all.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The second proviso is itself an exception that narrows the "summons not duly served" ground — technical irregularity alone is insufficient if actual notice and sufficient time are shown.

The Explanation's bar does not apply where the appeal was disposed of specifically on the ground of withdrawal — an appellant who withdraws the appeal can still potentially pursue a Rule 13 application.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is one of the most frequently litigated provisions in the Code — build a Rule 13 application around concrete, documented facts (process-server discrepancies, medical/travel sufficient-cause evidence) rather than bare assertions, since the second proviso means courts increasingly look past technical service defects to ask whether the defendant genuinely knew and had time to respond; and always check first whether an appeal against the same ex-parte decree has already been filed and decided, since the Explanation can extinguish the Rule 13 route entirely.

sections.title: Order IX, Rule 14 — No decree to be set aside without notice to opposite party
sections.raw_text: 14. No decree to be set aside without notice to opposite party.—No decree shall be set aside on any such application as aforesaid unless notice thereof has been served on the opposite party.

breakdown.plain_summary: An ex-parte decree cannot be set aside under Rule 13 unless the plaintiff (the opposite party) has first been served notice of the setting-aside application — the same natural-justice safeguard that Rule 9(2) applies to restoration of a plaintiff-default dismissal.
essential_elements: Mandatory notice to the opposite party before any order setting aside a decree under this Order.
breakdown.how_to_read: Always confirm proof of notice/service on the opposite party is on record before expecting a Rule 13 application to be decided — an order setting aside a decree without this notice is itself vulnerable to challenge for violating this mandatory safeguard.

sections.title: Order X — Examination of Parties by the Court (Overview)
sections.raw_text:
ORDER X
Examination of parties by the court

This short but pivotal Order governs the first hearing's admission/denial exercise, the mandatory direction to attempt Section 89 alternative dispute resolution, the Court's power to orally examine parties (and their accompanying knowledgeable persons) to narrow the real controversy, the requirement that such examination be recorded, and the consequence when a pleader cannot answer a material question that only the party personally could answer.

breakdown.plain_summary: Order X operationalises the first hearing as a genuine issue-narrowing exercise, not a formality. Rule 1 requires the Court to go through the plaint and written statement allegation by allegation, asking each party or pleader to admit or deny what hasn't already been expressly or impliedly admitted/denied, and record the result. Rules 1A-1C then mandate that, once admissions and denials are recorded, the Court must direct the parties to choose one of the Section 89 ADR modes (arbitration, conciliation, judicial settlement, Lok Adalat, or mediation), send them to that forum, and — if conciliation efforts fail — have the matter referred back for continuation before the Court. Rule 2 empowers (and partly mandates) oral examination of parties present in Court, and even of any knowledgeable person accompanying a party or pleader, to elucidate the matters genuinely in controversy, with the Court free to put either party's suggested questions. Rule 3 requires the substance of any such examination to be reduced to writing as part of the record. Rule 4 addresses the scenario where a pleader cannot answer a material question that the party personally could likely answer: the Court may postpone the hearing (up to seven days) and order personal appearance, with judgment or any suitable order available against a party who then fails to appear without lawful excuse.
essential_elements: Rule 1's admission/denial exercise is mandatory at the first hearing and is recorded — forming a binding part of the record that narrows what actually remains in dispute going forward.

Rules 1A-1C make the Section 89 ADR reference a mandatory first-hearing step (not optional case management) once admissions/denials are recorded, with a built-in return-to-Court mechanism if conciliation is judged unlikely to succeed.

Rule 2(1)(a) makes oral examination of present parties mandatory ("shall") where it would elucidate the controversy, while examining an accompanying knowledgeable person is discretionary ("may") under Rule 2(1)(b).
Rule 3's written-record requirement means the oral examination becomes part of the formal case record, usable later (e.g., as an admission) much like pleadings themselves.

Rule 4 is a targeted tool against pleaders who are unable to answer party-specific material questions — it forces personal appearance within seven days, backed by a judgment-against sanction for unexcused non-appearance.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Rule 2(3) lets the Court put either party's suggested questions during the examination — this is not a free-for-all cross-examination by opposing counsel but a Court-controlled, Court-put inquiry.

Rule 4's postponement is capped at seven days from the first hearing date and is triggered only when the pleader (or accompanying person) is unable/refuses to answer AND the Court believes the party personally could likely answer if asked directly.
breakdown.how_to_read: Order X's first-hearing sequence (Rule 1 admissions/denials -> Rule 1A-1C ADR reference -> Rule 2 oral examination) is the Code's primary case-management tool for narrowing a suit before the expense of a full trial — advocates should prepare clients for the real possibility of being orally examined by the Court at the first hearing and should likewise be ready with a considered ADR-mode preference, since the Rule 1A direction is now a mandatory step, not a discretionary suggestion.

sections.title: Order X, Rule 1 — Ascertainment whether allegations in pleadings are admitted or denied
sections.raw_text: 1. Ascertainment whether allegations in pleadings are admitted or denied.—At the first hearing of the suit the Court shall ascertain from each party or his pleader whether he admits or denies such allegations of fact as are made in the plaint or written statement (if any) of the opposite party, and as are not expressly or by necessary implication admitted or denied by the party against whom they are made. The Court shall record such admissions and denials.

breakdown.plain_summary: At the first hearing, the Court must go through the opposite party's pleading and directly ask each party (or their pleader) whether they admit or deny any factual allegation that hasn't already been clearly admitted or denied (expressly or by necessary implication) — and must record the resulting admissions and denials.
essential_elements: Mandatory exercise at the first hearing.
Covers only allegations not already expressly/impliedly admitted or denied.
Admissions and denials elicited this way must be recorded by the Court.
breakdown.how_to_read: This Rule is the live, in-Court counterpart to Order VI Rule 5's deemed-admission-by-silence-in-pleading rule — a party should walk into the first hearing having already rehearsed exactly what will be admitted and denied, since the Court's own recorded ascertainment here carries evidentiary weight independent of the written pleadings.

sections.title: Order X, Rule 1A — Direction of the court to opt for any one mode of alternative dispute resolution
sections.raw_text: 1A. Direction of the court to opt for any one mode of alternative dispute resolution.—After recording the admissions and denials, the court shall direct the parties to the suit to opt either mode of the settlement outside the court as specified in sub-section (1) of section 89. On the option of the parties, the court shall fix the date of appearance before such forum or authority as may be opted by the parties.

breakdown.plain_summary: Once admissions and denials are recorded, the Court must direct the parties to choose one of the out-of-court settlement modes listed in Section 89(1) (arbitration, conciliation, judicial settlement including Lok Adalat, or mediation). Once the parties choose, the Court fixes a date for them to appear before that chosen forum/authority.
essential_elements: Mandatory direction after Rule 1's admission/denial recording.
Parties choose the specific Section 89(1) ADR mode.
Court fixes an appearance date before the chosen forum/authority.
breakdown.how_to_read: Prepare a considered ADR-mode preference (and rationale) before the first hearing rather than treating this as a pro forma step — courts increasingly expect parties to engage substantively with Section 89, and a well-chosen forum (e.g., mediation for a continuing commercial relationship versus Lok Adalat for a straightforward money claim) can resolve the dispute far more efficiently than full trial.

sections.title: Order X, Rule 1B — Appearance before the conciliatory forum or authority
sections.raw_text: 1B. Appearance before the conciliatory forum or authority.—Where a suit is referred under rule 1A, the parties shall appear before such forum or authority for conciliation of the suit.

breakdown.plain_summary: Once a suit is referred to an ADR mode under Rule 1A, the parties must actually appear before that chosen forum or authority for conciliation of the dispute.
essential_elements: Mandatory appearance before the Rule 1A-referred forum/authority.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat the ADR appearance date with the same seriousness as a Court hearing date — non-appearance before the referred forum can trigger adverse consequences when the matter is reported back to the Court under Rule 1C.

sections.title: Order X, Rule 1C — Appearance before the court consequent to the failure of efforts of conciliation
sections.raw_text: 1C. Appearance before the court consequent to the failure of efforts of conciliation.—Where a suit is referred under rule 1A, and the presiding officer of conciliation forum or authority is satisfied that it would not be proper in the interest of justice to proceed with the matter further, then, it shall refer the matter again to the court and direct the parties to appear before the court on the date fixed by it.

breakdown.plain_summary: If the ADR forum's presiding officer concludes that continuing conciliation efforts would not serve the interest of justice, the matter is referred back to the Court, and the parties are directed to appear before the Court on a date it fixes — resuming the regular suit.
essential_elements: Triggered by the conciliation forum's own assessment that further proceedings would not be proper in the interest of justice.
Results in automatic referral back to the Court with a fixed appearance date.
breakdown.how_to_read: A failed ADR attempt under this Rule is not a dead end — the suit simply resumes before the Court on the fixed date, so parties should not view an unsuccessful Section 89 reference as wasted effort but as a genuine (if unsuccessful) attempt that the Code expects before full trial proceeds.

sections.title: Order X, Rule 2 — Oral examination of party, or companion of party
sections.raw_text:
2. Oral examination of party, or companion of party.—(1) At the first hearing of the suit, the Court—
(a) shall, with a view to elucidating matters in controversy in the suit examine orally such of the parties to the suit appearing in person or present in Court, as it deems fit; and
(b) may orally examine any person, able to answer any material question relating to the suit, by whom any party appearing in person or present in Court or his pleader is accompanied.
(2) At any subsequent hearing, the Court may orally examine any party appearing in person or present in Court, or any person, able to answer any material question relating to the suit, by whom such party or his pleader is accompanied.
(3) The Court may, if it thinks fit, put in the course of an examination under this rule questions suggested by either party.

breakdown.plain_summary: At the first hearing, the Court must orally examine parties present in Court (as it deems fit) to clarify the real matters in controversy, and may also examine any knowledgeable person accompanying a party or pleader. At later hearings, the same oral-examination power (for both parties and accompanying knowledgeable persons) continues, but becomes discretionary throughout. In either case, the Court may put questions suggested by either party during the examination.
essential_elements: Sub-rule (1)(a): mandatory oral examination of present parties at the first hearing, for elucidation purposes, as the Court deems fit.
Sub-rule (1)(b): discretionary oral examination of an accompanying knowledgeable person at the first hearing.
Sub-rule (2): both types of examination become fully discretionary at subsequent hearings.
Sub-rule (3): Court may incorporate either party's suggested questions into the examination.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The examination is always Court-conducted, not direct cross-examination by opposing counsel — parties/counsel can only suggest questions for the Court to ask, under sub-rule (3).
breakdown.how_to_read: Prepare clients for the realistic possibility of direct oral questioning by the Judge at the first hearing — this is a genuine fact-finding tool the Court uses to narrow the controversy early, and an unprepared client's answers here become part of the record under Rule 3.

sections.title: Order X, Rule 3 — Substance of examination to be written
sections.raw_text: 3. Substance of examination to be written.—The substance of the examination shall be reduced to writing by the Judge, and shall form part of the record.

breakdown.plain_summary: Whatever emerges from an oral examination under Rule 2 must be written down by the Judge (in substance) and becomes a formal part of the case record.
essential_elements: Mandatory written record of the examination's substance, made by the Judge.
Becomes part of the official case record.
breakdown.how_to_read: Always ask to review the Judge's recorded note of any oral examination for accuracy before it is finalised — since this written record becomes part of the case file and can later be relied upon, an inaccurate recording of a party's oral answers can have lasting evidentiary consequences.

sections.title: Order X, Rule 4 — Consequence of refusal or inability of pleader to answer
sections.raw_text:
4. Consequence of refusal or inability of pleader to answer.—(1) Where the pleader of any party who appears by a pleader or any such person accompanying a pleader as is referred to in rule 2, refuses or is unable to answer any material question relating to the suit which the Court is of opinion that the party whom he represents ought to answer, and is likely to be able to answer if interrogated in person, the Court may postpone the hearing of the suit to a day not later than seven days from the date of first hearing and direct that such party shall appear in person on such day.
(2) If such party fails without lawful excuse to appear in person on the day so appointed, the Court may pronounce judgment against him, or make such order in relation to the suit as it thinks fit.

breakdown.plain_summary: If a party's pleader (or an accompanying knowledgeable person) can't or won't answer a material question that the Court believes the party personally could likely answer, the Court can postpone the hearing — up to seven days from the first hearing date — and order the party to appear in person. If that party then fails to appear in person without lawful excuse, the Court can pronounce judgment against him or make any other order it thinks fit.
essential_elements: Triggered by a pleader's (or accompanying person's) refusal or inability to answer a material question the Court believes the party personally could likely answer.
Remedy: postponement, capped at seven days from the first hearing, with a personal-appearance direction.
Sanction for unexcused non-appearance on the appointed day: judgment against the party, or any other order the Court thinks fit.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The party retains an escape valve: appearing with a lawful excuse for not appearing in person avoids the adverse consequence — it is specifically unexcused non-appearance that triggers judgment.
breakdown.how_to_read: If a pleader anticipates being unable to answer case-specific factual questions at the first hearing, arrange for the client to be present in Court (or readily reachable) from the outset — being caught by a Rule 4 postponement-and-personal-appearance order, followed by a missed appointment, risks an adverse judgment on a technicality unrelated to the substantive merits.

sections.title: Order XI — Discovery and Inspection (Overview)
sections.raw_text:
ORDER XI
Discovery and Inspection

This Order supplies the pre-trial fact-gathering toolkit available between the parties themselves (as distinct from Order XVI's third-party witness/document summonses): discovery by interrogatories (written questions a party must answer on oath), discovery and production of documents, and inspection of documents referred to in pleadings or affidavits. A parallel, self-contained Order XI (Rules 1-7) applies instead to suits before the Commercial Division of a High Court or a Commercial Court, replacing this general regime with a front-loaded, deadline-driven disclosure code introduced by the Commercial Courts Act, 2015.

breakdown.plain_summary: Order XI lets one party compel the other to answer written questions on oath (interrogatories) and to disclose and produce documents relevant to the suit, all with leave of the Court so the tool isn't abused for fishing expeditions or harassment. Rules 1-11 cover interrogatories: how they're delivered (with Court leave), how objections and costs are handled, and how to compel further answers. Rules 12-14 cover discovery and production of documents generally. Rules 15-19 cover inspection of documents already referred to in pleadings/affidavits, the notice-to-produce mechanism, and verified copies in lieu of originals. Rule 20 lets the Court defer discovery/inspection until a threshold issue is decided. Rule 21 is the enforcement teeth — non-compliance can get a plaintiff's suit dismissed (with a bar on a fresh suit on the same cause of action) or a defendant's defence struck out. Rule 22 governs using interrogatory answers at trial, and Rule 23 extends the whole Order to minors' suits via their next friends/guardians.
essential_elements: Every significant step (delivering interrogatories, ordering document discovery, ordering inspection) requires leave/order of the Court — this is not a self-executing party-to-party procedure like some common-law discovery regimes.
The Court's gatekeeping standard throughout is whether the step is 'necessary either for disposing fairly of the suit or for saving costs' — irrelevant, vexatious, or premature discovery is refused.
Non-compliance carries real teeth under Rule 21: dismissal of the suit (plaintiff) or striking out of the defence (defendant), not merely costs.
exceptions_and_qualifications: A separate, self-contained Order XI (Rules 1-7) applies to commercial-division/commercial-court suits instead of this general Order — see the 'O-XI-CC' entries below.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat Order XI as a scalpel, not a hammer — Courts routinely refuse interrogatories or discovery applications that aren't tightly tied to a genuine disputed issue, so draft any Order XI application with a clear statement of exactly which facts or documents are sought and why they are necessary for fairly disposing of the suit or saving costs, anticipating the Rule 6/Rule 20 objections an opponent will raise.

sections.title: Order XI, Rule 1 — Discovery by interrogatories
sections.raw_text: 1. Discovery by interrogatories.—In any suit the plaintiff or defendant by leave of the Court may deliver interrogatories in writing for the examination of the opposite parties or any one or more of such parties and such interrogatories when delivered shall have a note at the foot thereof stating which of such interrogatories each of such person is required to answer: Provided that no party shall deliver more than one set of interrogatories to the same party without an order for that purpose: Provided also that interrogatories which do not relate to any matters in question in the suit shall be deemed irrelevant, notwithstanding that they might be admissible on the oral cross-examination of a witness.

breakdown.plain_summary: Either side may, with the Court's leave, serve written questions (interrogatories) on the opposite party for them to answer on oath, with a note specifying who must answer which question. A party can't deliver a second set without a fresh order, and questions unrelated to matters actually in issue are irrelevant even if they'd have been fair game in oral cross-examination.
essential_elements: Leave of the Court is a precondition.
A note at the foot must specify which person answers which interrogatory.
Only one set per party absent a further order.
Must relate to matters in question in the suit.
breakdown.how_to_read: Interrogatories are a pre-trial tool for pinning down an opponent's position on oath before trial — draft each question tightly to a disputed fact in issue, since a scattershot set invites both a relevance objection under Rule 6 and a striking-out application under Rule 7.

sections.title: Order XI, Rule 2 — Particular interrogatories to be submitted
sections.raw_text: 2. Particular interrogatories to be submitted.—On an application for leave to deliver interrogatories, the particular interrogatories proposed to be delivered shall be submitted to the Court and that court shall decide within seven days from the day of filing of the said application.
