Rule 7 draws the line: admitted documents (or substituted copies) become part of the record; rejected documents don't, and are returned. Rule 8 gives the Court an overriding power to impound any document or book for sufficient cause, regardless of the Rule 5/7 scheme. Rule 9 governs when and how documents already on record get returned to their producers — generally only after the suit (or any appeal) concludes, subject to a certified-copy-substitution shortcut for earlier return, and never for documents rendered void/useless by the decree. Rule 10 lets the Court call for records from its own files or another Court's, subject to an affidavit-of-materiality safeguard and without overriding the law of evidence on admissibility. Rule 11 extends this entire documentary scheme to material objects tendered as evidence.
essential_elements: Rule 1's production deadline is 'on or before the settlement of issues' — a firm, early-case checkpoint, not something that can be left to the eve of trial.
The endorsement scheme (Rules 4-6) creates a clear, judge-authenticated paper trail distinguishing admitted from rejected documents.

Rule 8's impounding power is expressly non-obstante ('notwithstanding') against Rules 5 and 7 and Order VII Rule 17 — it overrides the normal admit-or-return scheme whenever the Court sees sufficient cause.

Rule 9's return mechanism is timed to finality — ordinarily only after the suit (where no appeal lies) or after the appeal period has lapsed/the appeal is disposed of (where one does lie) — though earlier return is possible via certified-copy substitution.
breakdown.how_to_read: Build document production into the pre-issues checklist, not the eve-of-trial scramble — Rule 1's 'at or before settlement of issues' deadline, combined with the Rule 3 rejection power and the Rule 4/6 endorsement regime, means the documentary record of the suit is substantially locked in early, and a late, unexplained attempt to introduce a fresh original invites both a relevance/admissibility challenge and scrutiny over why it wasn't produced on time.

sections.title: Order XIII, Rule 1 — Original documents to be produced at or before the settlement of issues
sections.raw_text:
1. Original documents to be produced at or before the settlement of issues.—(1) The parties or their pleader shall produce on or before the settlement of issues, all the documentary evidence in original where the copies thereof have been filed along with plaint or written statement.
(2) The Court shall receive the documents so produced: Provided that they are accompanied by an accurate list thereof prepared in such form as the High Court directs.
(3) Nothing in sub-rule (1) shall apply to documents—
(a) produced for the cross-examination of the witnesses of the other party; or
(b) handed over to a witness merely to refresh his memory.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where copies of documents were filed along with the plaint or written statement, the parties (or their pleaders) must produce the corresponding originals on or before the settlement of issues. The Court receives them provided they're accompanied by an accurate list in the High-Court-prescribed form. This production requirement doesn't apply to documents used only for cross-examining the other side's witnesses, or handed to a witness merely to refresh their memory.
essential_elements: Deadline: on or before settlement of issues.
Applies where copies were already filed with the plaint/written statement.
Court's receipt of the originals is conditioned on an accompanying accurate list in the prescribed form.
Two carve-outs: cross-examination-only documents and memory-refreshing documents.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Cross-examination-only and memory-refreshing documents are exempt from this production deadline.
breakdown.how_to_read: Prepare and file the accurate list of original documents in the High-Court-prescribed form alongside production — the Rule 1(2) proviso makes the list a precondition to the Court actually receiving the documents, so an undocumented bundle of originals handed up in Court risks simply not being accepted onto the record.

sections.title: Order XIII, Rule 3 — Rejection of irrelevant or inadmissible documents
sections.raw_text: 3. Rejection of irrelevant or inadmissible documents.—The Court may at any stage of the suit reject any document which it considers irrelevant or otherwise inadmissible, recording the grounds of such rejection.

breakdown.plain_summary: The Court can reject a document it considers irrelevant or otherwise inadmissible at any stage of the suit, but must record the grounds for doing so.
essential_elements: Exercisable at any stage of the suit.
Covers both irrelevance and inadmissibility.
Grounds for rejection must be recorded.
breakdown.how_to_read: If a document you've produced is rejected under this Rule, obtain and preserve the Court's recorded grounds — they're essential both for any immediate re-argument and for preserving the point in a future appeal against the eventual decree.

sections.title: Order XIII, Rule 4 — Endorsements on documents admitted in evidence
sections.raw_text:
4. Endorsements on documents admitted in evidence.—(1) Subject to the provisions of the next following sub-rule, there shall be endorsed on every document which has been admitted in evidence in the suit the following particulars, namely:—
(a) the number and title of the suit,
(b) the name of the person producing the document,
(c) the date on which it was produced, and
(d) a statement of its having been so admitted,
and the endorsement shall be signed or initialled by the Judge.
(2) Where a document so admitted is an entry in a book, account or record, and a copy thereof has been substituted for the original under the next following rule, the particulars aforesaid shall be endorsed on the copy and the endorsement thereon shall be signed or initialled by the Judge.

breakdown.plain_summary: Every document admitted in evidence must be endorsed with the suit number and title, the producer's name, the production date, and a statement of admission — signed or initialled by the Judge. Where a copy was substituted for an original book/account entry under Rule 5, the same endorsement goes on the copy instead.
essential_elements: Four mandatory endorsement particulars for every admitted document.
Endorsement must be Judge-signed or initialled.
Where a Rule 5 copy-substitution applies, the endorsement moves to the copy.
breakdown.how_to_read: Check that every document tendered and admitted actually carries the full Rule 4 endorsement, Judge-signed — an unendorsed 'admitted' document can later create ambiguity about whether it was genuinely taken on record, which matters if its admissibility is challenged on appeal.

sections.title: Order XIII, Rule 5 — Endorsements on copies of admitted entries in books, accounts and records
sections.raw_text:
5. Endorsements on copies of admitted entries in books, accounts and records.—(1) Save in so far as is otherwise provided by the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891 (XVIII of 1891) where a document admitted in evidence in the suit is an entry in a letter-book or a shop-book or other account in current use, the party on whose behalf the book or account is produced may furnish a copy of the entry.
(2) Where such a document is an entry in a public record produced from a public office or by a public officer, or an entry in a book or account belonging to a person other than a party on whose behalf the book or account is produced, the Court may require a copy of the entry to be furnished—
(a) where the record, book or account is produced on behalf of a party, then by that party, or
(b) where the record, book or account is produced in obedience to an order of the Court acting of its own motion, then by either or any party.
(3) Where a copy of an entry is furnished under the foregoing provisions of this rule, the Court shall, after causing the copy to be examined, compared and certified in manner mentioned in rule 17 of Order VII, mark the entry and cause the book, account or record in which it occurs to be returned to the person producing it.

breakdown.plain_summary: For entries in current-use letter-books, shop-books, or accounts, the producing party may furnish a certified copy instead of leaving the original book on record (subject to the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891, for banking records). For public records or third-party books/accounts, the Court can require a copy to be furnished by the producing party, or by any party where the Court called for the record itself. Once such a copy is examined, compared, and certified per Order VII Rule 17's procedure, the Court marks the entry and returns the original book/account/record to its producer.
essential_elements: Current-use books: producing party may voluntarily furnish a copy (Bankers' Books Evidence Act takes precedence where applicable).
Public records / third-party books: Court can require a copy to be furnished.
Copy must be examined, compared, and certified per Order VII Rule 17 before the original is returned.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Banking records are governed by the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891 rather than this Rule where the two conflict.
breakdown.how_to_read: This Rule is particularly valuable for banks, shops, and businesses that need their active ledgers and account books back in daily use — invoke the copy-substitution mechanism promptly rather than leaving an operationally essential book tied up with the Court record for the suit's duration.

sections.title: Order XIII, Rule 6 — Endorsements on documents rejected as inadmissible in evidence
sections.raw_text: 6. Endorsements on documents rejected an inadmissible in evidence.—Where a document relied on as evidence by either party is considered by the Court to be inadmissible in evidence, there shall be endorsed thereon the particulars mentioned in clauses (a), (b) and (c) of rule 4, sub-rule (1) together with a statement of its having been rejected, and the endorsement shall be signed or initialled by the Judge.

breakdown.plain_summary: A document found inadmissible gets endorsed with the suit number/title, producer's name, and production date (the same first three particulars as Rule 4), plus a statement that it was rejected — again signed or initialled by the Judge.
essential_elements: Mirrors Rule 4's first three endorsement particulars.
Adds a rejection statement instead of an admission statement.
Judge-signed or initialled.
breakdown.how_to_read: A properly endorsed rejection is important appellate ammunition — if the rejection is later challenged, the endorsed document (with the Judge's own rejection statement) forms part of the record showing exactly what was tendered and why it was kept out.

sections.title: Order XIII, Rule 7 — Recording of admitted and return of rejected documents
sections.raw_text:
7. Recording of admitted and return of rejected documents.—(1) Every documents which has been admitted in evidence, or a copy thereof where a copy has been substituted for the original under rule 5, shall form part of the record of the suit.
(2) Documents not admitted in evidence shall not form part of the record and shall be returned to the persons respectively producing them.

breakdown.plain_summary: Admitted documents (or their Rule 5 copy substitutes) become part of the official suit record. Documents that aren't admitted don't become part of the record at all, and must be returned to whoever produced them.
essential_elements: Admitted documents/copies: become part of the record.
Rejected documents: excluded from the record, returned to the producer.
breakdown.how_to_read: Promptly collect rejected documents once Rule 7(2) entitles their return — there's no reason to leave them with the Court, and retrieving them ensures they remain available for any other purpose (e.g., a different proceeding) without needing a fresh application.

sections.title: Order XIII, Rule 8 — Court may order any document to be impounded
sections.raw_text: 8. Court may order any document to be impounded.—Notwithstanding anything contained in rule 5 or rule 7 of this Order or in rule 17 of Order VII, the Court may, if it sees sufficient cause, direct any document or book produced before it in any suit to be impounded and kept in the custody of an officer of the Court, for such period and subject to such conditions as the Court thinks fit.

breakdown.plain_summary: Regardless of the normal copy-substitution (Rule 5) or record/return (Rule 7) scheme, the Court can, for sufficient cause, order any document or book produced before it to be impounded — kept in the custody of a court officer, for whatever period and on whatever conditions the Court thinks fit.
essential_elements: Non-obstante power — overrides Rules 5 and 7 and Order VII Rule 17.
Triggered by the Court's own view of sufficient cause.
Document held by a court officer, for a Court-determined period and conditions.
breakdown.how_to_read: If a document's authenticity or chain of custody is genuinely in doubt (e.g., suspected fabrication), consider urging the Court to exercise its Rule 8 impounding power rather than allowing the document to be returned under the ordinary Rule 7/9 scheme — impounding preserves the original for further scrutiny, including potential criminal reference, that a mere endorsed-and-returned document would not.

sections.title: Order XIII, Rule 9 — Return of admitted documents
sections.raw_text:
9. Return of admitted documents.—(1) Any person, whether a party to the suit or not, desirous of receiving back any documents produced by him in the suit and placed on the record shall, unless the document is impounded under rule 8, be entitled to receive back the same,—
(a) where the suit is one in which an appeal is not allowed, when the suit has been disposed of, and
(b) where the suit is one in which an appeal is allowed, when the Court is satisfied that the time for preferring an appeal has elapsed and that no appeal has been preferred or, if an appeal has been preferred, when the appeal has been disposed of:
Provided that a document may be returned at any time earlier then that prescribed by this rule if the person applying therefor—
(a) delivers to the proper officer for being substituted for the original,—
(i) in the case of a party to the suit, a certified copy, and
(ii) in the case of any other person, an ordinary copy which has been examined, compared and certified in the manner mentioned in sub-rule (2) of rule 17 of Order VII, and
(b) undertakes to produce the original, if required to do so:
Provided also, that no document shall be returned with, by force of the decree, has become wholly void or useless.
(2) On the return of a document admitted in evidence, a receipt shall be given by the person receiving it.

breakdown.plain_summary: Anyone (party or not) who produced a document now on record is entitled to get it back — unless it's been impounded under Rule 8 — once the suit concludes (where no appeal lies) or once the appeal period has lapsed without an appeal, or any appeal filed has been disposed of (where an appeal does lie). An earlier return is possible if the applicant substitutes a certified copy (for a party) or a duly examined/compared/certified ordinary copy (for a non-party), while undertaking to produce the original again if required. No document is returned if the decree has rendered it wholly void or useless. A receipt must be given on return.
essential_elements: Available to any producer of an admitted document, party or not.
Impounded documents (Rule 8) are excluded from this return entitlement.
Default timing: suit disposal (no-appeal suits) or appeal-period lapse/appeal disposal (appealable suits).
Earlier return available via certified/examined-copy substitution plus an undertaking to re-produce the original if required.
Absolute bar: documents rendered wholly void or useless by the decree are never returned.
breakdown.how_to_read: If an original document is urgently needed elsewhere before the suit (and any appeal) concludes, use the certified-copy-substitution proviso rather than waiting out the full timeline — but be prepared to honour the undertaking to re-produce the original if the Court later calls for it.

sections.title: Order XIII, Rule 10 — Court may send for papers from its own records or from other Courts
sections.raw_text:
10. Court may send for papers from its own records or from other Courts.—(1) The Court may of its own motion, and may in its discretion upon the application of any of the parties to a suit, send for, either from its own records or from any other Court, the record of any other suit or proceeding, and inspect the same.
(2) Every application made under this rule shall (unless the Court otherwise directs) be supported by an affidavit showing how the record is material to the suit in which the application is made, and that the applicant cannot without unreasonable delay or expense obtain a duly authenticated copy of the record or of such portion thereof as the applicant requires, or that the production of the original is necessary for the purposes of justice.
(3) Nothing contained in this rule shall be deemed to enable the Court to use in evidence any document which under the law of evidence would be inadmissible in the suit.

breakdown.plain_summary: The Court can, suo motu or on a party's application, call for and inspect the record of another suit or proceeding — from its own files or another Court's. Such an application must (absent a contrary direction) be backed by an affidavit showing the record's materiality and either unreasonable delay/expense in obtaining an authenticated copy, or the necessity of the original for justice. This power doesn't override the ordinary law of evidence on admissibility — calling for a record doesn't make inadmissible material usable.
essential_elements: Exercisable suo motu or on party application.
Covers records from the same Court or any other Court.
Application generally requires a materiality-and-necessity affidavit.
Does not expand admissibility beyond what the law of evidence otherwise permits.
breakdown.how_to_read: File the Rule 10(2) affidavit with precision — vaguely asserting that another suit's record is 'relevant' invites refusal; instead, identify specifically why a duly authenticated copy is unreasonably delayed/costly to obtain, or why the original specifically (not just its contents) is necessary for justice.

sections.title: Order XIII, Rule 11 — Provisions as to documents applied to material objects
sections.raw_text: 11. Provisions as to documents applied to material objects.—The provisions therein contained as to documents shall, so far as may be, apply to all other material objects producible as evidence.

breakdown.plain_summary: Everything this Order provides for documents — production deadlines, rejection, endorsement, impounding, return, and so on — applies equally, so far as practicable, to other material objects tendered as evidence (not just paper documents).
essential_elements: Extends the whole of Order XIII's document regime to material objects, to the extent applicable.
breakdown.how_to_read: Don't assume Order XIII's safeguards are limited to paper — physical exhibits (weapons, damaged goods, samples, etc.) are governed by the same production, endorsement, impounding, and return regime, so handle and document their production with the same procedural discipline as any documentary exhibit.

sections.title: Order XIII-A — Summary Judgment (Overview)
sections.raw_text:
ORDER XIII-A
Summary Judgment

Applicable to commercial disputes of a specified value by Act 4 of 2016, s. 16 and the Sch. (w.e.f. 23-10-2015). This Order, inserted by the Commercial Courts Act, 2015, gives Commercial Division/Commercial Court judges a mechanism to decide a Commercial Dispute claim without recording oral evidence, wherever a claim or defence has no real prospect of success and there is no other compelling reason for a full trial.

breakdown.plain_summary: Order XIII-A lets a Commercial Division or Commercial Court dispose of a claim (or part of one, a discrete question, or a counterclaim) without recording oral evidence, where it's satisfied the opposing side has no real prospect of success on the claim or defence, and there's no other compelling reason to let the matter go to trial. Rule 1 scopes the Order to Commercial Disputes and excludes suits already proceeding as summary suits under Order XXXVII. Rule 2 lets the application be made any time after summons is served, but bars it once issues have been framed. Rule 3 states the twin test (no real prospect of success + no other compelling reason for trial). Rule 4 prescribes a detailed, document-and-reasons-driven application and reply procedure with a thirty-day notice and thirty-day reply window. Rule 5 governs additional documentary evidence timelines for the hearing itself (fifteen days for the respondent, five days for the applicant's reply evidence). Rule 6 lists the Court's full range of dispositive options — from full judgment to dismissal, partial judgment, striking out pleadings, or routing the matter into Order XV-A case management — all requiring recorded reasons. Rule 7 introduces the 'conditional order' middle ground for claims/defences that are possible but improbable to succeed, which can be conditioned on deposits, specified steps, security, or other terms, with a stated consequence (including judgment against the non-complying party) for breach. Rule 8 lets the Court impose costs under Sections 35 and 35A.
essential_elements: Available only for Commercial Disputes (of specified value) and not for suits already proceeding as Order XXXVII summary suits.
Can only be applied for after summons is served and before issues are framed — a defined procedural window.
The governing test is twofold: no real prospect of success/defence, AND no other compelling reason for a full trial — both limbs must be satisfied.
The application/reply procedure is heavily document- and reasons-driven, with specific content requirements (Rule 4) and tight evidentiary timelines (Rule 5).

The Court's outcome options span a full spectrum — outright judgment, dismissal, partial disposal, pleading strike-out, conditional orders, or redirection to case management — every one of which must be reasoned.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Not available once the Court has already framed issues in the suit.
Not available for suits originally filed as Order XXXVII summary suits.
breakdown.how_to_read: Order XIII-A is the commercial-litigation analogue of summary judgment found in many common-law systems — use it aggressively where a commercial claim or defence is genuinely weak on the merits, since it can avoid the time and cost of a full trial, but file promptly (before issues are framed) and build the application around precise, documented reasons under Rule 4 rather than general assertions, since a bare or conclusory application is unlikely to meet the 'no real prospect of success' threshold.

sections.title: Order XIII-A, Rule 1 — Scope of and classes of suits to which this Order applies
sections.raw_text:
1. Scope of and classes of suits to which this Order applies.—(1) This Order sets out the procedure by which Courts may decide a claim pertaining to any Commercial Dispute without recording oral evidence.
(2) For the purposes of this Order, the word "claim" shall include—
(a) part of a claim;
(b) any particular question on which the claim (whether in whole or in part) depends; or
(c) a counterclaim, as the case may be.
(3) Notwithstanding anything to the contrary, an application for summary judgment under this Order shall not be made in a suit in respect of any Commercial Dispute that is originally filed as a summary suit under Order XXXVII.

breakdown.plain_summary: This Order applies to Commercial Dispute claims and lets the Court decide them without recording oral evidence. 'Claim' is defined broadly to include part of a claim, a particular dependent question, or a counterclaim. It cannot be invoked in a suit that was originally filed as an Order XXXVII summary suit.
essential_elements: Scope limited to Commercial Disputes.
'Claim' broadly defined to include partial claims, dependent questions, and counterclaims.
Express exclusion for suits originally filed under Order XXXVII.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Order XXXVII summary suits are categorically excluded from this Order's procedure, since they already have their own summary mechanism.
breakdown.how_to_read: Confirm at the outset that the suit is a genuine Commercial Dispute (not merely a suit that happens to be commercial in a lay sense) and was not originally filed under Order XXXVII, since either disqualifier defeats a Rule 1 application before its merits are even reached.

sections.title: Order XIII-A, Rule 2 — Stage for application for summary judgment
sections.raw_text: 2. Stage for application for summary judgment.—An applicant may apply for summary judgment at any time after summons has been served on the defendant: Provided that, no application for summary judgment may be made by such applicant after the Court has framed the issues in respect of the suit.

breakdown.plain_summary: A summary judgment application can be made any time after the defendant has been served with summons, but it must be made before the Court frames issues in the suit — once issues are framed, the window closes.
essential_elements: Earliest trigger: service of summons on the defendant.
Latest cutoff: before the Court frames issues.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat issue-framing as a hard deadline for a summary judgment strategy — if a claim or defence looks weak early on, file the Rule 2 application promptly rather than waiting, since delay risks the window closing once issues are framed.

sections.title: Order XIII-A, Rule 3 — Grounds for summary judgment
sections.raw_text:
3. Grounds for summary judgment.—The Court may give a summary judgment against a plaintiff or defendant on a claim if it considers that—
(a) the plaintiff has no real prospect of succeeding on the claim or the defendant has no real prospect of successfully defending the claim, as the case may be; and
(b) there is no other compelling reason why the claim should not be disposed of before recording of oral evidence.

breakdown.plain_summary: The Court can grant summary judgment against either side if it finds both that the plaintiff has no real prospect of succeeding (or the defendant no real prospect of successfully defending), and that there's no other compelling reason to avoid disposing of the claim without oral evidence.
essential_elements: Two-limb conjunctive test: no real prospect of success/defence, AND no other compelling reason for trial.
Available against either a plaintiff's claim or a defendant's defence.
breakdown.how_to_read: Both limbs of the Rule 3 test must be met — even a claim or defence that looks weak on the papers can survive summary judgment if there's a compelling reason (e.g., a genuine need for cross-examination on a disputed fact, or a developing area of law) why the matter should still go to trial, so address both limbs squarely in any application or opposition.

sections.title: Order XIII-A, Rule 4 — Procedure

breakdown.plain_summary: A summary judgment application must expressly identify itself as such, precisely disclose all material facts and legal points, attach and pinpoint any relied-upon documentary evidence, explain why there's no real prospect of success/defence, and specify the relief sought with grounds. Once a hearing is fixed, the respondent gets at least thirty days' notice of the date and the claim to be decided. The respondent then has thirty days (from whichever of the application notice or hearing notice comes first) to file a mirror-image reply: disclosing material facts and legal points, explaining why relief shouldn't be granted, attaching and pinpointing its own documentary evidence, explaining why there are real prospects of success/defence, concisely stating proposed trial issues, identifying what further trial-stage evidence couldn't be brought at the summary stage, and explaining why summary judgment shouldn't proceed.
essential_elements: Application must satisfy six specified content requirements (a)-(f), including documentary evidence pinpointing.
Minimum thirty-day hearing notice to the respondent, specifying date and the claim to be decided.
Respondent's reply deadline: thirty days from the earlier of the application notice or hearing notice.
Reply must satisfy its own six specified content requirements (a)-(f), mirroring but distinct from the application's.
breakdown.how_to_read: Draft both the application and any reply as self-contained, evidence-anchored documents satisfying every listed sub-clause — because the Rule is this prescriptive, a generic application or reply that omits any required element (e.g., failing to identify proposed trial issues in a reply) risks being treated as non-compliant or unpersuasive on its own terms.

sections.title: Order XIII-A, Rule 5 — Evidence for hearing of summary judgment
sections.raw_text:
5. Evidence for hearing of summary judgment.—(1) Notwithstanding anything in this Order, if the respondent in an application for summary judgment wishes to rely on additional documentary evidence during the hearing, the respondent must:—(a) file such documentary evidence; and (b) serve copies of such documentary evidence on every other party to the application at least fifteen days prior to the date of the hearing.
(2) Notwithstanding anything in this Order, if the applicant for summary judgment wishes to rely on documentary evidence in reply to the defendant's documentary evidence, the applicant must:—(a) file such documentary evidence in reply; and (b) serve a copy of such documentary evidence on the respondent at least five days prior to the date of the hearing.
(3) Notwithstanding anything to the contrary, sub-rules (1) and (2) shall not require documentary evidence to be:—(a) filed if such documentary evidence has already been filed; or (b) served on a party on whom it has already been served.

breakdown.plain_summary: If the respondent wants to introduce additional documentary evidence at the hearing beyond what's in the reply, it must be filed and served on every other party at least fifteen days before the hearing. If the applicant then wants to respond with its own documentary evidence, it must be filed and served at least five days before the hearing. Neither requirement applies to documents already filed or already served on the relevant party.
essential_elements: Respondent's additional evidence: fifteen-day pre-hearing filing/service deadline.
Applicant's reply evidence: five-day pre-hearing filing/service deadline.
No duplicate filing/service required for material already on record/served.
breakdown.how_to_read: Plan backward from the hearing date using these two deadlines — the fifteen-day respondent deadline and the five-day applicant reply deadline are sequential and tight, so identify any additional documentary evidence well before the hearing rather than attempting a late introduction that would breach Rule 5.

sections.title: Order XIII-A, Rule 6 — Orders that may be made by Court
sections.raw_text:
6. Orders that may be made by Court.—(1) On an application made under this Order, the Court may make such orders that it may deem fit in its discretion including the following:—(a) judgment on the claim; (b) conditional order in accordance with Rule 7 mentioned hereunder; (c) dismissing the application; (d) dismissing part of the claim and a judgment on part of the claim that is not dismissed; (e) striking out the pleadings (whether in whole or in part); or (f) further directions to proceed for case management under Order XV-A.
(2) Where the Court makes any of the orders as set forth in sub-rule (1) (a) to (f), the Court shall record its reasons for making such order.

breakdown.plain_summary: On a summary judgment application, the Court has a wide discretionary menu of outcomes: full judgment on the claim, a conditional order under Rule 7, dismissing the application outright, partially dismissing/partially granting judgment on a claim, striking out pleadings wholly or partly, or simply directing the matter into Order XV-A case management. Whichever option is chosen, the Court must record its reasons.
essential_elements: Six listed dispositive options, non-exhaustively framed ('including').
Every order under this Rule requires recorded reasons.
breakdown.how_to_read: Don't assume a summary judgment application is a binary win-or-lose proposition — the Rule 6 menu includes partial judgment, pleading strike-out, and case-management redirection, so frame submissions (and anticipate outcomes) across this full spectrum rather than arguing only for outright judgment or outright dismissal.

sections.title: Order XIII-A, Rule 7 — Conditional order
sections.raw_text:
7. Conditional order.—(1) Where it appears to the Court that it is possible that a claim or defence may succeed but it is improbable that it shall do so, the Court may make a conditional order as set forth in Rule 6 (1) (b).
(2) Where the Court makes a conditional order, it may:—(a) make it subject to all or any of the following conditions:—(i) require a party to deposit a sum of money in the Court; (ii) require a party to take a specified step in relation to the claim or defence, as the case may be; (iii) require a party, as the case may be, to give such security or provide such surety for restitution of costs as the Court deems fit and proper; (iv) impose such other conditions, including providing security for restitution of losses that any party is likely to suffer during the pendency of the suit, as the Court may deem fit in its discretion; and (b) specify the consequences of the failure to comply with the conditional order, including passing a judgment against the party that have not complied with the conditional order.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where a claim or defence is possible but improbable to succeed, the Court can make a conditional order instead of an outright judgment or dismissal — requiring a deposit, a specified step, security/surety for costs, or other conditions (including security for likely losses pending the suit) — and must specify what happens if the party fails to comply, which can include judgment against them.
essential_elements: Threshold: 'possible but improbable' success — the middle ground between 'no real prospect' and a genuinely triable claim/defence.
Conditions can include monetary deposits, specified steps, costs security/surety, or other Court-fashioned conditions.
Non-compliance consequences must be specified, up to and including adverse judgment.
breakdown.how_to_read: A conditional order is a practical tool to flush out a genuinely weak-but-not-hopeless claim or defence — if facing one, be prepared to actually satisfy the imposed condition (e.g., a deposit) promptly, since non-compliance can result directly in judgment against you without further proceedings.

sections.title: Order XIII-A, Rule 8 — Power to impose costs
sections.raw_text: 8. Power to impose costs.—The Court may make an order for payment of costs in an application for summary judgment in accordance with the provisions of sections 35 and 35A of the Code.

breakdown.plain_summary: The Court can order costs on a summary judgment application, governed by the Code's general costs provisions under Sections 35 (costs) and 35A (compensatory costs for false or vexatious claims/defences).
essential_elements: Costs power is tied to Sections 35 and 35A of the main Code.
breakdown.how_to_read: Remember that Section 35A's compensatory-costs exposure for false or vexatious claims/defences is available in the summary judgment context too — a party who forces a summary judgment hearing on a hopeless claim or defence risks more than simply losing the application.

sections.title: Order XIV — Settlement of Issues and Determination of Suit on Issues of Law or on Issues Agreed Upon
sections.raw_text: Order XIV governs the framing of issues — the formal statement of the precise questions of fact and law on which a suit will be tried — along with the Court's power to decide preliminary issues of law or jurisdiction first, and the special procedure for suits where the parties agree to submit a specific question to the Court's decision.

breakdown.plain_summary: Order XIV is the hinge between pleadings and trial. Once pleadings close, the Court reads the plaint, written statement, and the Order X Rule 2 oral examination, and distils the dispute into a numbered list of 'issues' — the only questions the trial will actually be about. Everything at trial (evidence, arguments, the final judgment) is organised around these issues. Rule 2 lets the Court decide a pure issue of law first — if it goes to jurisdiction or a statutory bar to the suit — without wading into the facts at all, potentially disposing of the whole case on a threshold point. Rules 6-7 provide a rare procedural shortcut: if both sides agree to frame their entire dispute as a single stated question and bind themselves to its answer, the Court can try just that question and decree accordingly.
essential_elements: Rule 1: issues arise from a 'material proposition' of fact or law affirmed by one side and denied by the other; every such proposition gets its own distinct issue, framed at the first hearing after reading the pleadings, the Order X Rule 2 oral examination, and hearing the parties; no issues need be framed if the defendant puts up no defence at all.

Rule 2: the Court must ordinarily decide all issues and pronounce judgment on all of them even if the case could be disposed of on one preliminary issue — but as an exception, if there are mixed issues of law and fact, the Court may try a pure issue of law first if it goes to (a) the Court's jurisdiction or (b) a statutory bar to the suit, postponing the rest pending that decision.
Rule 3: issues may be framed from oath-based allegations by parties/their pleaders, from the pleadings or interrogatory answers, or from the contents of produced documents.

Rule 4: if issues cannot be correctly framed without examining an absent person or inspecting an unproduced document, the Court may adjourn framing (to a day not later than seven days) and compel attendance/production by summons.

Rule 5: the Court retains a continuing power, at any time before passing a decree, to amend issues, frame additional issues necessary to determine the real controversy, or strike out wrongly framed or unnecessary issues.

Rules 6-7: where parties agree on a question of fact or law and execute a written agreement binding themselves to a stated consequence (payment of a sum, delivery of property, or doing/abstaining from an act) depending on the Court's finding, the Court — after satisfying itself the agreement was duly executed, the parties have a substantial interest in the question, and it is fit to be tried — records and tries that question as if it were a Court-framed issue, then pronounces judgment according to the agreement's terms, upon which a decree follows.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Rule 2's 'decide jurisdiction/bar-to-suit issues first' power is discretionary ('may'), not mandatory — a Court can still choose to try all issues together.
The Rule 5 amendment power is available only before the decree is passed, not after.

Rules 6-7's agreed-issue procedure is distinct from an Order XXIII compromise — here the Court still tries the stated question and renders a genuine adjudication; it is not a mere recording of settlement terms.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Rule 1 as defining what an issue even is before reading anything else — a lawyer disputing a draft issue list should test each proposed issue against the 'material proposition... affirmed by one, denied by the other' definition. Rule 2's proviso is a favourite defence tool: frame the limitation or jurisdiction objection as a threshold issue of law and press the Court to decide it first under Rule 2(2) before the expense of a full trial. Rules 6-7 are rarely used in ordinary litigation but valuable in commercial/technical disputes where the parties can isolate one dispositive legal or valuation question.

sections.title: Order XIV, Rule 1 — Framing of Issues
sections.raw_text: 1. Framing of issues.—(1) Issues arise when a material proposition of fact or law is affirmed by the one party and denied by the other. (2) Material propositions are those propositions of law or fact which a plaintiff must allege in order to show a right to sue or a defendant must allege in order to constitute his defence. (3) Each material proposition affirmed by one party and denied by the other shall form the subject of a distinct issue. (4) Issues are of two kinds: (a) issues of fact, (b) issues of law. (5) At the first hearing of the suit the Court shall, after reading the plaint and the written statements if any, and after examination under rule 2 of Order X and after hearing the parties or their pleaders, ascertain upon what material propositions of fact or of law the parties are at variance, and shall thereupon proceed to frame and record the issues on which the right decision of the case appears to depend. (6) Nothing in this rule requires the Court to frame and record issues where the defendant at the first hearing of the suit makes no defence.

breakdown.plain_summary: Rule 1 defines an 'issue' as a material proposition — something the plaintiff must allege to show a right to sue, or the defendant to show a defence — that one side affirms and the other denies. Every genuinely disputed material proposition gets its own issue, split into fact-issues and law-issues, framed at the first hearing after the Court has read the pleadings and conducted the Order X Rule 2 examination. If the defendant offers no defence at all, there is nothing to frame issues on.
essential_elements: A 'material proposition' is tied to the cause of action/defence — not every factual assertion in the pleadings generates an issue, only those essential to the right to sue or the defence.
Affirmation by one side and denial by the other is the triggering test — admitted facts never become issues.
Framing happens at the first hearing, informed by the pleadings and the Order X Rule 2 oral examination of parties.
No issues are required where the defendant makes no defence at the first hearing (the matter proceeds under Order VIII/Order XV instead).
exceptions_and_qualifications: A fact admitted in the written statement is not an 'issue' even if mentioned in the plaint — Rule 1 applies only to genuinely contested propositions.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the foundational definitional rule — every later Order XIV rule (amendment, striking out, preliminary trial) operates on 'issues' as defined here. A practitioner reviewing a draft issue list should check each item traces back to a specific pleaded-and-denied material proposition.

sections.title: Order XIV, Rule 2 — Court to Pronounce Judgment on All Issues
sections.raw_text: 2. Court to pronounce judgment on all issues.—(1) Notwithstanding that a case may be disposed of on a preliminary issue, the Court shall, subject to the provisions of sub-rule (2), pronounce judgment on all issues. (2) Where issues both of law and of fact arise in the same suit, and the Court is of opinion that the case or any part thereof may be disposed of on an issue of law only, it may try that issue first if the issue relates to— (a) the jurisdiction of the Court, or (b) a bar to the suit created by any law for the time being in force, and for that purpose may, if it thinks fit, postpone the settlement of the other issues until after that issue has been determined, and may deal with the suit in accordance with the decision on that issue.

breakdown.plain_summary: The default rule (sub-rule 1) is that a Court must decide every framed issue, even if one issue alone would dispose of the whole case — this guards against piecemeal appeals and ensures a complete record. Sub-rule (2) is the narrow, defence-friendly exception: where a pure issue of law touches jurisdiction or a statutory bar to the suit (limitation, res judicata, lack of cause of action, etc.), the Court may try that one issue first and dispose of the suit on it without ever reaching the facts.
essential_elements: General rule: all issues must be decided, even after a preliminary issue disposes of the case — this avoids remand loops if the preliminary finding is later reversed in appeal.
Exception threshold: the issue must be a pure issue of law (not mixed fact-and-law) and must relate specifically to jurisdiction or a statutory bar to the suit.
The power to try that issue first and postpone the rest is discretionary, not mandatory.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This sub-rule (2) exception is narrower than it looks: 'bar to the suit created by any law' means a statutory bar (e.g., limitation, Section 80 notice, res judicata) — not any issue the Court subjectively regards as dispositive.
Rule 2 interacts with Order VII Rule 11 (rejection of plaint) and Section 9A-style preliminary jurisdictional objections where applicable.
breakdown.how_to_read: Defence counsel plead jurisdiction or limitation prominently and early precisely to invoke Rule 2(2) — framing the issue as 'law only' is the tactical move, since a mixed fact-law issue cannot be tried preliminarily under this rule. Plaintiffs resisting a preliminary trial should argue the issue is in truth mixed (requires evidence) to keep it bundled with the rest under sub-rule (1).

sections.title: Order XIV, Rule 3 — Materials from Which Issues May Be Framed
sections.raw_text: 3. Materials from which issues may be framed.—The Court may frame the issues from all or any of the following materials:— (a) allegations made on oath by the parties, or by any persons present on their behalf, or made by the pleaders of such parties; (b) allegations made in the pleadings or in answers to interrogatories delivered in the suit; (c) the contents of documents produced by either party.

breakdown.plain_summary: Rule 3 lists the Court's raw material for framing issues: sworn statements by parties or counsel, the pleadings themselves (including interrogatory answers), and the content of produced documents. It confirms issue-framing is not limited mechanically to the plaint/written statement text but can draw on anything already properly before the Court by the first hearing.
essential_elements: Three sources: oath-based allegations (party/representative/pleader), pleadings/interrogatory answers, and document contents.
The list is permissive ('all or any') — the Court is not required to consult every source for every issue.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This rule does not let the Court import extraneous material not yet on the suit's record — the sources are all things already before the Court through the ordinary pleading/interrogatory/document process.
breakdown.how_to_read: Useful where the written statement is vague or evasive — counsel can point the Court to interrogatory answers or produced documents to sharpen a properly-framed issue instead of accepting an issue drafted only off the bare pleadings.

sections.title: Order XIV, Rule 4 — Court May Examine Witnesses or Documents Before Framing Issues
sections.raw_text: 4. Court may examine witnesses or documents before framing issues.—Where the Court is of opinion that the issues cannot be correctly framed without the examination of some person not before the Court or without the inspection of some document not produced in the suit, it may adjourn the framing of issues to a day not later than seven days and may (subject to any law for the time being in force) compel the attendance of any person or the production of any document by the person in whose possession or power it is by summons or other process.

breakdown.plain_summary: If the Court genuinely cannot frame correct issues without input from an absent person or an unproduced document, it can pause issue-framing (for up to seven days) and use summons/process to compel that person's attendance or that document's production, then resume framing with the fuller picture.
essential_elements: Trigger: issues 'cannot be correctly framed' without the missing testimony/document — a genuine necessity, not routine delay.
The adjournment is capped at seven days.
The compulsion power is exercised 'subject to any law for the time being in force' (e.g., Evidence Act privilege rules still apply).
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a narrow, time-boxed power distinct from the general discovery/interrogatories machinery of Order XI — it operates specifically to enable correct issue-framing at the threshold, not general evidence-gathering.
breakdown.how_to_read: Rarely invoked in practice since most issue-framing proceeds on the pleadings alone; relevant where a critical document (e.g., a disputed contract) is referenced but not yet filed and its content is essential to state the issue accurately.

sections.title: Order XIV, Rule 5 — Power to Amend and Strike Out Issues
sections.raw_text: 5. Power to amend and strike out issues.—(1) The Court may at any time before passing a decree amend the issues or frame additional issues on such terms as it thinks fit, and all such amendments or additional issues as may be necessary for determining the matters in controversy between the parties shall be so made or framed. (2) The Court may also, at any time before passing a decree, strike out any issues that appear to it to be wrongly framed or introduced.

breakdown.plain_summary: Issue-framing is not frozen at the first hearing — Rule 5 gives the Court a continuing power, right up until the decree is passed, to amend existing issues, add new ones necessary to resolve the real dispute, or delete issues that were wrongly framed or unnecessarily introduced.
essential_elements: Time limit: any time before the decree is passed — this is a trial-stage power, not a post-decree one.

Amendment/addition is actually mandatory where 'necessary for determining the matters in controversy' — the discretionary word is only 'on such terms as it thinks fit' for conditions, not whether to act at all when necessity is shown.
Striking out targets issues wrongly framed or introduced — e.g., issues not supported by any pleaded material proposition.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This power must be read alongside Order VI Rule 17 (amendment of pleadings) — a pleading amendment often necessitates a corresponding Rule 5 issue amendment.
breakdown.how_to_read: Counsel who discover mid-trial that a crucial issue was omitted (e.g., limitation was pleaded but never framed as an issue) should move promptly under Rule 5 rather than waiting for appeal, since appellate courts are reluctant to entertain issues never tried below.

sections.title: Order XIV, Rule 6 — Questions of Fact or Law May by Agreement Be Stated in Form of Issues
sections.raw_text: 6. Questions of fact or law may by agreement be stated in form of issues.—(1) Where the parties to a suit are agreed as to the question of fact or of law to be decided between them, they may state the same in the form of an issue, and enter into an agreement in writing that, upon the finding of the Court in the affirmative or the negative of such issue,— (a) a sum of money specified in the agreement or to be ascertained by the Court, or in such manner as the Court may direct, shall be paid by one of the parties to the other of them, or that one of them be declared entitled to some right or subject some liability specified in the agreement; (b) some property specified in the agreement and in dispute in the suit shall be delivered by one of the parties to the other of them, or as that other may direct; or (c) one or more of the parties shall do or abstain from doing some particular act specified in the agreement and relating to the matter in dispute.

breakdown.plain_summary: This rule lets parties shortcut a full trial by isolating a single agreed question (of fact or law) and binding themselves in writing to a specific consequence depending on how the Court answers it — payment of a sum, a declared right/liability, delivery of specified property, or doing/abstaining from a specified act.
essential_elements: Requires genuine party agreement on both the question and the written consequence structure.
Three permitted consequence types: money payment/right-liability declaration, property delivery, or an act/omission order.
The agreement must specify (or provide a mechanism to ascertain) the consequence precisely.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is not a compromise under Order XXIII — the Court still genuinely adjudicates the stated question; the agreement only fixes what follows from the answer.
breakdown.how_to_read: Useful in disputes that genuinely turn on one clean legal or valuation question (e.g., 'is the sale deed a benami transaction?') where both sides would rather bind themselves to the answer than litigate every ancillary issue.

sections.title: Order XIV, Rule 7 — Court, If Satisfied That Agreement Was Executed in Good Faith, May Pronounce Judgment
sections.raw_text: 7. Court, if satisfied that agreement was executed in good faith, may pronounce judgment.—Where the Court is satisfied, after making such inquiry as it deems proper,— (a) that the agreement was duly executed by the parties, (b) that they have a substantial interest in the decision of such question as aforesaid, and (c) that the same is fit to be tried and decided, it shall proceed to record and try the issue and state its finding or decision thereon in the same manner as if the issue had been framed by the Court; and shall, upon the finding or decision on such issue, pronounce judgment according to the terms of the agreement; and, upon the judgment so pronounced, a decree shall follow.

breakdown.plain_summary: Rule 7 is the operative follow-through to Rule 6: once the Court verifies (i) the agreement was duly executed, (ii) the parties have a genuine substantial interest in the question, and (iii) the question is fit to be tried, it tries that single issue exactly as it would a Court-framed issue, then pronounces judgment strictly according to the agreement's pre-fixed consequence — and a decree follows automatically.
essential_elements: Three-part satisfaction test before the Court will act: due execution, substantial interest, fitness for trial.
The trial of the agreed issue proceeds exactly as an ordinary issue trial (evidence, arguments, findings).
Judgment is bound by the agreement's terms — the Court does not independently fashion relief once the issue is answered.
exceptions_and_qualifications: If the Court is not satisfied on any of the three conditions, it declines to use this shortcut and the suit proceeds on ordinary issues instead — Rule 7 does not compel the Court to accept a defective or collusive agreement.
breakdown.how_to_read: Advocates drafting a Rule 6 agreement should pre-empt Rule 7 scrutiny by making due execution easy to prove (registered/notarised where possible) and by articulating each party's substantial interest expressly in the agreement's recitals.

sections.title: Order XV — Disposal of the Suit at the First Hearing
sections.raw_text: Order XV lets the Court shortcut the trial at the very first hearing where the parties either are not genuinely at issue on any question, or are at issue but the available evidence and argument are already sufficient to decide — avoiding a wasted full trial where the real dispute is thin or absent.

breakdown.plain_summary: Order XV operates at the opposite end of the spectrum from a protracted trial: Rules 1-2 let the Court pronounce judgment immediately if, on reading the pleadings, there is simply no real dispute (either overall or as against one of several defendants). Rule 3 lets the Court decide the suit on the spot if the parties are at issue but nothing further needs to be adduced for a sufficient decision. Rule 4 penalises a party who, despite the summons being for final disposal, fails without sufficient cause to produce evidence — the Court may decide against them immediately. Note: this Order is extended to apply to specified-value Commercial Disputes by the Commercial Courts Act, 2015.
essential_elements: Rule 1: if at the first hearing the parties are not at issue on any question of law or fact at all, the Court may pronounce judgment at once.

Rule 2: where there are multiple defendants and one is not at issue with the plaintiff, the Court may pronounce judgment for/against that defendant alone and continue the suit only against the remaining defendants; whenever judgment is so pronounced, the decree is drawn up dated to the judgment date.

Rule 3: where parties are at issue and issues are framed, but the Court is satisfied no further argument or evidence is required for a sufficient decision and no injustice results from proceeding forthwith, it may decide the issues and pronounce judgment immediately — whether summons was for issue-settlement only or for final disposal (with a proviso requiring party/pleader presence and no objection if summons was for issues only).

Rule 4: if summons was for final disposal and a party fails without sufficient cause to produce relied-upon evidence, the Court may pronounce judgment at once, or adjourn (after framing issues) for production of necessary evidence if it thinks fit.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Rule 3's shortcut applies even where summons was issued only for settling issues, but only with the proviso's safeguards (presence, no objection).
Order XV is applied to Commercial Disputes of specified value by the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 (Act 4 of 2016) alongside the ordinary civil suit context.
breakdown.how_to_read: A defendant with a genuinely undisputed claim against them (e.g., admitting liability in the written statement) should expect judgment under Rule 1/2 at the first hearing itself — delay tactics gain nothing once there is truly nothing to contest. Plaintiffs facing a party who stonewalls on evidence despite a final-disposal summons should press for Rule 4 relief rather than accepting repeated adjournments.

sections.title: Order XV, Rule 1 — Parties Not at Issue
sections.raw_text: 1. Parties not at issue.—(1) Where at the first hearing of a suit it appears that the parties are not at issue on any question of law or of fact, the Court may at once pronounce judgment.

breakdown.plain_summary: If, at the very first hearing, it turns out there is no genuine dispute of law or fact between the parties at all, the Court need not go through framing issues or a trial — it may pronounce judgment immediately.
essential_elements: Applies only when there is no dispute whatsoever — any live question of law or fact takes the case out of this rule.
Operative at the first hearing specifically.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Distinguish from Rule 3, which applies where the parties are at issue but little remains to decide it — Rule 1 is for cases with no issue at all.
breakdown.how_to_read: Typically invoked where the written statement effectively admits the plaint's claim or raises only legally irrelevant objections.

sections.title: Order XV, Rule 2 — One of Several Defendants Not at Issue
sections.raw_text: 2. One of several defendants not at issue.—(1) Where there are more defendants than one, and any one of the defendants is not at issue with the plaintiff on any question of law or of fact, the Court may at once pronounce judgment for or against such defendant and the suit shall proceed only against the other defendants. (2) Whenever a judgment is pronounced under this rule, a decree shall be drawn up in accordance with such judgment and the decree shall bear the date on which the judgment was pronounced.

breakdown.plain_summary: In a multi-defendant suit, if one defendant simply has no live dispute with the plaintiff (e.g., admits the claim), the Court can resolve that defendant's part of the case immediately by judgment and decree, letting the suit continue only against the remaining, genuinely contesting defendants.
essential_elements: Applies specifically to multi-defendant suits where severance is possible.
The decree for the severed defendant is dated to the judgment date, not deferred to final disposal of the whole suit.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a true partial/severed judgment — distinct from staying the whole suit pending the other defendants' trial.
breakdown.how_to_read: Useful where a nominal or formal defendant (e.g., a bank holding disputed funds as a stakeholder) admits the claim while the real contest is against a different defendant — the suit need not wait for that second defendant's trial to conclude before relief issues against the first.

sections.title: Order XV, Rule 3 — Parties at Issue
sections.raw_text: 3. Parties at issue.—(1) Where the parties are at issue on some question of law or of fact, and issues have been framed by the Court as hereinbefore provided, if the Court is satisfied that no further argument or evidence that the parties can at once adduce is required upon such of the issues as may be sufficient for the decision of the suit, and that no injustice will result from proceeding with the suit forthwith, the Court may proceed to determine such issues, and, if the finding thereon is sufficient for the decision, may pronounce judgment accordingly, whether the summons has been issued for the settlement of issues only or for the final disposal of the suit: Provided that, where the summons has been issued for the settlement of issues only, the parties or their pleaders are present and none of them objects. (2) Where the finding is not sufficient for the decision, the Court shall postpone the further hearing of the suit, and shall fix a day for the production of such further evidence, or for such further argument as the case requires.

breakdown.plain_summary: Even where real issues exist, if the Court is satisfied the parties can immediately supply all the argument/evidence needed on the issues sufficient to decide the suit — and proceeding at once would cause no injustice — it may determine those issues then and there and pronounce judgment, even if the summons only called for settling issues (subject to the presence-and-no-objection proviso). If what emerges isn't enough, the Court instead fixes a future date for the missing evidence or argument.
essential_elements: Two-part satisfaction: (a) no further argument/evidence needed beyond what parties can give right away, and (b) no injustice from proceeding forthwith.
Works regardless of whether summons was for issue-settlement only or final disposal — but if the former, the proviso's presence-and-no-objection safeguard applies.
If findings prove insufficient after all, sub-rule (2) requires postponement with a fixed future date — not an indefinite adjournment.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 'no injustice' requirement is the key guardrail — a party ambushed without fair opportunity to adduce evidence can resist an immediate Rule 3 disposal on this ground.
breakdown.how_to_read: This rule rewards well-prepared counsel who come to the first hearing ready to argue the dispositive issues on the spot — it can compress months of litigation into a single hearing where the dispute is narrow.

sections.title: Order XV, Rule 4 — Failure to Produce Evidence
sections.raw_text: 4. Failure to produce evidence.—Where the summons has been issued for the final disposal of the suit and either party fails without sufficient cause to produce the evidence on which he relies, the Court may at once pronounce judgment, or may, if it thinks fit, after framing and recording issues, adjourn the suit for the production of such evidence as may be necessary for its decision upon such issues.

breakdown.plain_summary: If the summons was explicitly for final disposal and a party, without a good reason, fails to bring the evidence it relies on, the Court has a choice: decide the suit immediately (typically against the defaulting party), or — if it thinks that's unjust — frame issues and give one more adjourned date for producing the necessary evidence.
essential_elements: Precondition: summons must have been for final disposal, not merely issue-settlement.
Trigger: failure, without sufficient cause, to produce relied-upon evidence.
Two Court options: immediate judgment, or a single structured adjournment after issues are framed/recorded.
exceptions_and_qualifications: 'Sufficient cause' is assessed case-by-case — genuine, unavoidable circumstances differ from negligence or deliberate delay.
breakdown.how_to_read: A cautionary rule for litigants who treat the final-disposal hearing casually — showing up without evidence in hand risks an adverse judgment on the spot rather than an automatic adjournment.

sections.title: Order XV-A — Case Management Hearing (Commercial Disputes)
sections.raw_text: Order XV-A, inserted for Commercial Disputes of specified value by the Commercial Courts Act, 2015, introduces a structured Case Management Hearing regime that compresses issue-framing, evidence scheduling, and argument timetabling into Court-fixed, enforceable deadlines aimed at closing arguments within six months of the first such hearing.

breakdown.plain_summary: This Order is the Commercial Courts Act's answer to chronic trial delay: instead of open-ended adjournments, the Court holds a structured Case Management Hearing (within four weeks of the affidavit of admission/denial of documents) at which it frames issues, lists witnesses, and fixes dates for every remaining stage of the trial — evidence affidavits, cross-examination, written arguments, oral arguments — with a hard target of closing arguments within six months. Rule 6 gives the Court sweeping case-management powers (strike off irrelevant evidence, consolidate proceedings, delegate evidence recording, order cost budgets) and Rule 8 arms it with escalating sanctions — up to dismissal or judgment — for non-compliance.
essential_elements: Rule 1: first Case Management Hearing must be held not later than four weeks from the filing of the affidavit of admission or denial of documents by all parties.

Rule 2: once the Court finds triable issues of fact/law exist, it passes an order framing issues (per Order XIV, informed by Order X Rule 2 examination), listing witnesses, and fixing dates for evidence affidavits, recording of evidence, written arguments, and oral arguments, with time limits for advocates' oral submissions.
Rule 3: the Court must ensure arguments close not later than six months from the first Case Management Hearing.
Rule 4: evidence recording must, as far as possible, proceed day-to-day until cross-examination of all witnesses is complete.
Rule 5: further Case Management Hearings may be held during trial to enforce the fixed dates and speed disposal.

Rule 6: lists extensive case-management powers (deciding pending Order XIII-A applications before framing issues, directing document compilations, extending/shortening time, adjourning/advancing hearings, consolidating proceedings, striking irrelevant witnesses/evidence, directing commission-recorded evidence under Order XXVI, rejecting or striking argumentative affidavit content, ordering costs budgets, and general case-management directions) — orders under this Order may be made conditional (including deposit of money) with specified consequences for non-compliance; parties may be directed to attend personally if settlement seems possible.

Rule 7: a Case Management Hearing shall not be adjourned solely for the advocate's absence, though an advance application may secure an adjournment on costs, and a justified-reason absence may still be accommodated.

Rule 8: non-compliance with a Case Management order may be met with costs, foreclosure of the defaulting party's right to file affidavits/cross-examine/argue, or — where wilful, repeated, and costs are inadequate — dismissal of the plaint or allowing the suit outright.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Order XV-A applies only to Commercial Disputes of specified value under the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 — it does not govern ordinary civil suits, which remain under the more flexible Order XIV/XVII regime.

The six-month argument-closure target in Rule 3 is an administrative discipline requirement, not a jurisdictional limitation period — missing it doesn't void proceedings, but invites Rule 8-type scrutiny of the cause.
breakdown.how_to_read: Commercial litigators must treat the first Case Management Hearing as the single most important procedural event in the suit — the entire trial calendar, evidence strategy, and argument structure gets locked in there. Rule 8's escalating sanctions mean missed Case Management deadlines are not merely inconvenient; repeated or wilful non-compliance can forfeit a party's right to present its case at all.

sections.title: Order XV-A, Rule 1 — First Case Management Hearing
sections.raw_text: 1. First Case Management Hearing.—The Court shall hold the first Case Management Hearing, not later than four weeks from the date of filing of affidavit of admission or denial of documents by all parties to the suit.
key_terms: affidavit of admission or denial of documents

breakdown.plain_summary: The clock for the first Case Management Hearing starts running from the date all parties have filed their affidavits of admission/denial of documents (the Commercial Courts disclosure mechanism under Order XI-CC) — the Court must convene within four weeks of that date.
essential_elements: Trigger event: filing of the affidavit of admission/denial of documents by all parties.
Deadline: not later than four weeks thereafter.
breakdown.how_to_read: Counsel should track the affidavit-of-admission filing date closely, since it silently starts this four-week clock without a separate notice requirement.

sections.title: Order XV-A, Rule 2 — Orders to Be Passed in a Case Management Hearing
sections.raw_text: 2. Orders to be passed in a Case Management Hearing.—In a Case Management Hearing, after hearing the parties, and once it finds that there are issues of fact and law which require to be tried, the Court may pass an order–– (a) framing the issues between the parties in accordance with Order XIV of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908), after examining pleadings, documents and documents produced before it, and on examination conducted by the Court under Rule 2 of Order X, if required; (b) listing witnesses to be examined by the parties; (c) fixing the date by which affidavit of evidence to be filed by parties; (d) fixing the date on which evidence of the witnesses of the parties to be recorded; (e) fixing the date by which written arguments are to be filed before the Court by the parties; (f) fixing the date on which oral arguments are to be heard by the Court; and (g) setting time limits for parties and their advocates to address oral arguments.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the core scheduling order — once the Court determines there are triable issues, it frames them (per Order XIV, informed by the pleadings/documents/Order X Rule 2 examination) and, in the same breath, fixes the entire remaining trial calendar: witness list, evidence-affidavit deadline, evidence-recording date, written-argument deadline, oral-argument date, and time limits for oral submissions.
essential_elements: Seven distinct components bundled into one order: issue-framing plus six scheduling directions covering the rest of the trial.
Issue-framing under this rule expressly cross-references Order XIV and the Order X Rule 2 oral examination.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This order issues only after the Court first finds triable issues exist — if parties are not genuinely at issue, Order XV's immediate-disposal route applies instead.
breakdown.how_to_read: Advocates should come to this hearing prepared with a complete witness list and a realistic self-imposed timetable proposal — the dates fixed here bind the remainder of the case under the Rule 8 sanctions regime.

sections.title: Order XV-A, Rule 3 — Time Limit for the Completion of a Trial
sections.raw_text: 3. Time limit for the completion of a trial.—In fixing dates or setting time limits for the purposes of Rule 2 of this Order, the Court shall ensure that the arguments are closed not later than six months from the date of the first Case Management Hearing.

breakdown.plain_summary: Whatever specific dates the Court fixes under Rule 2, it must structure them so that oral/written arguments conclude within six months of the first Case Management Hearing — a hard outer ceiling on the whole evidence-and-argument phase.
essential_elements: The six-month clock runs from the first Case Management Hearing, not from suit filing or issue-framing alone.
It is the Court's obligation to structure the Rule 2 schedule to meet this ceiling.
breakdown.how_to_read: A practitioner can cite this provision to resist excessive piecemeal adjournment requests from the opposing side that threaten to blow past the six-month target.

sections.title: Order XV-A, Rule 4 — Recording of Oral Evidence on a Day-to-Day Basis
sections.raw_text: 4. Recording of oral evidence on a day-to-day basis.—The Court shall, as far as possible, ensure that the recording of evidence shall be carried on, on a day-to-day basis until the cross-examination of all the witnesses is complete.

breakdown.plain_summary: Evidence recording in a Commercial Dispute should, wherever feasible, run continuously day-to-day rather than in scattered, spread-out hearings, until every witness's cross-examination is finished — mirroring the Order XVII Rule 1 proviso for ordinary suits but stated as a specific Commercial Courts obligation.
essential_elements: Obligation qualified by 'as far as possible' — not an absolute bar on any gap.
Applies through completion of cross-examination of all witnesses, not just examination-in-chief.
breakdown.how_to_read: Useful leverage against a party seeking to fragment cross-examination across many separated dates to exhaust or confuse a witness, or simply to delay.

sections.title: Order XV-A, Rule 5 — Case Management Hearings During a Trial
sections.raw_text: 5. Case Management Hearings during a trial.—The Court may, if necessary, also hold Case Management Hearings anytime during the trial to issue appropriate orders so as to ensure adherence by the parties to the dates fixed under Rule 2 and facilitate speedy disposal of the suit.

breakdown.plain_summary: The Rule 1 hearing is not the only one — the Court can convene further Case Management Hearings at any point during the trial if needed to keep the parties on track with the Rule 2 schedule and push the suit toward speedy disposal.
essential_elements: Discretionary and need-triggered — not mandated at fixed intervals.
Purpose is enforcement of the existing schedule and acceleration, not re-opening settled issues.
breakdown.how_to_read: A party experiencing the other side's repeated non-compliance should proactively seek a mid-trial Case Management Hearing under this rule rather than waiting passively for the final hearing to raise the issue.

sections.title: Order XV-A, Rule 6 — Powers of the Court in a Case Management Hearing
sections.raw_text: 6. Powers of the Court in a Case Management Hearing.—(1) In any Case Management Hearing held under this Order, the Court shall have the power to— (a) prior to the framing of issues, hear and decide any pending application filed by the parties under Order XIII-A; (b) direct parties to file compilations of documents or pleadings relevant and necessary for framing issues; (c) extend or shorten the time for compliance with any practice, direction or Court order if it finds sufficient reason to do so; (d) adjourn or bring forward a hearing if it finds sufficient reason to do so; (e) direct a party to attend the Court for the purposes of examination under Rule 2 of Order X; (f) consolidate proceedings; (g) strike off the name of any witness or evidence that it deems irrelevant to the issues framed; (h) direct a separate trial of any issue; (i) decide the order in which issues are to be tried; (j) exclude an issue from consideration; (k) dismiss or give judgment on a claim after a decision on a preliminary issue; (l) direct that evidence be recorded by a Commission where necessary in accordance with Order XXVI; (m) reject any affidavit of evidence filed by the parties for containing irrelevant, inadmissible or argumentative material; (n) strike off any parts of the affidavit of evidence filed by the parties containing irrelevant, inadmissible or argumentative material; (o) delegate the recording of evidence to such authority appointed by the Court for this purpose; (p) pass any order relating to the monitoring of recording the evidence by a commission or any other authority; (q) order any party to file and exchange a costs budget; (r) issue directions or pass any order for the purpose of managing the case and furthering the overriding objective of ensuring the efficient disposal of the suit. (2) When the Court passes an order in exercise of its powers under this Order, it may— (a) make it subject to conditions, including a condition to pay a sum of money into Court; and (b) specify the consequence of failure to comply with the order or a condition. (3) While fixing the date for a Case Management Hearing, the Court may direct that the parties also be present for such Case Management Hearing, if it is of the view that there is a possibility of settlement between the parties.

breakdown.plain_summary: Rule 6 is the toolbox: eighteen distinct case-management powers ranging from deciding pending Order XIII-A summary judgment applications before issues are even framed, through document compilation directions, time extensions, consolidation, striking irrelevant witnesses/evidence, commission-based evidence recording, rejecting argumentative affidavits, cost-budget orders, and a general residuary power to further the 'overriding objective' of efficient disposal. Any order under this toolbox can be made conditional (including a money deposit) with pre-specified consequences for default, and the Court can require personal party attendance where settlement seems achievable.
essential_elements: Eighteen enumerated powers under sub-rule (1), spanning pre-issue applications, scheduling, evidence control, and consolidation/separation of issues.
Sub-rule (2) allows conditional orders (including a money-deposit condition) with specified default consequences — mirroring the Order XIII-A Rule 7 conditional-order mechanism.
Sub-rule (3) lets the Court compel personal party presence specifically where it sees settlement potential.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (a)'s pre-issue-framing disposal of Order XIII-A applications shows the two Orders are designed to interlock — summary judgment is meant to be resolved before full issue-framing wherever possible.
The 'overriding objective of ensuring the efficient disposal of the suit' residuary clause (r) gives this rule considerable breadth beyond the sixteen specifically enumerated powers.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the single most powerful case-management toolkit in the CPC — commercial litigators should anticipate that irrelevant witnesses, padded affidavits, and delay tactics face a much harder time surviving a Case Management Hearing than an ordinary civil trial's more permissive culture.

sections.title: Order XV-A, Rule 7 — Adjournment of Case Management Hearing
sections.raw_text: 7.
