exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a tactical option for the party beginning, not a right available to the other party — only the party with the right to begin can choose to reserve evidence this way.
The structure prevents the other party from being deprived of a chance to respond specifically to late-produced evidence, while preserving the beginning party's overall right of reply.
breakdown.how_to_read: Useful where the burden of proof is split across issues (e.g., plaintiff proves execution of a document, defendant must prove a specific defence like fraud or undue influence) — plan whether to lead all evidence up front or hold back evidence on issues the other side bears the burden on.

sections.title: Order XVIII Rule 3A — Party to appear before other witnesses
sections.raw_text: 3A. Party to appear before other witnesses.—Where a party himself wishes to appear as a witness, he shall so appear before any other witness on his behalf has been examined, unless the Court, for reasons to be recorded, permits him to appear as his own witness at a later stage.

breakdown.plain_summary: If a party to the suit wants to testify as a witness in his own case, he must do so before any of his other witnesses are examined — he cannot sit back, hear how his other witnesses testify, and then tailor his own evidence accordingly. The Court can permit a later appearance only for recorded reasons.
essential_elements: Party wishes to appear as his own witness.
General rule: must appear before any other witness on his behalf is examined.
Exception: Court permits later appearance, but only for reasons recorded in writing.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This rule exists precisely to prevent a party from shaping his own testimony after hearing what his other witnesses have said — a credibility safeguard.
The exception is narrowly available and requires the Court to record its reasons, not a routine indulgence.
breakdown.how_to_read: A short but important sequencing rule for any case where the party himself will testify — plan to call the party-witness first in the party's own evidence unless there is a genuine, recordable reason to depart from that order.

sections.title: Order XVIII Rule 4 — Recording of evidence
sections.raw_text:
4. Recording of evidence.—(1) In every case, the examination-in-chief of a witness shall be on affidavit and copies thereof shall be supplied to the opposite party by the party who calls him for evidence: Provided that where documents are filed and the parties rely upon the documents, the proof and admissibility of such documents which are filed along with affidavit shall be subject to the orders of the Court.
(1A) The affidavits of evidence of all witnesses whose evidence is proposed to be led by a party shall be filed simultaneously by that party at the time directed in the first Case Management Hearing.
(1B) A party shall not lead additional evidence by the affidavit of any witness (including of a witness who has already filed an affidavit) unless sufficient cause is made out in an application for that purpose and an order, giving reasons, permitting such additional affidavit is passed by the Court.
(1C) A party shall however have the right to withdraw any of the affidavits so filed at any time prior to commencement of cross-examination of that witness, without any adverse inference being drawn based on such withdrawal: Provided that any other party shall be entitled to tender as evidence and rely upon any admission made in such withdrawn affidavit.
(2) The evidence (cross-examination and re-examination) of the witness in attendance, whose evidence (examination-in-chief) by affidavit has been furnished to the Court, shall be taken either by the Court or by the Commissioner appointed by it: Provided that the Court may, while appointing a commission under this sub-rule, consider taking into account such relevant factors as it thinks fit.
(3) The Court or the Commissioner, as the case may be, shall record evidence either in writing or mechanically in the presence of the Judge or of the Commissioner, as the case may be, and where such evidence is recorded by the Commissioner he shall return such evidence together with his report in writing signed by him to the Court appointing him and the evidence taken under it shall form part of the record of the suit.
(4) The Commissioner may record such remarks as it thinks material respecting the demeanour of any witness while under examination: Provided that any objection raised during the recording of evidence before the Commissioner shall be recorded by him and decided by the Court at the stage of arguments.
(5) The report of the Commissioner shall be submitted to the Court appointing the commission within sixty days from the date of issue of the commission unless the Court for reasons to be recorded in writing extends the time.
(6) The High Court or the District Judge, as the case may be, shall prepare a panel of Commissioners to record the evidence under this rule.
(7) The Court may by general or special order fix the amount to be paid as remuneration for the services of the Commissioner.
(8) The provisions of rules 16, 16A, 17 and 18 of Order XXVI, in so far as they are applicable, shall apply to the issue, execution and return of such commission under this rule.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the modern engine for recording oral evidence. Examination-in-chief of every witness is taken on affidavit, filed with the opposite party, and — in the Commercial Courts regime — all of a party's witness affidavits must be filed together at the time fixed in the first Case Management Hearing. A party cannot sneak in extra affidavit evidence later without sufficient cause and a reasoned court order, though a filed affidavit can be withdrawn before cross-examination begins without penalty (though the other side can still use any admissions in it). Actual cross-examination and re-examination happen before the Court itself or before a Commissioner it appoints; whoever records it must note demeanour, defer objection-rulings to the argument stage, and submit the Commissioner's report within 60 days unless extended for recorded reasons. Courts maintain standing panels of Commissioners, fix their remuneration, and Order XXVI's commission-execution machinery (rules 16, 16A, 17, 18) applies to how the commission itself is issued and returned.
essential_elements: Examination-in-chief: affidavit, copies to opposite party, document-proof subject to Court's orders.
Simultaneous filing of all witness affidavits at the time fixed in the first Case Management Hearing.
Additional affidavit evidence: only on sufficient cause shown and a reasoned order.
Withdrawal of a filed affidavit: permitted before cross-examination starts, no adverse inference, but admissions in it remain usable by the other side.
Cross-examination/re-examination: before Court or an appointed Commissioner.
Commissioner's report: within 60 days (extendable for recorded reasons), demeanour remarks noted, objections deferred to arguments stage.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Sub-rules (1A)-(1C) tie this rule directly to the Case Management Hearing machinery introduced for commercial disputes under Order XV-A, though Rule 4 itself applies generally as substituted by the 2002 Amendment Act.
The Commissioner's demeanour-recording power under sub-rule (4) is advisory input for the Court, not a finding that binds the Court's own assessment of credibility.
Objections raised during Commissioner-recorded evidence are preserved but not decided at that stage — they wait until final arguments, which keeps the recording process moving.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the single most frequently invoked rule at the evidence stage of modern Indian civil trials — read sub-rule (1) for the affidavit-in-chief requirement, sub-rules (1A)-(1C) for filing discipline, sub-rule (2) for who conducts cross-examination, and sub-rules (3)-(8) for the mechanics of Commissioner-recorded evidence, timelines, and cost.

sections.title: Order XVIII Rule 5 — How evidence shall be taken in appealable cases
sections.raw_text:
5. How evidence shall be taken in appealable cases.—In case in which an appeal is allowed, the evidence of each witness shall be,—
(a) taken down in the language of the Court,—
(i) in writing by, or in the presence and under the personal direction and superintendence of, the Judge, or
(ii) from the dictation of the Judge directly on a typewriter; or
(b) if the Judge, for reasons to be recorded, so directs, recorded mechanically in the language of the Court in the presence of the Judge.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where a suit is of the kind in which an appeal lies, each witness's evidence must be taken down in the Court's own language — either in writing by or under the Judge's personal direction, or by the Judge dictating directly onto a typewriter. Mechanical recording (audio) is allowed only if the Judge records reasons for choosing that method, and it must still happen in the Judge's presence.
essential_elements: Case is one in which an appeal is allowed.
Evidence taken down in the language of the Court.
Method: writing under the Judge's personal direction/superintendence, or direct dictation to a typewriter, or (with recorded reasons) mechanical recording in the Judge's presence.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The requirement is tied to appealability because an appellate court needs a reliable, verbatim-equivalent record to review findings of fact.
Mechanical recording is the exception requiring justification, not the default method under this rule.
breakdown.how_to_read: Distinguish from Rule 13 (unappealable cases), which permits a lighter memorandum-only record — the appealability of the suit is the trigger that decides which evidence-recording standard applies.

sections.title: Order XVIII Rule 6 — When deposition to be interpreted
sections.raw_text: 6. When deposition to be interpreted.—Where the evidence is taken down in a language different from that in which it is given, and the witness does not understand the language in which it is taken down, the evidence as taken down in writing shall be interpreted to him in the language in which it is given.

breakdown.plain_summary: If the evidence is recorded in a language other than the one the witness actually testified in, and the witness cannot understand the language it was recorded in, the written deposition must be read back and interpreted to the witness in the language he actually gave the evidence in — so he can confirm its accuracy.
essential_elements: Evidence taken down in a language different from the language it was given in.
Witness does not understand the recording language.
Mandatory interpretation of the recorded deposition back to the witness in his own language.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This rule protects the integrity of the record by ensuring the witness can verify that what was written down accurately reflects what he said.
Applies specifically where there is a language mismatch — not a general requirement to interpret every deposition.
breakdown.how_to_read: A safeguard rule to keep in mind in multilingual courtrooms — if a witness testifies in a regional language but the court record is kept in the official court language, the deposition must be translated back for the witness's confirmation.

sections.title: Order XVIII Rule 7 — Evidence under section 138
sections.raw_text: 7. Evidence under section 138.—Evidence taken down under section 138 shall be in the form prescribed by rule 5 and shall be read over and signed and, as occasion may require, interpreted and corrected as if it were evidence taken down under that rule.

breakdown.plain_summary: Evidence recorded under Section 138 (which deals with evidence taken by commission or otherwise outside the ordinary trial) must follow the same form Rule 5 prescribes for appealable-case evidence, and must similarly be read over to the witness, signed, and — where needed — interpreted and corrected just as if it had been recorded directly under Rule 5.
essential_elements: Evidence taken down under Section 138.
Must follow Rule 5's prescribed form.
Must be read over, signed, and (where needed) interpreted and corrected as under Rule 5.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This rule simply extends Rule 5's formal safeguards to Section 138 evidence rather than creating a separate standard.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read together with Section 138 of the main Code and Order XVIII Rule 5 — this rule is a cross-reference ensuring consistency of form rather than an independent procedural innovation.

sections.title: Order XVIII Rule 8 — Memorandum when evidence not taken down by Judge
sections.raw_text: 8. Memorandum when evidence not taken down by Judge.—Where the evidence is not taken down in writing by the Judge, or from his dictation in the open Court, or recorded mechanically in his presence, he shall be bound, as the examination of each witness proceeds, to make a memorandum of the substance of what each witness deposes, and such memorandum shall be written and signed by the Judge and shall form part of the record.

breakdown.plain_summary: If evidence is not being taken down in writing by the Judge himself, by his open-court dictation, or by mechanical recording in his presence, then as each witness is examined the Judge must still make a signed memorandum capturing the substance of what the witness said, and that memorandum becomes part of the official record.
essential_elements: Evidence not taken down in writing by the Judge, from his dictation, or mechanically recorded in his presence.
Judge's obligation: make a substance-memorandum as each witness is examined.
Memorandum written and signed by the Judge; forms part of the record.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a fallback record-keeping duty ensuring that even where the primary recording methods of Rule 5 are not used, there is still an authenticated record of what each witness said.
breakdown.how_to_read: A residual safeguard rule — relevant mainly in lower courts or situations where full verbatim recording per Rule 5 was not practically done; ensures no examination goes completely unrecorded.

sections.title: Order XVIII Rule 9 — When evidence may be taken in English
sections.raw_text:
9. When evidence may be taken in English.—(1) Where English is not the language of the Court, but all the parties to the suit who appear in person, and the pleaders of such of the parties as appear by pleaders, do not object to having such evidence as is given in English, being taken down in English, the judge may so take it down or cause it to be taken down.
(2) Where evidence is not given in English but all the parties who appear in person, and the pleaders of such of the parties as appear by pleaders, do not object to having such evidence being taken down in English, the Judge may take down, or cause to be taken down, such evidence in English.

breakdown.plain_summary: Even where English is not the official language of the Court, the Judge may record evidence in English if every party and pleader present consents — whether the evidence was actually given in English (sub-rule 1) or given in another language but the parties agree it may be recorded in English anyway (sub-rule 2).
essential_elements: English is not the Court's official language.
No objection from any party or pleader present.
Judge's discretion to take down (or cause to be taken down) the evidence in English, whether or not it was given in English.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is consent-based — a single party's or pleader's objection blocks recording in English under this rule.
breakdown.how_to_read: A practical convenience rule for courts where English is commonly used among lawyers even though it is not the formal language of the Court — always confirm no party objects before relying on this provision.

sections.title: Order XVIII Rule 10 — Any particular question and answer may be taken down
sections.raw_text: 10. Any particular question and answer may be taken down.—The Court may, of its own motion or on the application of any party or his pleader, take down any particular question and answer, or any objection to any question, if there appears to be any special reason for so doing.

breakdown.plain_summary: Beyond the standard recording methods, the Court has a discretionary power — exercisable on its own or on a party's application — to specifically note down a particular question and its answer, or an objection raised to a question, whenever there is some special reason to preserve that exact exchange in the record.
essential_elements: Special reason for specifically recording a question/answer/objection.
Trigger: Court's own motion or application by a party/pleader.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a targeted, discretionary recording tool distinct from the general evidence-recording obligations of Rules 5-8 — used where a specific exchange may matter later (e.g., on appeal or for a perjury/contempt question).
breakdown.how_to_read: Useful tactically: if a particular answer is likely to be significant, a party's pleader can apply under this rule to have it specifically taken down verbatim rather than relying on the general memorandum.

sections.title: Order XVIII Rule 11 — Questions objected to and allowed by Court
sections.raw_text: 11. Questions objected to and allowed by Court.—Where any question put to a witness is objected to by a party or his pleader, and the Court allows the same to be put, the Judge shall take down the question, the answer, the objection and the name of the person making it, together with the decision of the Court thereon.

breakdown.plain_summary: If a question put to a witness is objected to, but the Court nonetheless allows the question to be asked, the Judge must record the question itself, the answer given, the objection raised, who raised it, and the Court's decision on the objection — preserving the full exchange for the record.
essential_elements: Objection raised to a question put to a witness.
Court allows the question to be put despite the objection.
Mandatory recording of: question, answer, objection, objector's name, and the Court's ruling.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This creates a complete, appeal-ready record of contested evidentiary exchanges, letting an appellate court assess both the evidence and the correctness of the trial court's ruling on admissibility.
breakdown.how_to_read: Pair with Rule 4(4)'s proviso (objections during Commissioner-recorded evidence are preserved but decided only at the arguments stage) — this rule is the direct-before-Court analogue, where the ruling happens immediately.

sections.title: Order XVIII Rule 12 — Remarks on demeanour of witnesses
sections.raw_text: 12. Remarks on demeanour of witnesses.—The Court may record such remarks as it thinks material respecting the demeanour of any witness while under examination.

breakdown.plain_summary: The Court may note down, as part of the record, any observations it considers material about how a witness behaved or conducted himself while being examined — useful later in assessing credibility.
essential_elements: Court's discretion to record demeanour remarks it considers material.
Applies while the witness is under examination.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This mirrors the Commissioner's demeanour-recording power under Rule 4(4), but here it is the Court's own direct observation when conducting the examination itself.
breakdown.how_to_read: A short enabling provision — demeanour notes made under this rule often become relevant when a judgment explains why one witness's testimony was preferred over another's.

sections.title: Order XVIII Rule 13 — Memorandum of evidence in unappealable cases
sections.raw_text: 13. Memorandum of evidence in unappealable cases.—In cases in which an appeal is not allowed it shall not be necessary to take down or dictate or record the evidence of the witnesses at length; but the Judge, as the examination of each witness proceeds shall make in writing, or dictate directly on the typewriter, or cause to be mechanically recorded, a memorandum of the substance of what the witness deposes, and such memorandum shall be signed by the Judge or otherwise authenticated, and shall form part of the record.
key_terms: memorandum in lieu of verbatim record

breakdown.plain_summary: For suits where no appeal lies, the Code relaxes the recording burden: the Judge need not take down evidence verbatim, and may instead make (in writing, by direct typewriter dictation, or mechanical recording) a substance-memorandum of each witness's testimony, signed or otherwise authenticated by the Judge, which then forms part of the record.
essential_elements: Case is one in which an appeal is not allowed.
Relaxed standard: substance-memorandum instead of verbatim record.
Memorandum signed or otherwise authenticated by the Judge.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The contrast with Rule 5 (appealable cases, requiring a near-verbatim or dictated record) is the core logic of this rule — the recording burden scales with the stakes of appellate review.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read directly against Rule 5 — whether a suit is appealable or not is the dividing line between the full recording regime of Rule 5 and the lighter memorandum regime of Rule 13.

sections.title: Order XVIII Rule 15 — Power to deal with evidence taken before another Judge
sections.raw_text:
15. Power to deal with evidence taken before another Judge.—(1) Where a Judge is prevented by death, transfer or other cause from concluding the trial of a suit, his successor may deal with any evidence or memorandum taken down or made under the foregoing rules as if such evidence or memorandum had been taken down or made by him or under his direction under the said rules and may proceed with the suit from the stage at which his predecessor left it.
(2) The provisions of sub-rule (1) shall, so far as they are applicable, be deemed to apply to evidence taken in a suit transferred under section 24.

breakdown.plain_summary: If a Judge cannot finish a trial — because of death, transfer, or any other cause — the Judge who succeeds him can treat all evidence and memoranda already recorded as if he himself had recorded them, and simply continue the suit from wherever his predecessor left off, without having to restart the trial. The same principle applies, so far as relevant, to a suit transferred to another court under Section 24.
essential_elements: Original Judge prevented from concluding the trial (death, transfer, or other cause).
Successor Judge's power to treat predecessor's recorded evidence/memoranda as his own.
Continuation from the stage the predecessor left, not a fresh trial.
Extension to Section 24 transfers.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This rule prevents the enormous waste and delay that would result if every change of Judge required a full re-trial.

It does not prevent a party from seeking re-examination of a witness where genuinely necessary (e.g., for cross-examination that was never completed) — it simply removes the default requirement to start over.
breakdown.how_to_read: An important continuity provision given how often judicial transfers occur in the Indian subordinate judiciary — read with Section 24 for suits that move between courts mid-trial.

sections.title: Order XVIII Rule 16 — Power to examine witness immediately
sections.raw_text:
16. Power to examine witness immediately.—(1) Where a witness is about to leave the jurisdiction of the Court, or other sufficient cause is shown to the satisfaction of the Court why his evidence should be taken immediately, the Court may, upon the application of any party or of the witness, at any time after the institution of the suit, take the evidence of such witness in manner hereinbefore provided.
(2) Where such evidence is not taken forthwith and in the presence of the parties, such notice as the Court thinks sufficient, of the day fixed for the examination, shall be given to the parties.
(3) The evidence so taken shall be read over to the witness, and, if he admits it to be correct, shall be signed by him, and the Judge shall, if necessary, correct the same, and shall sign it, and it may then be read at any hearing of the suit.

breakdown.plain_summary: If a witness is about to leave the Court's jurisdiction, or there is some other sufficient cause to take his evidence right away, the Court can — on application by any party or even the witness himself, at any point after the suit is filed — record that witness's evidence immediately, even before the regular hearing. If this isn't done at once in the parties' presence, they must be given sufficient notice of when it will happen. The recorded evidence is read back to the witness, signed by him if correct (with Judge's corrections as needed and signature), and can then be read into the record at any later hearing.
essential_elements: Witness about to leave jurisdiction, or other sufficient cause shown.
Application by any party or the witness.
Can be done at any time after institution of the suit.
Notice to parties if not taken forthwith in their presence.
Evidence read over, admitted as correct, signed by witness and Judge.
Admissible at any later hearing of the suit.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is an early/out-of-sequence evidence-taking power distinct from the ordinary trial sequence of Rules 1-4 — it exists specifically to prevent loss of testimony.
breakdown.how_to_read: A practical tool when a key witness (e.g., an elderly witness, or one relocating abroad) may not be available by the time the suit reaches its ordinary evidence stage — apply promptly once the risk becomes apparent.

sections.title: Order XVIII Rule 17 — Court may recall and examine witness
sections.raw_text: 17. Court may recall and examine witness.—The Court may at any stage of a suit recall any witness who has been examined and may (subject to the law of evidence for the time being in force) put such questions to him as the Court thinks fit.

breakdown.plain_summary: At any stage of the suit, the Court can recall a witness who has already testified and put its own questions to him, subject to the ordinary law of evidence — a power the Court exercises on its own initiative to clarify or complete the record, not merely at a party's request.
essential_elements: Witness already examined.
Court's discretion to recall at any stage of the suit.
Questions put subject to the law of evidence in force.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a Court-driven power distinct from either party seeking further examination — it reflects the Court's own truth-seeking role in civil trials.
breakdown.how_to_read: A frequently invoked residual power — useful where the Court itself identifies a gap or ambiguity in a witness's earlier testimony that needs clarification before judgment.

sections.title: Order XVIII Rule 18 — Power of Court to inspect
sections.raw_text: 18. Power of Court to inspect.—The Court may at any stage of a suit inspect any property or thing concerning which any question may arise and where the Court inspects any property or thing it shall, as soon as may be practicable, make a memorandum of any relevant facts observed at such inspection and such memorandum shall form a part of the record of the suit.

breakdown.plain_summary: The Court may, at any stage, personally inspect any property or item that is the subject of a question in the suit (for example, a disputed boundary, a piece of machinery, or the layout of premises). After such an inspection, the Court must, as soon as practicable, record a memorandum of the relevant facts it observed, and that memorandum becomes part of the trial record.
essential_elements: Property or thing concerning which a question arises in the suit.
Court's discretion to inspect at any stage.
Mandatory memorandum of relevant observed facts, made part of the record.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The memorandum requirement ensures the Court's personal, extra-courtroom observations are transparently captured and available for appellate scrutiny, rather than remaining an unrecorded impression.
breakdown.how_to_read: Common in property disputes (boundary suits, encroachment, specific performance involving immovable property) — a party seeking a local inspection should request it be followed by a recorded memorandum under this rule.

sections.title: Order XVIII Rule 19 — Power to get statements recorded on commission
sections.raw_text: 19. Power to get statements recorded on commission.—Notwithstanding anything contained in these rules, the court may, instead of examining witnesses in open court, direct their statements to be recorded on commission under rule 4A of Order XXVI.

breakdown.plain_summary: Overriding the ordinary rules requiring open-court examination, the Court may instead direct that a witness's statement be recorded on commission under Order XXVI Rule 4A — useful where open-court examination is impractical or unnecessary.
essential_elements: Non-obstante override of the ordinary open-court examination rules.
Court's discretion to direct recording on commission.
Mechanism: Order XXVI Rule 4A.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This rule is the general gateway into Order XXVI's commission machinery for recording evidence, distinct from Rule 4's specific affidavit-and-Commissioner regime for cross-examination.
breakdown.how_to_read: Cross-refer to Order XXVI (Commissions) whenever a case calls for evidence to be taken outside the ordinary courtroom setting — this rule is the enabling link from Order XVIII into that broader commission framework.

sections.title: Order XIX — Affidavits
sections.raw_text: Order XIX of the First Schedule to the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 governs proof of facts by affidavit: the Court's power to order a fact proved by affidavit, the right to demand the deponent's attendance for cross-examination, what an affidavit may properly contain, and — for specified-value commercial disputes under the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 — a detailed evidence-control, redaction, and formatting regime for affidavits of evidence.

breakdown.plain_summary: Order XIX lets a Court shortcut formal oral proof by allowing facts to be established through sworn affidavits (Rule 1), while preserving the other side's right to insist on the deponent's attendance for cross-examination if a witness is genuinely wanted and available (Rule 2). Rule 3 confines affidavits to facts within the deponent's own knowledge, except for interlocutory applications where stated belief is allowed if its grounds are given, and penalises affidavits cluttered with hearsay or argument through a costs sanction. Rules 4-6, applicable to specified-value commercial disputes under the Commercial Courts Act, 2015, add a far more structured regime: the Court's power to control what evidence is led and how, the power to redact or reject non-evidentiary portions of an affidavit of examination-in-chief, and detailed formatting rules an affidavit of evidence must follow (chronological, paragraphed, sourced for belief/information, paginated, annexed).
essential_elements: Rule 1's affidavit-proof power is discretionary and 'for sufficient reason' — not every fact can simply be proved by affidavit over objection.

Rule 2's cross-examination safeguard is the quid pro quo for allowing affidavit evidence: a party cannot hide a witness behind an affidavit if the other side genuinely wants, and can produce, that witness for cross-examination.

Rules 4-6 were inserted by the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 (Act 4 of 2016) and apply only to commercial disputes of specified value, layering a civil-litigation-reform regime of evidence control, redaction, and strict affidavit formatting on top of the general Rules 1-3.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Order XIX interacts directly with Order XVIII Rule 4's affidavit-in-chief regime — Rule 1 is the general affidavit-evidence power, while Order XVIII Rule 4 is the specific application of affidavit evidence to examination-in-chief at trial; Rules 5 and 6 here give the Commercial Courts machinery its teeth for weeding out argumentative or legally conclusory affidavits before they clutter the record.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Rules 1-3 as the general law of affidavit evidence applicable to every suit, then check whether the matter is a specified-value commercial dispute under the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 to see if Rules 4-6's evidence-control, redaction, and formatting regime also applies.

sections.title: Order XIX Rule 1 — Power to order any point to be proved by affidavit
sections.raw_text: 1. Power to order any point to be proved by affidavit.—Any Court may at any time for sufficient reason order that any particular fact or facts may be proved by affidavit, or that the affidavit of any witness may be read at the hearing, on such conditions as the Court thinks reasonable: Provided that where it appears to the Court that either party bona fide desires the production of a witness for cross-examination, and that such witness can be produced, an order shall not be made authorising the evidence of such witness to be given by affidavit.

breakdown.plain_summary: A Court can, for sufficient reason, order that a particular fact be proved by affidavit instead of oral testimony, or that a witness's affidavit be read at the hearing, subject to whatever conditions the Court thinks reasonable. But this shortcut is blocked where either party genuinely wants to cross-examine that witness and the witness can actually be produced — in that situation the Court must not allow the evidence to go in merely by affidavit.
essential_elements: Sufficient reason for ordering proof by affidavit.
Court's discretion over conditions attached to the order.
Bar: no such order where a party bona fide wants, and can secure, cross-examination of that witness.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The proviso is the key safeguard — it prevents affidavit evidence from being used to insulate a witness from cross-examination when the opposing party has a genuine and practically achievable demand to test that witness.
breakdown.how_to_read: The foundational affidavit-evidence power — read the proviso carefully whenever opposing a request to prove a contested fact purely by affidavit; a bona fide, practicable demand for cross-examination defeats the shortcut.

sections.title: Order XIX Rule 2 — Power to order attendance of deponent for cross-examination
sections.raw_text:
2. Power to order attendance of deponent for cross-examination.—(1) Upon any application evidence may be given by affidavit, but the Court may, at the instance of either party, order the attendance for cross-examination of the deponent.
(2) Such attendance shall be in Court, unless the deponent is exempted from personal appearance in Court or the Court otherwise directs.

breakdown.plain_summary: On any application, evidence can be given by affidavit, but either party can ask the Court to order the deponent to attend in person for cross-examination. That attendance must be in Court itself unless the deponent is exempt from personal appearance or the Court directs otherwise (e.g., examination elsewhere).
essential_elements: Affidavit evidence filed in connection with an application.
Either party's right to seek an order for the deponent's attendance for cross-examination.
Default venue: in Court, subject to exemption from personal appearance or a contrary Court direction.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This rule operationalises the Rule 1 proviso's cross-examination safeguard specifically for affidavit evidence filed on applications (as opposed to affidavits of evidence at trial, governed by Order XVIII Rule 4).
breakdown.how_to_read: Commonly invoked on interlocutory applications (e.g., injunction applications supported by affidavit) — if the opposing party doubts the deponent's assertions, this rule is the route to compel his attendance for cross-examination.

sections.title: Order XIX Rule 3 — Matters to which affidavits shall be confined
sections.raw_text:
3. Matters to which affidavits shall be confined.—(1) Affidavits shall be confined to such facts as the deponent is able of his own knowledge to prove, except on interlocutory applications, on which statements of his belief may be admitted: provided that the grounds thereof are stated.
(2) The costs of every affidavit which shall unnecessarily set forth matters of hearsay or argumentative matter, or copies of or extracts from documents, shall (unless the Court otherwise directs) be paid by the party filing the same.

breakdown.plain_summary: An affidavit must generally stick to facts the deponent personally knows to be true. The exception is interlocutory applications, where the deponent may state matters of belief, provided he also states the grounds for that belief. If an affidavit unnecessarily includes hearsay, argumentative content, or needless document copies/extracts, the party filing it bears the costs of that excess unless the Court directs otherwise.
essential_elements: General rule: affidavit confined to the deponent's own knowledge.
Exception: interlocutory applications permit stated belief, with grounds given.
Costs sanction for unnecessary hearsay, argumentative matter, or document copies/extracts.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The costs sanction under sub-rule (2) is a built-in discipline mechanism meant to keep affidavits factual and concise rather than argumentative pleadings in disguise.
breakdown.how_to_read: A drafting-discipline rule every practitioner should keep in mind when settling an affidavit — confine statements to personal knowledge (or clearly-grounded belief on interlocutory matters) and strip out argument, which belongs in submissions, not the affidavit.

sections.title: Order XIX Rule 4 — Court may control evidence
sections.raw_text:
4. Court may control evidence.—(1) The Court may, by directions, regulate the evidence as to issues on which it requires evidence and the manner in which such evidence may be placed before the Court.
(2) The Court may, in its discretion and for reasons to be recorded in writing, exclude evidence that would otherwise be produced by the parties.

[Applicable to commercial disputes of a specified value by Act 4 of 2016, s. 16 and the Schedule, w.e.f. 23-10-2015.]

breakdown.plain_summary: In specified-value commercial disputes, the Court has active case-management power over evidence: it can direct exactly which issues need evidence and how that evidence should be placed before it, and it can exclude evidence that would otherwise be led by the parties, provided it records its reasons in writing.
essential_elements: Applies to commercial disputes of specified value under the Commercial Courts Act, 2015.
Court's directive power over which issues require evidence and the manner of its presentation.
Court's discretionary exclusion power, conditioned on recorded reasons.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This rule is a direct product of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 reforms aimed at tightening and speeding up commercial litigation by letting the Court actively curate the evidence rather than leaving it entirely to party autonomy.
It does not apply to ordinary (non-commercial, or below the specified value) suits, which remain governed by the general affidavit regime of Rules 1-3.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read together with Order XV-A's case management hearing powers and Order XVIII Rule 4's affidavit-in-chief regime — this rule gives the Commercial Court teeth to actively shape what evidence is even placed on record in the first place.

sections.title: Order XIX Rule 5 — Redacting or rejecting evidence
sections.raw_text:
5. Redacting or rejecting evidence.—A Court may, in its discretion, for reasons to be recorded in writing,—
(i) redact or order the redaction of such portions of the affidavit of examination-in-chief as do not, in its view, constitute evidence; or
(ii) return or reject an affidavit of examination-in-chief as not constituting admissible evidence.

[Applicable to commercial disputes of a specified value by Act 4 of 2016, s. 16 and the Schedule, w.e.f. 23-10-2015.]

breakdown.plain_summary: In specified-value commercial disputes, the Court can, for reasons recorded in writing, either redact the parts of an examination-in-chief affidavit that are not really evidence (argument, legal submissions, etc.), or go further and reject or return the entire affidavit if it does not amount to admissible evidence at all.
essential_elements: Applies to commercial disputes of specified value.
Reasons must be recorded in writing.
Two tools: partial redaction of non-evidentiary portions, or outright rejection/return of a non-admissible affidavit.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This directly complements Order XIX Rule 3's general hearsay/argument costs-sanction by giving Commercial Courts a sharper tool — outright redaction or rejection — rather than just a costs penalty.
breakdown.how_to_read: Anticipate this scrutiny when drafting an affidavit of examination-in-chief in a commercial suit — portions that merely restate pleadings, argue law, or editorialise risk being redacted or the affidavit being rejected wholesale.

sections.title: Order XIX Rule 6 — Format and guidelines of affidavit of evidence

breakdown.plain_summary: In specified-value commercial disputes, an affidavit of evidence must follow a strict format: confined to and organised by the chronological sequence of relevant dates and events; liable to be struck out (wholly or partly) if it is a mere rehash of the pleadings or contains legal argument; each paragraph confined to a distinct topic as far as possible; must distinguish between statements from the deponent's own knowledge versus information/belief, and give the source for the latter; and must be consecutively paginated, divided into numbered paragraphs, use figures for all numbers/dates, and cross-reference annexures with page numbers.
essential_elements: Applies to commercial disputes of specified value.
Chronological organisation of dates and events.
Court's power to strike out pleadings-reproduction or legal-argument content.
Paragraph-per-topic discipline.
Mandatory disclosure of knowledge vs. belief, with sourcing for belief.
Formal requirements: pagination, numbered paragraphs, figures for numbers/dates, annexure cross-referencing.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This rule is a detailed drafting code specific to commercial disputes and goes well beyond the general, loosely worded requirements of Rule 3 — practitioners drafting affidavits of evidence in a Commercial Court must treat it as a checklist.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this as a drafting checklist for every affidavit of examination-in-chief filed in a specified-value commercial dispute — non-compliance invites striking out under clause (b) or redaction/rejection under Rule 5.

sections.title: Order XX — Judgment and Decree
sections.raw_text: Order XX of the First Schedule to the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 governs the final stage of a trial: the timeline and manner of pronouncing judgment, who may pronounce a judgment written but not pronounced by a predecessor, signing and dating the judgment and decree, the mandatory contents of a decree, the timeline for preparing the decree, and detailed rules for framing decrees in specific categories of suits — possession and mesne profits, instalment payments, specific performance, administration, pre-emption, partnership dissolution, accounts, partition, and set-off/counter-claim.

breakdown.plain_summary: Order XX closes out the trial. Rule 1 sets the timeline for pronouncing judgment — open court, as soon as practicable, with a general endeavour to pronounce within 30 days (extendable to 60 in exceptional circumstances) for ordinary suits, and a stricter 90-day post-arguments deadline for Commercial Courts/Divisions. Rules 2-5A deal with signing, dating, the contents required of judgments from different courts, and informing unrepresented parties of their appeal rights. Rules 6-8 prescribe the contents of the decree, a 15-day decree-preparation timeline, the date the decree bears, and what happens if the Judge leaves office before signing it. Rules 9-19 then give detailed, suit-type-specific decree-drafting rules: immovable and movable property, instalment payments, possession-with-mesne-profits, specific performance of sale/lease contracts, administration suits, pre-emption suits, partnership dissolution, principal-agent accounts, special accounting directions, partition suits, and set-off/counter-claim decrees. Rule 20 entitles parties to certified copies of the judgment and decree.
essential_elements: Rule 1 exists in two textual forms: the general 30/60-day endeavour-based timeline (substituted by the 1999/2002 amendments) and the stricter, absolute 90-day Commercial Court/Division/Appellate Division timeline (inserted by the Commercial Courts Act, 2015) — documented together within the Rule 1 entry below per the Order XV/Order XVIII Rule 2 precedent.
A decree must 'agree with the judgment' (Rule 6) — any mismatch between the operative portion of the judgment and the decree as drawn up is a correctable error, typically via Section 152.

Several specific-suit-type rules (Rules 12-18) produce preliminary decrees (declaring rights, directing further inquiry) followed by final decrees once the inquiry concludes — a structural feature of accounts, partition, administration, and partnership-dissolution litigation that practitioners must track across both decree stages.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Order XX is where trial strategy converts into an enforceable decree — errors here (wrong decree contents, mismatched judgment/decree, missed instalment or mesne-profits directions) routinely become fresh grounds for execution objections or appeals, so decree-drawing is a distinct skill from arguing the case.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read Rule 1 for the pronouncement timeline (checking the general vs. Commercial Court track), Rules 6-8 for the decree's mandatory contents and preparation timeline, and then the relevant suit-type-specific rule (9-19) depending on what kind of suit and relief is involved.

sections.title: Order XX Rule 1 — Judgment when pronounced
sections.raw_text:
1. Judgment when pronounced.—
General-suit version (substituted by Act 22 of 2002):
(1) The Court, after the case has been heard, shall pronounce judgment in an open Court, either at once, or as soon thereafter as may be practicable and when the judgment is to be pronounced on some future day, the Court shall fix a day for that purpose, of which due notice shall be given to the parties or their pleaders: Provided that where the judgment is not pronounced at once, every endeavour shall be made by the Court to pronounce the judgment within thirty days from the date on which the hearing of the case was concluded but, where it is not practicable so to do on the ground of the exceptional and extraordinary circumstances of the case, the Court shall fix a future day for the pronouncement of the judgment, and such day shall not ordinarily be a day beyond sixty days from the date on which the hearing of the case was concluded, and due notice of the day so fixed shall be given to the parties or their pleaders.

Commercial Courts version (applicable to commercial disputes of specified value by Act 4 of 2016, s. 16 and the Schedule):
(1) The Commercial Court, Commercial Division, or Commercial Appellate Division, as the case may be, shall, within ninety days of the conclusion of arguments, pronounce judgment and copies thereof shall be issued to all the parties to the dispute through electronic mail or otherwise.

(2) Where a written judgment is to be pronounced, it shall be sufficient if the findings of the Court on each issue and the final order passed in the case are read out and it shall not be necessary for the Court to read out the whole judgment.
(3) The judgment may be pronounced by dictation in open Court to a shorthand writer if the Judge is specially empowered by the High Court in this behalf: Provided that, where the judgment is pronounced by dictation in open Court, the transcript of the judgment so pronounced shall, after making such correction therein as may be necessary, be signed by the judge, bear the date on which it was pronounced, and form a part of the record.

breakdown.plain_summary: After hearing concludes, the Court must pronounce judgment in open court — either immediately or on a fixed future day with notice to the parties. For ordinary suits, the Court must make every endeavour to pronounce within 30 days of the conclusion of hearing, extendable up to 60 days only for exceptional and extraordinary circumstances (with a fixed, notified future date). For commercial disputes of specified value, the deadline is stricter and absolute: judgment within 90 days of the conclusion of arguments, with copies issued to all parties by email or otherwise. A written judgment need not be read out in full — reading the issue-wise findings and final order suffices — and a specially empowered Judge may pronounce judgment by dictating it in open court to a shorthand writer, with the corrected, signed, dated transcript becoming part of the record.
essential_elements: Judgment pronounced in open Court, at once or on a notified future date.
General suits: 30-day endeavour, extendable to 60 days only for exceptional/extraordinary circumstances, with notice of the fixed date.
Commercial disputes of specified value: absolute 90-day deadline from conclusion of arguments, with electronic or other distribution of copies.
Reading issue-wise findings and the final order suffices for a written judgment.
Dictation to a shorthand writer permitted only for specially empowered Judges, with signed, dated, corrected transcript forming the record.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Two timeline regimes coexist: the general 30/60-day endeavour-based standard (directory in tone, built around 'every endeavour') and the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 90-day absolute deadline applicable only to commercial disputes of specified value — practitioners must identify which track their suit falls into.
The 60-day outer limit for general suits is itself not absolute ('shall not ordinarily be a day beyond sixty days'), preserving some flexibility for truly exceptional cases.
breakdown.how_to_read: Check first whether the suit is a specified-value commercial dispute (90-day absolute deadline) or an ordinary suit (30-day endeavour / 60-day outer limit), then read sub-rules (2)-(3) for the mechanics of how the judgment may actually be delivered (full reading vs. issue-wise reading, dictation to a shorthand writer).

sections.title: Order XX Rule 2 — Power to pronounce judgment written by judge's predecessor
sections.raw_text: 2. Power to pronounce judgment written by judge's predecessor.—A Judge shall pronounce a judgment written, but not pronounced, by his predecessor.

breakdown.plain_summary: If a Judge has written a judgment but leaves office (or is otherwise unable to pronounce it) before pronouncing it, his successor must pronounce that already-written judgment — the successor does not need to rewrite or rehear the case.
essential_elements: Judgment written but not pronounced by the predecessor Judge.
Mandatory duty of the successor Judge to pronounce it.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This complements Order XVIII Rule 15's continuity principle for evidence — here the continuity extends all the way to a finished, written judgment that simply needs formal pronouncement.
breakdown.how_to_read: A narrow but important continuity rule — distinguish from Order XVIII Rule 15, which concerns evidence recorded by a predecessor mid-trial; this rule concerns a judgment already fully written but not yet pronounced.

sections.title: Order XX Rule 3 — Judgment to be signed
sections.raw_text: 3. Judgment to be signed.—The judgment shall be dated and signed by the Judge in open Court at the time of pronouncing it and, when once signed, shall not afterwards be altered or added to save as provided by section 152 or on review.

breakdown.plain_summary: The judgment must be dated and signed by the Judge in open court at the moment it is pronounced. Once signed, it is final and cannot be altered or added to, except through Section 152's correction-of-errors mechanism or on a formal review.
essential_elements: Dating and signing in open Court at the time of pronouncement.
Finality: no alteration or addition thereafter.
Exceptions: Section 152 corrections, or review.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This finality rule is what gives a pronounced, signed judgment its binding character — any change outside Section 152 or review risks being set aside as without jurisdiction.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read with Section 152 (correction of clerical or arithmetical mistakes) and the review provisions (Section 114/Order XLVII) — those are the only lawful routes to touch a signed judgment.

sections.title: Order XX Rule 4 — Judgments of Small Cause Courts
sections.raw_text:
4. Judgments of Small Cause Courts.—(1) Judgments of a Court of Small Causes need not contain more than the points for determination and the decision thereon.
(2) Judgments of other Courts.—Judgments of other Courts shall contain a concise statement of the case, the points for determination, the decision thereon, and the reasons for such decision.

breakdown.plain_summary: A Small Cause Court's judgment can be brief — just the points for determination and the decision on them, without detailed reasoning. Every other court's judgment, however, must contain a concise statement of the case, the points for determination, the decision, and the reasons for that decision.
essential_elements: Small Cause Courts: points for determination plus decision, nothing more required.
All other courts: concise case statement, points for determination, decision, and reasons.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The lighter Small Cause Court standard reflects the summary, low-value nature of that jurisdiction, where detailed reasoned judgments are not proportionate to the stakes.
breakdown.how_to_read: A useful contrast when drafting or reviewing a judgment for correctness of form — ordinary civil court judgments must show reasoning, not just a bare conclusion, while Small Cause Court judgments are deliberately streamlined.

sections.title: Order XX Rule 5 — Court to state its decision on each issue
sections.raw_text: 5. Court to state its decision on each issue.—In suits in which issues have been framed, the Court shall state its finding or decision, with the reasons therefor, upon each separate issue, unless the finding upon any one or more of the issue is sufficient for the decision of the suit.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where issues have been framed in a suit, the judgment must give a finding with reasons on each separate issue — unless the finding on one or more particular issues is by itself sufficient to dispose of the whole suit, in which case the Court need not labour through every remaining issue.
essential_elements: Issues framed in the suit.
Issue-wise findings with reasons required.
Exception: a dispositive finding on one or more issues makes further issue-wise findings unnecessary.
exceptions_and_qualifications: A judgment that fails to address framed issues without falling within the dispositive-finding exception is vulnerable to challenge in appeal as incomplete or non-speaking on material issues.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read together with Order XIV (framing of issues) — this rule is the payoff requiring the trial court to actually resolve, with reasons, every issue it earlier framed as material to the suit.

sections.title: Order XX Rule 5A — Court to inform parties as to where an appeal lies in cases where parties are not represented by pleaders
sections.raw_text: 5A. Court to inform parties as to where an appeal lies in cases where parties are not represented by pleaders.—Except where both the parties are represented by pleaders, the Court shall, when it pronounces its judgment in a case subject to appeal, inform the parties present in Court as to the Court to which an appeal lies and the period of limitation for the filing of such appeal and place on record the information so given to the parties.

breakdown.plain_summary: If one or both parties are not represented by pleaders (i.e., appearing in person), the Court must, when pronouncing an appealable judgment, tell the parties present which court the appeal lies to and what the limitation period for filing it is, and must record on file that this information was given.
essential_elements: At least one party unrepresented by a pleader.
Judgment is one subject to appeal.
Mandatory disclosure: appellate forum and limitation period.
Mandatory record of the disclosure.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a protective provision for unrepresented litigants, who may not otherwise know their appellate rights or the time within which to exercise them.
No equivalent duty arises where both parties are represented by pleaders, who are presumed to know the appellate forum and limitation period.
breakdown.how_to_read: A litigant-protection rule worth flagging whenever a party is self-represented — if the Court omits this information, it may be relevant to any later condonation-of-delay application in the appeal.

sections.title: Order XX Rule 6 — Contents of decree
sections.raw_text:
6. Contents of decree.—(1) The decree shall agree with the judgment it shall contain the number of the suit, the names and descriptions of the parties, their registered addresses, and particulars of the claim, and shall specify clearly the relief granted or other determination of the suit.
(2) The decree shall also state the amount of costs incurred in the suit, and by whom or out of what property and in what proportions such costs are to be paid.
(3) The Court may direct that the costs payable to one party by the other shall be set off against any sum which is admitted or found to be due from the former to the latter.

breakdown.plain_summary: The decree must agree with the judgment and must include the suit number, the parties' names, descriptions, and registered addresses, the particulars of the claim, and a clear statement of the relief granted or other determination. It must also state the costs incurred, who bears them (and out of what property, in what proportions), and the Court may order that costs owed by one party to the other be set off against any admitted or found-due sum between them.
essential_elements: Agreement between decree and judgment.
Mandatory particulars: suit number, parties' names/descriptions/registered addresses, claim particulars, relief/determination.
Mandatory costs statement: amount, payer, source property, proportions.
Discretionary set-off of cross-owed costs/sums.
exceptions_and_qualifications: A decree that departs from the judgment on any of these particulars is open to correction (typically under Section 152) or challenge — the 'agree with the judgment' requirement is the anchor for that scrutiny.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this as the master checklist for drafting or scrutinising any decree — every decree should be checked against sub-rules (1)-(3) before it is signed and acted upon.

sections.title: Order XX Rule 6A — Preparation of decree
sections.raw_text:
6A. Preparation of decree.—(1) Every endeavour shall be made to ensure that the decree is drawn up as expeditiously as possible and, in any case, within fifteen days from the date on which the judgment is pronounced.
(2) An appeal may be preferred against the decree without filing a copy of the decree and in such a case the copy made available to the party by the court shall for the purposes of rule 1 of Order XLI be treated as the decree. But as soon as the decree is drawn, the judgment shall cease to have the effect of a decree for the purposes of execution or for any other purpose.

breakdown.plain_summary: The decree should be drawn up as quickly as possible, and in any case within 15 days of the judgment's pronouncement. Until the formal decree is drawn, a party may still appeal using the judgment copy made available by the Court, which is treated as the decree for the purpose of Order XLI Rule 1 (the appeal-memorandum rule). But once the decree is actually drawn up, the judgment loses its stand-in effect as a decree for execution or any other purpose.
essential_elements: Fifteen-day target for drawing up the decree.
Interim mechanism: judgment copy treated as the decree for filing an appeal under Order XLI Rule 1, pending the formal decree.
Judgment's stand-in effect as a decree ceases once the actual decree is drawn.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This rule balances expeditious finality (letting an appeal proceed without waiting for decree paperwork) against the formal distinction between a judgment and a decree, which matters for execution purposes — execution can only proceed on the actual decree once drawn.
breakdown.how_to_read: Important for appeal-filing strategy: a party need not wait for the formal decree to file an appeal, but must track when the decree is actually drawn since that is the trigger point after which only the decree (not the judgment) governs execution.

sections.title: Order XX Rule 6B — Copies of judgments when to be made available
sections.raw_text: 6B. Copies of judgments when to be made available.—Where the judgment is pronounced, copies of the judgment shall be made available to the parties immediately after the pronouncement of the judgment for preferring an appeal on payment of such charges as may be specified in the rule made by the High Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: As soon as judgment is pronounced, copies must be made available to the parties right away so they can file an appeal, on payment of whatever charges the High Court's rules specify.
essential_elements: Immediate availability of judgment copies post-pronouncement.
Purpose: enabling appeal.
Charges as specified by High Court rules.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This rule works together with Rule 6A(2) — the prompt availability of judgment copies is what makes the 'judgment copy as interim decree' mechanism for filing an appeal practically workable.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read with Rule 6A — together these rules ensure a party is never stuck unable to appeal merely because the formal decree is still being prepared.

sections.title: Order XX Rule 7 — Date of decree
sections.raw_text: 7. Date of decree.—The decree shall bear the day on which the judgment was pronounced, and, when the judge has satisfied himself that the decree has been drawn up in accordance with the judgment, he shall sign the decree.

breakdown.plain_summary: A decree is dated to the day the judgment was pronounced, not the (often later) day it is actually drawn up. The Judge signs it only after satisfying himself that the decree correctly reflects the judgment.
essential_elements: Decree dated to the judgment-pronouncement date.
Judge's verification that the decree matches the judgment, as a precondition to signing.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This date rule matters for computing limitation periods and other time-bound rights tied to 'the date of the decree' — it is always the judgment date, regardless of drafting delay.
breakdown.how_to_read: A small but consequential rule for limitation computation — always check the judgment pronouncement date, not the decree's drawing-up date, when calculating time limits that run from 'the date of the decree'.

sections.title: Order XX Rule 8 — Procedure where Judge has vacated office before signing decree
sections.raw_text: 8. Procedure where Judge has vacated office before signing decree.—Where a Judge has vacated office after pronouncing judgment but without signing the decree, a decree drawn up in accordance with such judgment may be signed by his successor or, if the Court has ceased to exist, by the Judge of any Court to which such Court was subordinate.

breakdown.plain_summary: If a Judge pronounces judgment but leaves office before signing the decree, his successor may sign the decree once it is drawn up in accordance with that judgment. If the very Court has ceased to exist, a Judge of any court to which it was subordinate may sign it instead.
essential_elements: Judge vacated office after pronouncing judgment but before signing the decree.
Successor Judge's power to sign.
Fallback: Judge of a superior court if the original Court itself has ceased to exist.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This rule, together with Rule 2 (pronouncing a predecessor's written judgment) and Order XVIII Rule 15 (dealing with predecessor's evidence), forms a complete continuity scheme ensuring no civil proceeding is derailed merely by a change or disappearance of the presiding Judge or Court.
breakdown.how_to_read: A practical continuity rule relevant whenever there has been a transfer, retirement, or death of the Judge, or reorganisation of courts, between pronouncement of judgment and signing of the decree.

sections.title: Order XX Rule 9 — Decree for recovery of immovable property
sections.raw_text: 9. Decree for recovery of immovable property.—Where the subject-matter of the suit is immovable property, the decree shall contain a description of such property sufficient to identify the same, and where such property can be identified by boundaries or by numbers in a record of settlement or survey, the decree shall specify such boundaries or numbers.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where the suit concerns immovable property, the decree must describe the property precisely enough to identify it, and where the property can be identified by boundaries or by settlement/survey record numbers, the decree must specify those boundaries or numbers.
essential_elements: Subject-matter is immovable property.
Sufficiently identifying description required.
Boundaries or survey/settlement numbers specified where available.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Imprecise property description is a classic ground for execution difficulties in suits for possession — an executing court cannot deliver possession of property it cannot identify from the decree.
breakdown.how_to_read: Critical in property-recovery suits — ensure the decree's property description (boundaries, survey numbers) is precise enough to allow trouble-free execution, since vague descriptions routinely generate execution-stage litigation.

sections.title: Order XX Rule 10 — Decree for delivery of movable property
sections.raw_text: 10. Decree for delivery of movable property.—Where the suit is for movable property, and the decree is for the delivery of such property, the decree shall also state the amount of money to be paid as an alternative if delivery cannot be had.

breakdown.plain_summary: In a suit for movable property where the decree orders delivery of that property, the decree must also fix an alternative sum of money payable if actual delivery turns out not to be possible.
essential_elements: Suit for movable property.
Decree for delivery of the property.
Mandatory alternative money sum if delivery cannot be had.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This alternative-money mechanism prevents a decree from becoming unenforceable merely because the specific movable property can no longer be delivered (destroyed, lost, disposed of) by the time of execution.
breakdown.how_to_read: Always ensure a decree for delivery of movable property includes the alternative money figure — its absence can stall execution entirely if the property is unavailable.

sections.title: Order XX Rule 11 — Decree may direct payment by instalments
sections.raw_text:
11. Decree may direct payment by instalments.—(1) Where and in so far as a decree is for the payment of money, the Court may for any sufficient reason incorporate in the decree, after hearing such of the parties who had appeared personally or by pleader at the last hearing, before judgment, an order that payment of the amount decreed shall be postponed or shall be made by instalments, with or without interest, notwithstanding anything contained in the contract under which the money is payable.
(2) Order, after decree, for payment by instalments.—After the passing of any such decree the Court may, on the application of the judgment-debtor and with the consent of the decree-holder, order that payment of the amount decreed shall be postponed or shall be made by instalments on such terms as to the payment of interest, the attachment of the property of the judgment-debtor, or the taking of security from him, or otherwise, as it thinks fit.

breakdown.plain_summary: For money decrees, the Court can — for sufficient reason, and after hearing the parties who appeared at the last hearing before judgment — build an instalment or postponed-payment schedule directly into the decree, overriding any contrary contractual term, with or without interest. Separately, even after the decree is passed, the Court can order postponement or instalments on the judgment-debtor's application, but only with the decree-holder's consent, on whatever terms (interest, attachment, security) it thinks fit.
essential_elements: Sub-rule (1): instalment/postponement built into the decree itself, for sufficient reason, after hearing the parties who appeared at the last pre-judgment hearing, overriding contrary contract terms.
Sub-rule (2): post-decree instalment order, on judgment-debtor's application AND decree-holder's consent, on Court-determined terms.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The two mechanisms differ sharply on consent: sub-rule (1) is the Court's own power exercised at the judgment stage without needing the decree-holder's consent, while sub-rule (2) post-decree relief absolutely requires the decree-holder's consent.
breakdown.how_to_read: Distinguish the two sub-rules carefully — relief under sub-rule (1) must be sought before or at judgment, while post-decree relief under sub-rule (2) is consent-gated and unavailable if the decree-holder refuses.

sections.title: Order XX Rule 12 — Decree for possession and mesne profits

breakdown.plain_summary: In a suit for possession of immovable property plus rent or mesne profits, the decree can cover possession itself, pre-suit accrued rent (either fixed or sent for inquiry), mesne profits (fixed or sent for inquiry), and — crucially — a running inquiry into rent or mesne profits from the date the suit was filed until whichever happens first: possession is delivered, the judgment-debtor relinquishes possession with notice, or three years pass from the decree's date. Wherever an inquiry is ordered, a separate final decree on rent/mesne profits follows once that inquiry concludes.
essential_elements: Suit for possession plus rent/mesne profits.

Decree components: possession; pre-suit rent (fixed or inquiry-directed); mesne profits (fixed or inquiry-directed); post-suit running inquiry capped at delivery, relinquishment-with-notice, or three years from decree, whichever first.
Final decree on rent/mesne profits follows the inquiry's result.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The three-year cap on the running mesne-profits inquiry is a deliberate limitation preventing open-ended post-decree accounting disputes from dragging on indefinitely.
This rule creates a preliminary/final decree structure for the rent/mesne-profits component even while the possession component is finally decided upfront.
breakdown.how_to_read: A heavily litigated rule in property-recovery suits — track the distinction between the possession decree (final and immediate) and the rent/mesne-profits component (often preliminary, pending inquiry, and time-capped at three years).

sections.title: Order XX Rule 12A — Decree for specific performance of contract for the sale or lease of immovable property
sections.raw_text: 12A. Decree for specific performance of contract for the sale or lease of immovable property.—Where a decree for the specific performance of a contract for the sale or lease of immovable property orders that the purchase-money or other sum be paid by the purchaser or lessee, it shall specify the period within which the payment shall be made.

breakdown.plain_summary: When a decree for specific performance of a contract to sell or lease immovable property requires the purchaser or lessee to pay the purchase-money or other sum, the decree must specify the time period within which that payment must be made.
essential_elements: Decree for specific performance of a sale or lease contract concerning immovable property.
Order to pay purchase-money or other sum.
Mandatory specification of the payment period.
exceptions_and_qualifications: A clear payment-period specification prevents disputes at the execution stage over whether the purchaser/lessee has defaulted and avoids open-ended obligations.
breakdown.how_to_read: Essential drafting checklist item in every specific-performance decree involving immovable property — the absence of a specified payment period invites later disputes over compliance and default.

sections.title: Order XX Rule 13 — Decree in administration suit
sections.raw_text:
13. Decree in administration suit.—(1) Where a suit is for an account of any property and for its due administration under the decree of the Court, the Court shall, before passing the final decree, pass a preliminary decree ordering such accounts and inquiries to be taken and made, and giving such other directions as it thinks fit.
(2) In the administration by the Court of the property of any deceased person, if such property proves to be insufficient for the payment in full of his debts and liabilities, the same rules shall be observed as to the respective rights of secured and unsecured creditors and as to debts and liabilities provable, and as to the valuation of annuities and future and contingent liabilities respectively, as may be in force for the time being, within the local limits of the Court in which the administration-suit is pending with respect to the estates of persons adjudged or declared insolvent; and all persons who in any such case would be entitled to be paid out of such property, may come in under the preliminary decree, and make such claims against the same as they may respectively be entitled to by virtue of this Code.

breakdown.plain_summary: In an administration suit (seeking an account of property and its due administration under the Court's decree), the Court must first pass a preliminary decree ordering the necessary accounts and inquiries and giving other directions it thinks fit, before any final decree. If the deceased's property is insufficient to pay all debts in full, the same rules that apply to insolvent estates in that Court's jurisdiction govern the respective rights of secured and unsecured creditors, provable debts/liabilities, and valuation of annuities and contingent liabilities — and anyone entitled to be paid from the property may come in under the preliminary decree to stake their claim.
essential_elements: Preliminary decree mandatory before final decree in administration suits, ordering accounts/inquiries.
Insufficiency of estate triggers application of local insolvency-estate rules for creditor priority and claims valuation.
All entitled claimants may come in under the preliminary decree.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This rule effectively imports insolvency-law creditor-priority principles into administration suits whenever the estate cannot satisfy all claims — a significant cross-reference practitioners handling administration suits must be alert to.
breakdown.how_to_read: A structurally important rule for administration suits — always check whether the estate is sufficient; insufficiency triggers a whole separate body of insolvency-style creditor-priority rules via this provision.

sections.title: Order XX Rule 14 — Decree in pre-emption suit
sections.raw_text:
14. Decree in pre-emption suit.—(1) Where the Court decrees a claim to pre-emption in respect of a particular sale of property and the purchase-money has not been paid into Court, the decree shall—
(a) specify a day on or before which the purchase-money shall be so paid, and
(b) direct that on payment into Court of such purchase-money, together with the costs (if any) decreed against the plaintiff, on or before the day referred to in clause (a), the defendant shall deliver possession of the property to the plaintiff, whose title thereto shall be deemed to have accrued from the date of such payment, but that, if the purchase-money and the costs (if any) are not so paid, the suit shall be dismissed with costs.
(2) Where the Court has adjudicated upon rival claims to pre-emption, the decree shall direct,—
(a) if and in so far as the claims decreed are equal in degree, that the claim of each pre-emptor complying with the provisions of sub-rule (1) shall take effect in respect of a proportionate share of the property including any proportionate share in respect of which the claim of any pre-emptor failing to comply with the said provisions would, but for such default, have taken effect; and
(b) if and in so far as the claims decreed are different in degree, that the claim of the inferior pre-emptor shall not take effect unless and until the superior pre-emptor has failed to comply with the said provisions.

breakdown.plain_summary: Where a pre-emption claim is decreed and the purchase-money has not yet been paid into Court, the decree must fix a deadline for payment and direct that, if paid (with any decreed costs) by that date, the defendant must deliver possession to the plaintiff with title deemed to accrue from the payment date — but if not paid by the deadline, the suit itself is dismissed with costs. Where multiple rival pre-emptors have been adjudicated, claims of equal degree share proportionately (including absorbing the share of any defaulting pre-emptor), while claims of unequal degree give the superior pre-emptor first right, with the inferior pre-emptor's claim taking effect only if the superior one defaults.
essential_elements: Fixed deadline for depositing purchase-money (plus costs) into Court.
Consequence of timely payment: possession delivered, title accruing from payment date.
Consequence of default: suit dismissed with costs.
Equal-degree rival pre-emptors: proportionate sharing, absorbing defaulters' shares.
Unequal-degree rival pre-emptors: superior pre-emptor's claim prevails unless/until that pre-emptor defaults.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The hard payment deadline with automatic dismissal on default makes pre-emption decrees unusually self-executing compared to most other decree types — there is no need for a separate application to dismiss on default.
breakdown.how_to_read: A specialised rule for the increasingly rare but still litigated pre-emption suits — the self-executing deadline-and-dismissal mechanism and the rival-pre-emptor priority scheme are both distinctive features worth flagging to clients in such suits.

sections.title: Order XX Rule 15 — Decree in suit for dissolution of partnership
sections.raw_text: 15. Decree in suit for dissolution of partnership.—Where a suit is for the dissolution of a partnership, or the taking of partnership accounts, the Court, before passing a final decree, may pass a preliminary decree declaring the proportionate shares of the parties, fixing the day on which the partnership shall stand dissolved or be deemed to have been dissolved, and directing such accounts to be taken, and other acts to be done, as it thinks fit.
