(4) Where the judgment-debtor has obeyed the decree and paid all costs of executing the same which he is bound to pay, or where, at the end of six months from the date of the attachment no application to have the property sold has been made, or if made has been refused, the attachment shall cease.
(5) Where a decree for the specific performance of a contract or for an injunction has not been obeyed, the Court may, in lieu of or in addition to all or any of the processes aforesaid, direct that the act required to be done may be done so far as practicable by the decree-holder or some other person appointed by the Court, at the cost of the judgment-debtor, and upon the act being done the expenses incurred may be ascertained in such manner as the Court may direct and may be recovered as if they were included in the decree.
Explanation.—For the removal of doubts, it is hereby declared that the expression "the act required to be done" covers prohibitory as well as mandatory injunctions.
key_terms: act done by decree-holder at judgment-debtor's cost

breakdown.plain_summary: These three decree types (specific performance, conjugal rights, injunction) are enforced only against a party who had a genuine opportunity to comply and wilfully refused. Conjugal-rights decrees can only be enforced through property attachment, never personal detention (reflecting the personal, non-coercible nature of that relief); specific-performance and injunction decrees additionally allow civil imprisonment. A corporate judgment-debtor is enforced against through attachment of its property or, with leave, detention of its directors/officers. A six-month attachment sunset clause mirrors Rule 31's, and — distinctively for these decree types — the Court can simply get the act done itself (by the decree-holder or a Court-appointed person) and recover the cost from the judgment-debtor as part of the decree.
essential_elements: 'Wilful failure to obey' after a genuine opportunity is a precondition for coercive enforcement under this rule — mere non-compliance without that opportunity does not trigger it.

Sub-rule (1)'s exclusion of civil imprisonment for conjugal-rights decrees is a deliberate, named carve-out — Parliament has consistently declined to let the state physically compel resumption of cohabitation.
The Explanation confirms sub-rule (5)'s 'act done' mechanism works for both prohibitory injunctions (restraining an act) and mandatory injunctions (compelling an act).
exceptions_and_qualifications: Corporate enforcement via director/officer detention requires the Court's leave — it is not an automatic fallback alongside corporate-property attachment.
breakdown.how_to_read: For injunction and specific-performance decrees, the sub-rule (5) 'get it done and recover the cost' route is often more practical than pursuing detention or lengthy attachment — plead it as an express alternative prayer in the execution application.

sections.title: Order XXI Rule 33 — Discretion of Court in executing decrees for restitution of conjugal rights
sections.raw_text:
33. Discretion of Court in executing decrees for restitution of conjugal rights.—(1) Notwithstanding anything in rule 32, the Court, either at the time of passing a decree against a husband for the restitution of conjugal rights or at any time afterwards, may order that the decree shall be executed in the manner provided in this rule.
(2) Where the Court has made an order under sub-rule (1), it may order that, in the event of the decree not being obeyed within such period as may be fixed in this behalf, the judgment-debtor shall make to the decree-holder such periodical payments as may be just, and, if it thinks fit, require that the judgment-debtor shall, to its satisfaction, secure to the decree-holder such periodical payments.
(3) The Court may from time to time vary or modify any order made under sub-rule (2) for the periodical payment of money, either by altering the times of payment or by increasing or diminishing the amount, or may temporarily suspend the same as to the whole or any part of the money so ordered to be paid, and again review the same, either wholly or in part as it may think just.
(4) Any money ordered to be paid under this rule may be recovered as though it were payable under a decree for the payment of money.

breakdown.plain_summary: As an alternative enforcement route specific to a conjugal-rights decree passed against a husband, the Court may instead order periodical payments to the wife if the decree is not obeyed within a fixed period, optionally requiring security for those payments. The Court retains ongoing power to vary, increase, decrease, or temporarily suspend these payments as circumstances change, and any amount so ordered is recoverable exactly like money payable under an ordinary money decree.
essential_elements: Operates 'notwithstanding' Rule 32 — it is a freestanding alternative enforcement track the Court can adopt instead of (or structure alongside) the attachment-based route.
Built-in flexibility (sub-rule 3) lets the Court respond to the parties' changing financial circumstances over time, unlike a one-off attachment order.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Textually confined to a decree 'against a husband' — reflecting the rule's historical origin; modern constitutional and gender-neutral reading of conjugal-rights provisions should be checked against current case law before assuming the converse does not apply.
breakdown.how_to_read: This periodical-payment mechanism is often a more realistic practical remedy than property attachment where a conjugal-rights decree is disobeyed and the real issue is the decree-holder's maintenance rather than forced cohabitation.

sections.title: Order XXI Rule 34 — Decree for execution of document, or endorsement of negotiable instrument
sections.raw_text:
34. Decree for execution of document, or endorsement of negotiable instrument.—(1) Where a decree is for the execution of a document or for the endorsement of a negotiable instrument and the judgment-debtor neglects or refuses to obey the decree, the decree-holder may prepare a draft of the document or endorsement in accordance with the terms of the decree and deliver the same to the Court.
(2) The Court shall thereupon cause the draft to be served on the judgment-debtor together with a notice requiring his objections (if any) to be made within such time as the Court fixes in this behalf.
(3) Where the judgment-debtor objects to the draft, his objections shall be stated in writing within such time, and the Court shall make such order approving or altering the draft, as it thinks fit.
(4) The decree-holder shall deliver to the Court a copy of the draft with such alterations (if any) as the Court may have directed upon the proper stamp-paper if a stamp is required by the law for the time being in force; and the Judge or such officer as may be appointed in this behalf shall execute the document so delivered.
(5) The execution of a document or the endorsement of a negotiable instrument under this rule may be in the following form, namely:— "C. D., Judge of the Court of, (or as the case may be), for A. B., in a suit by E. F against A. B.", and shall have the same effect as the execution of the document or the endorsement of the negotiable instrument by the party ordered to execute or endorse the same.
(6)(a) Where the registration of the document is required under any law for the time being in force, the Court, or such officer of the Court as may be authorised in this behalf by the Court, shall cause the document to be registered in accordance with such law.
(b) Where the registration of the document is not so required, but the decree-holder desires it to be registered, the Court may make such order as it thinks fit.
(c) Where the Court makes any order for the registration of any document, it may make such order as it thinks fit as to the expenses of registration.
key_terms: Judge executes document on debtor's behalf

breakdown.plain_summary: If a judgment-debtor refuses to sign a document or endorse a negotiable instrument as decreed, the decree-holder prepares a draft, the Court serves it on the judgment-debtor for objections, resolves any objections by approving or altering the draft, and then the Judge (or an appointed officer) formally executes it on the judgment-debtor's behalf — with the same legal effect as if the judgment-debtor had signed it himself. Where registration is legally required, the Court ensures it happens; where not required but desired, the Court has discretion.
essential_elements: This is the Code's substitute-signature mechanism — the Judge effectively stands in for an unwilling judgment-debtor, rather than requiring indefinite coercive process to extract an actual signature.

Mandatory registration (sub-rule 6(a)) tracks the ordinary law of registration (e.g., Registration Act requirements for documents affecting immovable property) — this rule does not exempt the document from otherwise-applicable registration law.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Proper stamping is a precondition to execution by the Judge under sub-rule (4) — an unstamped or inadequately stamped draft cannot simply be executed judicially.
breakdown.how_to_read: A decree-holder facing a recalcitrant judgment-debtor on a document-execution decree should move swiftly under this rule rather than pursuing contempt-style coercion — it provides a complete, self-sufficient substitute-execution mechanism.

sections.title: Order XXI Rule 35 — Decree for immovable property
sections.raw_text:
35. Decree for immovable property.—(1) Where a decree is for the delivery of any immovable property, possession thereof shall be delivered to the party to whom it has been adjudged, or to such person as he may appoint to receive delivery on his behalf, and, if necessary, by removing any person bound by the decree who refuses to vacate the property.
(2) Where a decree is for the joint possession of immovable property, such possession shall be delivered by affixing a copy of the warrant in some conspicuous place on the property and proclaiming by beat of drum, or other customary mode, at some convenient place, the substance of the decree.
(3) Where possession of any building on enclosure is to be delivered and the person in possession, being bound by the decree, does not afford free access, the Court, through its officers, may, after giving reasonable warning and facility to any woman not appearing in public according to the customs of the country to withdraw, remove or open any lock or bolt or break open any door or do any other act necessary for putting the decree-holder in possession.

breakdown.plain_summary: Sole possession under an immovable-property decree is delivered by physically putting the decree-holder in possession, forcibly removing a resisting person bound by the decree if necessary; joint possession is instead delivered symbolically, by affixing the warrant on the property and public proclamation. Where forced entry into a building is needed, the Court's officers must first give reasonable warning and allow any woman observing purdah to withdraw before breaking locks, doors, or bolts.
essential_elements: Sole vs. joint possession triggers two genuinely different delivery mechanisms (physical installation and removal, versus symbolic warrant-affixing and proclamation) — the two are not interchangeable.
Sub-rule (3)'s purdah-nashin safeguard is a mandatory procedural courtesy, not a discretionary option, before forced entry.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Removal of a resisting occupant is limited to a 'person bound by the decree' — a third party in independent possession is not simply removable under this rule and instead falls within Rules 97-106's resistance-to-possession machinery.
breakdown.how_to_read: Where the person resisting delivery claims to hold independently of the judgment-debtor, flag Rule 97 onwards rather than relying on Rule 35 alone — forcibly removing a genuine third-party occupant without going through the Rule 97-106 adjudication route is a common and serious execution irregularity.

sections.title: Order XXI Rule 36 — Decree for delivery of immovable property when in occupancy of tenant
sections.raw_text: 36. Decree for delivery of immovable property when in occupancy of tenant.—Where a decree is for the delivery of any immovable property in the occupancy of a tenant or other person entitled to occupy the same and not bound by the decree to relinquish such occupancy, the Court shall order delivery to be made by affixing a copy of the warrant in some conspicuous place on the property, and proclaiming to the occupant by beat of drum or other customary mode, at some convenient place, the substance of the decree in regard to the property.

breakdown.plain_summary: When the decreed property is occupied by a tenant (or other lawful occupant) who is not himself bound by the decree to give up occupancy, the Court delivers only symbolic/constructive possession to the decree-holder — by affixing the warrant and proclaiming the decree's substance to the occupant — rather than physically evicting the tenant.
essential_elements: Protects a lawful tenant's possessory rights from being disturbed by a decree to which the tenant was not a party and by which the tenant is not bound.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Applies only where the tenant/occupant genuinely is 'not bound by the decree' — a tenant who is himself a judgment-debtor or otherwise bound is not protected by this rule and is instead subject to Rule 35's physical-delivery mechanism.
breakdown.how_to_read: This rule commonly protects sub-tenants and licensees in landlord-tenant execution scenarios — a decree-holder gets symbolic possession (and thereby steps into the landlord's shoes vis-à-vis rent) rather than an actual eviction of the occupying tenant.

sections.title: Order XXI Rule 37 — Discretionary power to permit judgment-debtor to show cause against detention in prison
sections.raw_text:
37. Discretionary power to permit judgment-debtor to show cause against detention in prison.—(1) Notwithstanding anything in these rules, where an application is for the execution of a decree for the payment of money by the arrest and detention in the civil prison of a judgment-debtor who is liable to be arrested in pursuance of the application, the Court shall, instead of issuing a warrant for his arrest, issue a notice calling upon him to appear before the Court on a day to be specified in the notice and show cause why he should not be committed to the civil prison:
Provided that such notice shall not be necessary if the Court is satisfied, by affidavit, or otherwise, that, with the object or effect of delaying the execution of the decree, the judgment-debtor is likely to abscond or leave the local limits of the jurisdiction of the Court.
(2) Where appearance is not made in obedience to the notice, the Court shall, if the decree-holder so requires, issue a warrant for the arrest of the judgment-debtor.

breakdown.plain_summary: Before actually arresting a judgment-debtor on a money decree, the Court must ordinarily first issue a show-cause notice calling him to explain why he should not be committed to civil prison — arrest-first is now the exception, not the default. That exception kicks in only where the Court is satisfied the judgment-debtor is likely to abscond or leave jurisdiction to delay execution. If the judgment-debtor ignores the notice, an arrest warrant follows on the decree-holder's request.
essential_elements: The 1936 amendment ('may' to 'shall') made the show-cause-first procedure mandatory, reversing what had been a discretionary practice — a straight-to-arrest warrant is now the carved-out exception rather than the norm.
The abscond/delay exception requires actual satisfaction by affidavit or other evidence, not mere assertion by the decree-holder.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Non-appearance alone does not automatically trigger arrest — sub-rule (2)'s warrant issues only 'if the decree-holder so requires', preserving decree-holder control over whether to escalate to arrest.
breakdown.how_to_read: A judgment-debtor served with a Rule 37 notice should appear and show cause rather than ignore it — non-appearance both forfeits the opportunity to contest detention on the merits and exposes him to an arrest warrant.

sections.title: Order XXI Rule 38 — Warrant for arrest to direct judgment-debtor to be brought up
sections.raw_text: 38. Warrant for arrest to direct judgment-debtor to be brought up.—Every warrant for the arrest of a judgment-debtor shall direct the officer entrusted with its execution to bring him before the Court with all convenient speed, unless the amount which he has been ordered to pay, together with the interest thereon and the costs (if any) to which he is liable, be sooner paid.

breakdown.plain_summary: An arrest warrant must direct the executing officer to bring the judgment-debtor before the Court promptly — unless the judgment-debtor pays off the decreed amount, interest, and costs before that happens, in which case arrest/production becomes unnecessary.
essential_elements: Builds in a payment escape valve directly into the warrant's own terms — a judgment-debtor located under an arrest warrant can still avoid being produced in custody by paying in full on the spot.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 'all convenient speed' standard is not a fixed timeline — what counts as prompt depends on practical circumstances of the arrest and transport to Court.
breakdown.how_to_read: A judgment-debtor arrested under this warrant should be advised that immediate full payment (decreed amount, interest, and costs) can still avert being produced and potentially detained.

sections.title: Order XXI Rule 39 — Subsistence allowance
sections.raw_text:
39. Subsistence allowance.—(1) No judgment-debtor shall be arrested in execution of a decree unless and until the decree-holder pays into Court such sum as the Judge thinks sufficient for the subsistence of the judgment-debtor from the time of his arrest until he can be brought before the Court.
(2) Where a judgment-debtor is committed to the civil prison in execution of a decree, the Court shall fix for his subsistence such monthly allowance as he may be entitled to according to the scales fixed under section 57, or, where no such scales have been fixed, as it considers sufficient with reference to the class to which he belongs.
(3) The monthly allowance fixed by the Court shall be supplied by the party on whose application the judgment-debtor has been arrested by monthly payments in advance before the first day of each month.
(4) The first payment shall be made to the proper officer of the Court for such portion of the current month as remains unexpired before the judgment-debtor is committed to the civil prison, and the subsequent payments (if any) shall be made to the officer in charge of the civil prison.
(5) Sums disbursed by the decree-holder for the subsistence of the judgment-debtor in the civil prison shall be deemed to be costs in the suit:
Provided that the judgment-debtor shall not be detained in the civil prison or arrested on account of any sum so disbursed.
key_terms: subsistence costs not separately recoverable by detention

breakdown.plain_summary: A decree-holder must deposit a Court-fixed subsistence sum before arrest can even happen, and must then keep funding the judgment-debtor's monthly subsistence (per Section 57 scales, or the Court's own assessment) in advance throughout the detention, with these sums ultimately treated as suit costs — but critically, the judgment-debtor can never be detained or re-arrested specifically for failing to repay this subsistence amount.
essential_elements: Subsistence funding is a genuine precondition to arrest, not a post-arrest formality — arrest without the prior deposit is procedurally defective.
The proviso's bar on detention/arrest for subsistence sums is an absolute humanitarian safeguard, distinguishing subsistence debt from the underlying decretal debt.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The decree-holder funds subsistence at his own initial cost/risk — recovery happens indirectly, by the sums being added to recoverable suit costs, not through any direct coercive mechanism against the judgment-debtor.
breakdown.how_to_read: A decree-holder pursuing arrest should budget for ongoing monthly subsistence payments in advance — failure to pay on time risks the judgment-debtor's release from civil prison, independent of whether the underlying decree remains unsatisfied.

sections.title: Order XXI Rule 40 — Proceedings on appearance of judgment-debtor in obedience to notice or after arrest
sections.raw_text:
40. Proceedings on appearance of judgment-debtor in obedience to notice or after arrest.—(1) When a judgment-debtor appears before the Court in obedience to a notice issued under rule 37, or is brought before the Court after being arrested in execution of a decree for the payment of money, the Court shall proceed to hear the decree-holder and take all such evidence as may be produced by him in support of his application for execution and shall then give the judgment-debtor an opportunity of showing cause why he should not be committed to the civil prison.
(2) Pending the conclusion of the inquiry under sub-rule (1) the Court may, in its discretion, order the judgment-debtor to be detained in the custody of an officer of the Court or release him on his furnishing security to the satisfaction of the Court for his appearance when required.
(3) Upon the conclusion of the inquiry under sub-rule (1) the Court may, subject to the provisions of section 51 and to the other provisions of this Code, make an order for the detention of the judgment-debtor in the civil prison and shall in that event cause him to be arrested if he is not already under arrest:
Provided that in order to give the judgment-debtor an opportunity of satisfying the decree, the Court may, before making the order of detention, leave the judgment-debtor in the custody of an officer of the Court for a specified period not exceeding fifteen days or release him on his furnishing security to the satisfaction of the Court for his appearance at the expiration of the specified period if the decree be not sooner satisfied.
(4) A judgment-debtor released under this rule may be re-arrested.
(5) When the Court does not make an order of detention under sub-rule (3) it shall disallow the application and, if the judgment-debtor is under arrest, direct his release.

breakdown.plain_summary: Once the judgment-debtor appears or is produced, the Court conducts a full inquiry — hearing the decree-holder's evidence and giving the judgment-debtor a genuine opportunity to show cause — before any detention order. Pending that inquiry, the Court can hold him in Court-officer custody or release him on security. Only after the inquiry, and subject to Section 51's restrictions, may detention be ordered, with a built-in final fifteen-day grace window (in Court-officer custody or on security) to let him satisfy the decree before actual civil-prison detention begins. A released judgment-debtor can be re-arrested if the decree remains unsatisfied; and if detention is ultimately not ordered, the application itself is disallowed and any arrested judgment-debtor must be released.
essential_elements: Mirrors natural-justice safeguards (right to be heard, opportunity to show cause) before the coercive remedy of civil imprisonment can be imposed.
The fifteen-day proviso is a final, mandatory-flavoured opportunity to pay before actual detention — it operates even after the Court has otherwise decided detention is warranted.
Sub-rule (5) makes clear the inquiry can end in the judgment-debtor's favour entirely — detention is not a foregone conclusion once the process starts.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Any detention order remains 'subject to the provisions of section 51' — even after a full inquiry favouring the decree-holder, the Court cannot order detention unless Section 51's substantive preconditions are independently satisfied.
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat this rule's inquiry as a genuine contested hearing, not a formality — press for an order under sub-rule (5) disallowing detention wherever the Section 51 preconditions or the 'wilful default' standard are not clearly made out on the evidence.
